fields.Date: 1958 (Giazotto, on a theme attributed to Albinoni)
fields.Description: Presented by Remo Giazotto as a reconstruction of a fragment by Tomaso Albinoni, but almost certainly Giazotto's own composition.
fields.Listen: This piece opens with a walking bass in the organ and plucked low strings before the violins enter with a slow, sighing G-minor melody.
fields.Clue: Its publisher claimed to have built it from a fragment of a trio sonata found in the ruins of the Saxon State Library in Dresden; it is almost certainly Remo Giazotto's own G-minor piece for strings and organ.

fields.Description: August Wilhelmj's arrangement of the second movement of Bach's third orchestral suite, transposed so it can be played entirely on the violin's lowest string.
Six concertos sent to the Margrave of Brandenburg in 1721 with a flattering dedication; there is no evidence he ever had them played.
Gives the harpsichord an enormous unaccompanied cadenza, making it a soloist rather than continuo for the first time.
fields.Listen: This movement's opening ritornello: the string band drives repeated D's in a bright D major before the solo flute, violin, and harpsichord begin trading figures.
fields.Clue: In its first movement the harpsichord breaks free of the continuo for a solo cadenza sixty-five bars long, the first great keyboard solo in a concerto; flute and violin are its other soloists.

fields.Description: The closing chorale of Bach's cantata Herz und Mund und Tat und Leben, universally known through Myra Hess's piano arrangement.

fields.Audio: [sound:Bach (St. Matthew Passion - O Sacred Head, Now Wounded).mp3]
fields.Description: Written for Good Friday in Leipzig for double choir and double orchestra; Mendelssohn's 1829 revival launched the modern Bach revival, and the chorale “O Sacred Head” recurs five times.
fields.Listen: The chorus sings the Passion Chorale, Hans Leo Hassler's melody, in a slow, homophonic four-part harmonization.
fields.Clue: The chorale “O Sacred Head, Now Wounded”, on a melody by Hans Leo Hassler, returns five times in different harmonizations in this Good Friday setting for double choir and double orchestra.

fields.Description: The most famous organ piece ever written, though its attribution to Bach has been doubted for decades on stylistic grounds; Leopold Stokowski's orchestration opens Disney's Fantasia.
fields.Listen: This piece opens with a mordent on A (A, G, A) in octaves, a plunging run down to a low C-sharp, and a rolled diminished-seventh chord over a D pedal.
fields.Clue: Leopold Stokowski's orchestration of this D-minor organ piece opens Disney's Fantasia; its authorship has been doubted, and some scholars think it began as a piece for solo violin.

fields.Description: The D minor toccata and fugue, BWV 565, the most famous organ piece written, though its attribution to Bach has been doubted for decades on stylistic grounds.
Two books of preludes and fugues in all twenty-four major and minor keys; the C-major prelude of Book I underlies Charles Gounod's “Ave Maria”.
fields.Listen: This prelude is nothing but broken chords: each bar arpeggiates one harmony in the same rising figure, starting C, E, G, C, E.
fields.Clue: Its first prelude, in C major, made entirely of arpeggiated chords, became the accompaniment to Charles Gounod's “Ave Maria”; its two books pair a prelude and fugue in each of the twenty-four keys.

fields.Description: Arranged from the slow movement of Barber's String Quartet; Arturo Toscanini premiered it in a 1938 radio broadcast, and it has become the standard music of American national mourning.
fields.Listen: This piece opens on a held B-flat in the first violins; the melody then rises and falls by step (B-flat, C, D-flat) in long, slow phrases over suspended string chords.
fields.Clue: Arranged from the slow movement of its composer's String Quartet, Op. 11, and premiered by Arturo Toscanini in a 1938 broadcast; it was played at the funerals of Franklin Roosevelt and John F. Kennedy.

fields.Description: A bagatelle unpublished in Beethoven's lifetime; the dedicatee's name is probably a misreading of Therese, for Therese Malfatti, whom he wanted to marry.
fields.Listen: This piece opens in 3/8 with the right hand rocking between E and D-sharp (E, D-sharp, E, D-sharp, E, B, D, C, A), the left hand answering with rising A-minor arpeggios.
fields.Clue: An A-minor bagatelle published forty years after its composer's death by Ludwig Nohl; its dedicatee's name is probably a misreading of Therese, for Therese Malfatti.

fields.Description: Marked quasi una fantasia; the “Moonlight” name came from a critic five years after Beethoven's death. It opens slowly instead of fast and ends with a furious presto.
fields.Listen: This sonata opens with right-hand triplets repeating G-sharp, C-sharp, E over octave C-sharps in the bass, while a dotted melody enters on repeated G-sharps above them.
fields.Clue: Dedicated to Giulietta Guicciardi and marked quasi una fantasia; Liszt called its D-flat-major middle movement “a flower between two abysses”, and the critic Ludwig Rellstab gave it its nickname.

fields.Description: The “Pathétique”, one of the few nicknames Beethoven approved. A slow introduction returns inside the first movement, which was unusual.
The four-note opening figure recurs across all four movements, and the scherzo runs without a break into the C-major finale.
fields.Listen: The second theme: the horns sound the four-note motif stretched into a fanfare (B-flat, B-flat, B-flat, E-flat, F, B-flat), then the violins sing a gentle E-flat-major tune while the basses mutter short-short-short-long beneath.
fields.Clue: Its four-note opening motif, which Anton Schindler claimed was “fate knocking at the door”, recurs in all four movements; the scherzo runs without a break into a C-major finale that ends with twenty-nine bars of tonic chords.

fields.Movement: mvt. IV · Presto – Allegro assai (“Ode to Joy”)
fields.Description: The first major symphony to use voices, setting Schiller's Ode to Joy in a finale that begins by rejecting the earlier movements' themes. Beethoven, completely deaf at the 1824 premiere, had to be turned round to see the applause.
fields.Listen: The finale opens with the Schreckensfanfare (“terror fanfare”), a shrieking dissonant chord for winds and timpani, answered by the cellos and basses in a wordless recitative.
fields.Clue: Its finale opens with a dissonant “terror fanfare” and a recitative for cellos and basses that rejects the earlier movements' themes one by one before Schiller's ode enters; its deaf composer had to be turned round at the 1824 premiere to see the applause.

fields.Description: Five movements with titles, including a brook scene whose birdcalls (nightingale, quail, and cuckoo) are named in the score, and a thunderstorm that runs straight into the finale. Beethoven called it “more the expression of feeling than painting”.
fields.Listen: The finale opens with a shepherd's call: the clarinet, then the horn, plays a yodelling pipe tune over a drone, before the violins sing the broad 6/8 hymn of thanksgiving.
fields.Clue: Its finale, a Shepherd's Song of thanks after the storm, follows a Scene by the Brook in which flute, oboe, and clarinet imitate a nightingale, quail, and cuckoo; its composer called it “more the expression of feeling than painting”.

fields.Description: Wagner called it the apotheosis of the dance; every movement is built on an obsessive rhythm, and the second was encored at the premiere.
fields.Listen: The Allegretto opens on a held woodwind chord; then the violas, cellos, and basses begin an A-minor tread in an unchanging long-short-short-long-long rhythm that spreads through the orchestra.
fields.Clue: Its A-minor Allegretto was encored at the 1813 Vienna premiere, a benefit for soldiers wounded at Hanau; Wagner called this symphony “the apotheosis of the dance”.

fields.Description: The first major symphony to use voices, setting Schiller's Ode to Joy in a finale that begins by rejecting the earlier movements' themes. Beethoven, completely deaf at the 1824 premiere, had to be turned round to see the applause.
fields.Listen: The scherzo opens with octave leaps hurled out by the strings and answered by the timpani, tuned to F in octaves, before a fugato on a driving three-beat motif.

fields.Audio: [sound:cmc-Berlioz (Symphonie fantastique mvt. V ( Songe d'une nuit du sabbat )).mp3][sound:Berlioz (Sym. Fan. mvV - the witches' sabbath)).mp3]
fields.Movement: mvt. V (Songe d'une nuit du sabbat)
fields.Description: A young artist, despairing of love, poisons himself with opium; his beloved recurs as an idée fixe, finally as a witch at a sabbath where the Dies irae tolls. Berlioz's own obsession was the actress Harriet Smithson, whom he later married.
fields.Listen: The witches' sabbath opens with eerie divided-string tremolos and distant horn calls, before a squealing E-flat clarinet mocks the beloved's idée fixe as a vulgar dance.
fields.Clue: Its last movement is a witches' sabbath at which funeral bells toll and tubas intone the Dies irae, the young artist having poisoned himself with opium; its composer wrote it for the actress Harriet Smithson, whom he later married.

fields.Description: The 1875 premiere shocked the Opéra-Comique with a cigarette-factory heroine stabbed on stage. Bizet died three months later, before its success.
fields.Listen: The refrain, turning from D minor to D major: the tune climbs A, D, D, E, E, F-sharp on “L'amour! L'amour!” over the cellos' habanera rhythm.
fields.Clue: Its heroine sings that “love is a rebellious bird” in a habanera adapted from a song by Sebastián Yradier, then throws a cassia flower at Don José.

fields.Description: The 1875 premiere shocked the Opéra-Comique with a cigarette-factory heroine stabbed on stage. Bizet died three months later, before its success.
fields.Listen: The brisk, festive bullfight march that opens the prelude: cymbals and full orchestra in a bright, swaggering duple metre.

fields.Description: The 1875 premiere shocked the Opéra-Comique with a cigarette-factory heroine stabbed on stage. Bizet died three months later, before its success.

fields.Audio: [sound:Borodin (Prince Igor - Polovtsian Dance 17 - Dance of the Maidens).mp3]
fields.Description: Left unfinished at Borodin's death and completed by Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov and Alexander Glazunov; its Polovtsian Dances later supplied “Stranger in Paradise” to the musical Kismet.
fields.Listen: The gliding dance of the maidens: a sinuous oboe melody beginning B, B, high F-sharp over gently rocking strings, later sung by the women's chorus.
fields.Clue: Its Gliding Dance of the Maidens became “Stranger in Paradise” in the musical Kismet; its captive hero is held by Khan Konchak of the Polovtsians, and left unfinished at its composer's death, it was completed by Rimsky-Korsakov and Glazunov.

fields.Audio: [sound:Borodin (Prince igor - Polovtsian Dance 17 - Dance of the Men).mp3]
fields.Description: Left unfinished at Borodin's death and completed by Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov and Alexander Glazunov; its Polovtsian Dances later supplied “Stranger in Paradise” to the musical Kismet.
fields.Listen: Savage, pounding accents and racing string figures as the full orchestra whips up the men's dance.

fields.Description: Twenty-one arrangements of tunes Brahms took to be Hungarian folk music; most are Romani café melodies by known composers, which caused a plagiarism row.
Written for the birth of a son to Bertha Faber, a singer Brahms had known in Hamburg; its accompaniment quietly quotes a Viennese song she used to sing to him.
fields.Listen: The gentle F-major lullaby “Guten Abend, gut' Nacht” over a lilting, off-beat accompaniment in the piano.
fields.Clue: Written in 1868 for the birth of a son to Bertha Faber, a singer its composer had known in Hamburg; its first verse comes from the folk collection Des Knaben Wunderhorn.

fields.Description: Its third movement is the funeral march everyone knows; the finale is a minute and a half of bare unison whispering that Schumann found baffling.
fields.Listen: The funeral march: a tolling left hand alternating B-flat-minor and G-flat chords under a dirge on repeated B-flats in dotted rhythm.
fields.Clue: Its third movement is the most famous funeral march ever written, and its finale is a minute and a half of whispered unison that Schumann found baffling; it is in B-flat minor.

fields.Description: The nickname means “small”, not sixty seconds. Published in 1847 as the first of the three Op. 64 waltzes and dedicated to Countess Delfina Potocka; its spinning figure is said to be George Sand's little dog chasing its tail.
fields.Listen: This piece opens with the right hand alone spinning a whirling D-flat figure round and round, leggiero, before the left hand's light oom-pah-pah enters.
fields.Clue: Published in 1847 as the first of its composer's Op. 64 and dedicated to Countess Delfina Potocka; its spinning figure is said to be George Sand's little dog chasing its tail, and its nickname means “small”, not sixty seconds.

fields.Audio: [sound:Chopin (Nocturne in Eb 1).mp3][sound:cmc-Chopin (Nocturne Op. 9 No. 2).mp3][sound:Chopin (Nocturne in EbM)_n.mp3]
fields.Description: Chopin's first published nocturnes, taking the form from the Irishman John Field. No. 2 in E-flat is the most played piece he wrote.
fields.Listen: The famous E-flat-major night piece in a lilting 12/8: the melody opens with a rising sixth (B-flat to G) over a waltz-like left hand.
fields.Clue: Its composer's first published set in a form he took from the Irishman John Field; this E-flat-major piece in 12/8 is the most played music he wrote.

fields.Description: Chopin's first published nocturnes, taking the form from the Irishman John Field. No. 2 in E-flat is the most played piece he wrote.
National dances in triple time raised to concert scale. The A major is the “Military”, the A-flat the “Heroic”, and Chopin wrote his first at seven.
fields.Listen: A grand dotted polonaise rhythm and ringing chords under a proud, march-like A-flat-major theme.
fields.Clue: A Chopin concert dance in A-flat major and triple time, from 1842, whose trio is built on thundering left-hand octaves; its nickname is not Chopin's.

fields.Description: National dances in triple time raised to concert scale. The A major is the “Military”, the A-flat the “Heroic”, and Chopin wrote his first at seven.
fields.Listen: A bright A-major polonaise in square, march-like phrases, with brassy chords in the dance's dotted rhythm.

fields.Description: A study for the left hand, written in 1831 when Chopin heard in Stuttgart that the Russians had taken Warsaw; the Op. 10 set is dedicated to Liszt.
fields.Listen: This piece opens with a crashing chord and a torrent of left-hand sixteenths plunging down the keyboard, under heroic, dotted octaves in the right hand.
fields.Clue: A study for the left hand, written in 1831 when Chopin heard in Stuttgart that the Russians had taken Warsaw; the Op. 10 set is dedicated to Liszt.

fields.Description: Written for Martha Graham, who supplied the title from a Hart Crane poem after the music was finished; it won the 1945 Pulitzer Prize.
fields.Listen: The Shaker hymn “Simple Gifts”: the solo clarinet states it plainly over a quiet accompaniment, and the variations pass it round the orchestra.
fields.Clue: Its seventh section varies a Shaker hymn as a pioneer couple marry on the Pennsylvania frontier; written for Martha Graham, who took its title from a Hart Crane poem after the music was finished, it won the 1945 Pulitzer Prize.

fields.Description: Written in 1942 for brass and percussion after a speech about the century of the common man; Copland reused it in his Third Symphony.
fields.Listen: Timpani, bass drum, and tam-tam strike; then the trumpets in unison climb a rising line of open fourths and fifths (F, B-flat, F).
fields.Clue: Written by Aaron Copland in 1942 for brass and percussion, after a wartime speech by Vice President Henry Wallace; Copland reused it in the finale of his Third Symphony.

fields.Description: Composed for Agnes de Mille's ballet about a cowgirl trying to win the Head Wrangler; its four episodes became a popular concert suite that ends with a square dance.
fields.Listen: Strings, woodblock, and xylophone vamp a square-dance rhythm; then the violins burst out with the fiddle tune “Bonyparte”.
fields.Clue: Its Hoedown quotes an American fiddle tune; Agnes de Mille's ballet, subtitled The Courting at Burnt Ranch, follows a cowgirl trying to win the Head Wrangler, through Buckaroo Holiday, Corral Nocturne, and Saturday Night Waltz.

fields.Nickname: (Prelude to the Afternoon of a Faun)
fields.Description: After Stéphane Mallarmé's poem. Boulez said modern music begins with it, and Vaslav Nijinsky's 1912 ballet caused a scandal.
fields.Listen: The solo flute, unaccompanied, slides down chromatically from C-sharp to G, a tritone, and winds back up, before the harp and muted horns enter.
fields.Clue: After Stéphane Mallarmé's poem. Boulez said modern music begins with it, and Vaslav Nijinsky's 1912 ballet caused a scandal.

fields.Description: Four pieces, Prélude, Menuet, Clair de lune, and Passepied; the third, named after a Paul Verlaine poem, is Debussy's most famous piano piece.
fields.Listen: This piece opens pianissimo in D-flat major with soft, drifting chords in thirds (F and A-flat) in a gently swaying 9/8.
fields.Clue: Four pieces, Prélude, Menuet, Clair de lune, and Passepied; the third, named after a Paul Verlaine poem, is Debussy's most famous piano piece.

fields.Description: Set in British India: a Brahmin priest's daughter falls in love with a British officer. The Flower Duet and the Bell Song are its famous numbers.
fields.Listen: Two sopranos, the heroine and her servant Mallika, twine in close parallel thirds over a flowing accompaniment as they glide down the river to gather flowers.
fields.Clue: A Brahmin priest's daughter sings the “Flower Duet” with her servant in this opera set in British India; she falls for the British officer Gérald, sings the coloratura “Bell Song”, and poisons herself with a datura leaf.

fields.Description: Set in British India: a Brahmin priest's daughter falls in love with a British officer. The Flower Duet and the Bell Song are its famous numbers.
After Goethe's ballad about a boy who enchants a broom to fetch water and cannot stop it; Mickey Mouse plays the apprentice in Disney's Fantasia.
fields.Listen: The hushed, mysterious introduction in muted, divided strings, before the bewitched broom's theme.
fields.Clue: Paul Dukas's tone poem after Goethe's ballad about a boy who enchants a broom to fetch water and cannot stop it; Mickey Mouse plays the boy in Disney's Fantasia.

fields.Description: The middle panel of a triptych of overtures on Nature, Life, and Love, and the only one still regularly played.
Written for piano duet and then orchestrated, at Brahms's suggestion, for his publisher Fritz Simrock after the success of Brahms's Hungarian Dances; the first set made Dvořák's name.
fields.Listen: A furious G-minor furiant for full orchestra, the accents shifting between groupings of two and three.
fields.Clue: Written for piano duet and then orchestrated for the publisher Fritz Simrock, at Brahms's suggestion, after the success of Brahms's own set of Hungarian pieces; the first set made its composer's name.

fields.Description: Written in New York while Dvořák ran the National Conservatory, drawing on spirituals and on Longfellow's Hiawatha. The Largo's cor anglais melody was later given words as “Goin' Home” by his pupil William Arms Fisher.
fields.Listen: This finale opens with the strings rocking on a half step, faster and louder over pounding chords; then the horns and trumpets blare the march-like E-minor main theme.
fields.Clue: Its finale recalls the themes of the earlier movements, including the Largo's cor anglais tune later sung as “Goin' Home”, and its last chord dies away in the winds; written in New York while its composer ran the National Conservatory, it drew on spirituals and Longfellow's Hiawatha.

fields.Description: Fourteen portraits of friends, each headed by initials. Nimrod is his publisher August Jaeger; Elgar claimed a larger unheard theme runs through it, never identified.
fields.Listen: A slow, noble E-flat-major hymn in 3/4 for the strings, beginning pianissimo and swelling to one radiant climax.
fields.Clue: Its ninth section, a slow E-flat-major Adagio, portrays its composer's publisher August Jaeger, whose surname means “hunter”, and recalls their talk about Beethoven's slow movements; it is played each year at the Cenotaph.

fields.Description: Gershwin's tone poem of an American strolling through Paris, blending blues with a French promenade; later the basis of a Gene Kelly film.
fields.Listen: Bluesy, jazz-inflected orchestral writing, with bright, brash brass, from a tone poem of a stroll through a foreign capital.
fields.Clue: Its composer brought real taxi horns back from France for its score, and a muted-trumpet blues stands for homesickness; Walter Damrosch conducted the premiere in 1928, and it became the basis of a 1951 Gene Kelly film.

fields.Description: Premiered in 1924 at a concert billed as an experiment in modern music. The opening clarinet glissando was a rehearsal joke that stayed; Ferde Grofé did the orchestration.
fields.Listen: This piece opens with a low clarinet trill that smears up in a long glissando into a jazzy, swaggering theme.
fields.Clue: Commissioned by Paul Whiteman for his 1924 concert “An Experiment in Modern Music”, it was sketched partly on a rattling train to Boston; Ferde Grofé orchestrated it, and its opening clarinet glissando began as a rehearsal joke by Ross Gorman.

fields.Description: A short piano piece later orchestrated, used as the theme for Alfred Hitchcock Presents.
Incidental music for Ibsen's play, containing Morning Mood, Åse's Death, Anitra's Dance, and In the Hall of the Mountain King.
fields.Listen: An Andante doloroso for muted strings: a slow, mournful B-minor lament that grows from a hush to an anguished climax.
fields.Clue: Its slow lament mourns the hero's mother, who dies as he spins her a tale of a sleigh ride to Soria Moria Castle; this incidental music for an Ibsen play also includes a dance for a Bedouin chief's daughter and a chase through a troll king's hall.

fields.Description: Incidental music for Ibsen's play, containing Morning Mood, Åse's Death, Anitra's Dance and In the Hall of the Mountain King.

fields.Audio: [sound:Grieg (Peer Gynt - In the Hall of the Mountain King).mp3]
fields.Movement: In the Hall of the Mountain King
fields.Description: Incidental music for Ibsen's play, containing Morning Mood, Åse's Death, Anitra's Dance, and In the Hall of the Mountain King.
fields.Listen: Under a held horn note, the bassoons and pizzicato cellos and basses creep up a B-minor theme (B, C-sharp, D, E, F-sharp, D, long F-sharp), repeated faster and louder until it explodes.

fields.Description: Incidental music for Ibsen's play, containing Morning Mood, Åse's Death, Anitra's Dance, and In the Hall of the Mountain King.
fields.Listen: The flute opens with a pentatonic pastoral tune in E major that falls from B to E and climbs back (B, G-sharp, F-sharp, E, F-sharp, G-sharp), and the oboe answers.

fields.Description: Grieg's only concerto; it opens with a timpani roll and the piano crashing down the keyboard, and Liszt played it at sight from the manuscript.
Composed in twenty-four days and premiered in Dublin for charity. The tradition of standing for the Hallelujah chorus is attributed to George II.
fields.Listen: The “Hallelujah” chorus: the choir hammers out “Hallelujah!” in D major with trumpets and timpani, alternating block chords with imitative entries.
fields.Clue: Its “Hallelujah” chorus ends Part II and sets “and he shall reign for ever and ever” as a fugue; composed in twenty-four days on texts compiled by Charles Jennens, it premiered in Dublin in 1742, and George II supposedly began the custom of standing for that chorus.

fields.Audio: [sound:Handel (Music for the Royal Fireworks - La Rejouissance).mp3]
fields.Description: For George II's celebration of the Peace of Aix-la-Chapelle; the rehearsal caused a London traffic jam and the display itself set the building on fire.
fields.Listen: La Réjouissance: a jubilant, bustling D-major dance for trumpets, horns, oboes, and drums, with running figures passed between the groups.
fields.Clue: Its La Réjouissance and 12/8 La Paix celebrated the Peace of Aix-la-Chapelle, which ended the War of the Austrian Succession; a public rehearsal at Vauxhall Gardens caused a three-hour traffic jam on London Bridge, George II wanted only martial instruments and no fiddles, and the pavilion caught fire on the night.

fields.Audio: [sound:Handel (Solomon - Arrival of the Queen of Sheba).mp3]

fields.Description: Three suites played by musicians on a barge following George I up the Thames in 1717; the king is said to have had them repeated three times.
fields.Listen: The Alla Hornpipe: trumpets and horns blaze a bold, syncopated tune in 3/2, answered by the strings.
fields.Clue: Its Alla Hornpipe, from the D-major suite with trumpets, is one of the pieces played on a barge following George I up the Thames in 1717; the king is said to have had them repeated three times.

fields.Description: Written for George II's coronation in 1727 and sung at every British coronation since.
fields.Listen: The chorus and orchestra in full cry, trumpets and drums blazing in D major, on the acclamation “God save the King! Long live the King!”
fields.Clue: One of four Coronation Anthems written for George II in 1727 and sung at every British coronation since; a long string introduction of rising arpeggios builds to the choir's blazing entry, its text tells how Solomon was anointed king, and Tony Britten adapted it for the UEFA Champions League anthem.

fields.Description: The joke is said to have been aimed at dozing London audiences, hence the nickname. One of the twelve symphonies Haydn wrote for Johann Peter Salomon's concerts.
fields.Listen: This movement opens with a nursery-simple C-major tune in the strings (C, C, E, E, G, G, long E), repeated even more softly before a sudden fortissimo chord with a timpani stroke.
fields.Clue: Its slow movement's joke, said to be aimed at dozing audiences, gives it its nickname; one of twelve symphonies its composer wrote for Johann Peter Salomon's London concerts, its tune is whistled by a ploughman in his oratorio The Seasons.

fields.Description: Seven movements on astrological character, not astronomy, so there is no Earth and no Pluto. Mars was written before the First World War began.
fields.Listen: Bustling, jovial orchestral writing: syncopated horn tunes ringing out over busy, scurrying strings.
fields.Clue: Its fourth movement, the Bringer of Jollity, contains a broad tune its composer later set to Cecil Spring Rice's poem “I Vow to Thee, My Country”; its seven movements portray astrological character, so there is no Earth, and the last fades out on an offstage women's chorus.

fields.Description: Seven movements on astrological character, not astronomy, so there is no Earth and no Pluto. Mars was written before the First World War began.
fields.Listen: This movement opens with strings struck col legno, harp, and timpani hammering a relentless 5/4 rhythm on G, under a creeping theme in the bassoons and horns.

fields.Description: An orchestral suite drawn from incidental music for a children's play; the Galop is the most recognisable piece Dmitry Kabalevsky wrote.
fields.Listen: Short brash circus-flavoured orchestral numbers; the Galop is a xylophone-and-brass sprint.

fields.Description: A Soviet ballet set on an Armenian collective farm; its Sabre Dance became a worldwide hit, and its Adagio was used in Stanley Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey.
fields.Listen: Hammering repeated chords set a frantic pace in G minor, and the xylophone dashes out the snapping main tune.
fields.Clue: Its “Sabre Dance” sets the xylophone dashing over hammering chords in this Soviet ballet on an Armenian collective farm, whose heroine exposes her husband's arson; its Adagio was used in Stanley Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey.

fields.Description: The most famous of nineteen, in slow lassan and fast friska halves, and the soundtrack to more cartoons than any other classical piece.
Three piano nocturnes transcribed from Liszt's own songs; the third, on a poem beginning O lieb, is the famous one.
Opens with a solo trumpet funeral march; the Adagietto was a love letter to Alma Mahler and became famous through Luchino Visconti's film Death in Venice.
fields.Listen: The Adagietto: harp arpeggios and hushed strings alone, then a slow, yearning F-major melody in the violins that hangs on its suspensions.
fields.Clue: Its fourth movement, for strings and harp alone, was a love letter to Alma Schindler and became famous through Luchino Visconti's film Death in Venice; it opens with a solo trumpet's funeral march in C-sharp minor.

fields.Description: An Alexandrian courtesan is converted by a monk who then falls in love with her; the violin Méditation is the interlude between her conversion scenes.
fields.Listen: The Méditation: after a harp introduction, the solo violin sings a serene D-major melody over muted strings.
fields.Clue: Its violin Méditation is the interlude in which the Alexandrian courtesan resolves to follow the monk Athanaël, who then falls in love with her himself; after Anatole France's novel.

fields.Description: Also called Fingal's Cave, from a visit to Staffa; Mendelssohn sent the opening bars home in a letter the same day.
fields.Listen: This overture opens with a rolling B-minor figure in the violas, cellos, and bassoons (F-sharp, D, C-sharp, D, B, low F-sharp), rising a third every two bars like waves.
fields.Clue: A concert overture from its composer's 1829 visit to the Scottish island of Staffa and its basalt sea grotto; he sent its opening bars home in a letter the same day, and Wagner called him a first-rate landscape painter on its strength.

fields.Audio: [sound:Mendelssohn (Wedding March from A Midsummer Night's Dream).mp3]
fields.Description: Mendelssohn wrote the overture at seventeen and the rest of the incidental music sixteen years later. Its Wedding March became the standard recessional.
fields.Listen: Trumpets sound a fanfare of repeated triplets; then the full orchestra enters on chords that lean toward E minor before the C-major march arrives.
fields.Clue: Its Wedding March, which opens with a trumpet fanfare, became the standard recessional after Victoria, Princess Royal, walked out to it in 1858; its composer wrote the overture at seventeen and the rest of the incidental music sixteen years later.

fields.Description: A witches' sabbath, known almost entirely in Rimsky-Korsakov's posthumous rewriting rather than Mussorgsky's own version.
fields.Listen: This piece opens with swirling, rushing strings and woodwinds; then the trombones and tuba blast out a menacing theme over hammering timpani.
fields.Clue: A witches' sabbath on St John's Eve, known almost entirely in Rimsky-Korsakov's posthumous rewriting, which ends with a church bell and a peaceful dawn; Walt Disney's Fantasia paired it with Schubert's “Ave Maria”.

fields.Description: His last completed instrumental work, written for Anton Stadler and originally for basset clarinet, which reaches lower than the modern instrument.
fields.Listen: The Adagio: the clarinet sings a serene D-major melody rising A, long D, F-sharp, echoed by the strings.
fields.Clue: Its D-major Adagio opens with the soloist rising A, D, F-sharp; its composer's last completed instrumental work, written for Anton Stadler on an instrument Theodor Lotz had extended downward, and published only after his death.

fields.Description: A serenade for strings, K. 525, written in 1787 while Mozart was working on Don Giovanni. One of its five original movements is lost.
fields.Listen: The Romanze: a gentle, singing C-major melody in the violins over a soft accompaniment.
fields.Clue: Its Romanze in C major has a scampering C-minor middle section; written in 1787 while its composer was working on Don Giovanni, this serenade for strings, K. 525, has lost one of its five movements, a minuet.

fields.Description: A serenade for strings, K. 525, written in 1787 while Mozart was working on Don Giovanni. One of its five original movements is lost.

fields.Audio: [sound:cmc-Mozart (Die Zauberflote Der Holle Rache (Queen of the Night))_n.mp3]
fields.Movement: Act II · “Der Hölle Rache” (Queen of the Night)
fields.Description: A Singspiel with spoken dialogue, full of Masonic symbolism, premiered in a suburban Vienna theatre weeks before Mozart's death. The Queen of the Night's aria reaches top F.
A Singspiel with spoken dialogue, full of Masonic symbolism, premiered in a suburban Vienna theatre weeks before Mozart's death. The Queen of the Night's aria reaches top F.
After Pierre Beaumarchais's banned play, with the political speech removed to satisfy the censor. Its second act ends in a twenty-minute continuous finale.
After Pierre Beaumarchais's banned play, with the political speech removed to satisfy the censor. Its second act ends in a twenty-minute continuous finale.
Completed in Vienna in March 1785, a month after the D-minor concerto, K. 466.
fields.Listen: The slow movement: muted violins sing a long, floating F-major melody over soft, pulsing triplets and pizzicato bass.
fields.Clue: Its slow movement was used in a 1967 Swedish film about a tightrope walker and her lover, which gave the concerto its nickname; its first movement begins with a quiet march in the strings.

fields.Description: Entered in Mozart's catalogue in June 1788 as “a little keyboard sonata for beginners”, the summer of his last three symphonies; Edvard Grieg added a second piano part to it.
fields.Listen: The opening: the C-major melody C, E, G, then B, C, D, C, over a broken-chord Alberti bass in the left hand, before running scales.
fields.Clue: The best-known teaching sonata, its first movement's recapitulation begins unusually in F major, the subdominant, and its slow movement is an Andante in G major.

fields.Description: Commissioned anonymously by a count who wanted to pass it off as his own. Mozart died at the Lacrimosa; Franz Xaver Süssmayr completed it, and the widow concealed the fact.
fields.Listen: The Dies irae: the chorus hammers out “Dies irae, dies illa” in D minor over plunging tremolo strings, trumpets, and drums.
fields.Clue: Its Dies irae hurls the chorus at “the day of wrath” over tremolo strings; commissioned anonymously by Count Walsegg, who meant to pass it off as his own, it was left unfinished at its composer's death and completed by Franz Xaver Süssmayr.

fields.Description: Commissioned anonymously by a count who wanted to pass it off as his own. Mozart died at the Lacrimosa; Franz Xaver Süssmayr completed it, and the widow concealed the fact.
fields.Listen: The Lacrimosa: sighing string figures rise and fall in a slow 12/8; then the chorus enters softly on “Lacrimosa dies illa” and swells to a cry.

fields.Description: Unusually, none of its movements is in sonata form: it opens with a theme and variations in siciliana rhythm, has a minuet in the middle, and ends with the Rondo alla turca.
fields.Listen: This rondo opens with a scurrying A-minor turn in the right hand (B, A, G-sharp, A, C), then breaks into A major, with drum-like left-hand chords imitating a Janissary band.
fields.Clue: Its finale imitates a Janissary band; in this keyboard work, none of whose movements is in sonata form, it opens with a theme and variations in siciliana rhythm, and four pages of its autograph turned up in Budapest in 2014.

fields.Description: Written in Salzburg in 1773, at seventeen, in the stormy Sturm und Drang manner, and unusually scored with four horns.
fields.Listen: The opening: urgent syncopated repeated notes in the strings, G, then D, E-flat, and F-sharp, rising in agitation in G minor.
fields.Clue: One of only two minor-key symphonies by Mozart, it shares its key with No. 40 and is called the “little” one; its first movement plays as the film Amadeus opens.

fields.Description: One of only two he wrote in a minor key, opening without any introduction on a whispered viola accompaniment before the tune.
Written for piano after a memorial show of Viktor Hartmann's drawings, with a Promenade between pictures representing the viewer walking. Ravel's orchestration is standard.
fields.Listen: The Promenade: a stately theme on solo trumpet, G, F, B-flat, C, F, D, alternating bars of 5/4 and 6/4, then answered by the full brass.
fields.Clue: Its recurring Promenade, first on solo trumpet in Ravel's orchestration, depicts the viewer walking between drawings; written for piano after a memorial show of Viktor Hartmann's art, it also depicts chicks in their shells and the witch Baba Yaga's hut.

fields.Audio: [sound:Offenbach (Genevieve De Brabant - Galop 1).mp3][sound:cmc-Offenbach (Genevieve de Brabant Galop).mp3]

fields.Description: Offenbach's parody of the Orpheus myth and of Second Empire society; its Infernal Galop is the tune of the can-can.
fields.Listen: Light, bustling operetta music for full orchestra in a quick, galloping duple metre, bright and satirical.
fields.Clue: Its gods revolt against a diet of nectar and ambrosia and descend to Pluto's realm for a party, where they dance the Galop infernal, the tune of the can-can; Public Opinion forces a violinist to fetch back a wife he is glad to be rid of, and Jupiter buzzes his way to her disguised as a fly.

fields.Description: Offenbach's parody of the Orpheus myth and of Second Empire society; its Infernal Galop is the tune of the can-can.
fields.Listen: This overture, Carl Binder's 1860 potpourri, opens with a bold, dramatic flourish for full orchestra, then quiets to a tender woodwind melody; later a solo violin, the hero's instrument, takes over before the galop.

fields.Description: Offenbach's last work, left unfinished at his death: the poet Hoffmann tells of three lost loves, the doll Olympia, the singer Antonia, and the courtesan Giulietta.
fields.Listen: The Barcarolle: a gently rocking 6/8 in D major, a lilting gondola tune over swaying, lapping accompaniment, sung as the duet “Belle nuit, ô nuit d'amour”.
fields.Clue: Its Venetian act opens with a Barcarolle sung by the courtesan Giulietta and Nicklausse, the poet's Muse in disguise; its composer died before finishing it, and in other acts the hero loves a mechanical doll, Olympia, and the consumptive singer Antonia.

fields.Description: Sets medieval goliard poems found at Benediktbeuern. The opening and closing chorus, O Fortuna, addresses fortune as a turning wheel, and Orff disowned everything he had written before it.
fields.Listen: The opening chorus “O Fortuna”: full chorus and orchestra crash in on a D-minor chord over pounding timpani, a slow, massive declamation of fate's turning wheel.
fields.Clue: Its opening and closing chorus addresses Fortune, “Empress of the World”, who waxes and wanes like the moon; a “scenic cantata” on medieval goliard poems found at Benediktbeuern, in sections for spring, the tavern, and the court of love, where a roasted swan laments on the spit.

fields.Description: Pachelbel's only widely known work, long forgotten until a 1968 recording made it a wedding staple.
fields.Listen: The cello plays the two-bar ground bass alone (D, A, B, F-sharp, G, D, G, A); then the first violin enters stepping down F-sharp, E, D, C-sharp, B, A, B, C-sharp, and the second and third follow in strict imitation.
fields.Clue: Three violins play in strict imitation over a bass of eight notes repeated twenty-eight times; originally paired with a gigue in the same key, it was long forgotten until Jean-François Paillard's 1968 recording made it a wedding staple.

fields.Description: Three violins in canon over a two-bar ground bass repeated twenty-eight times; long forgotten, it became a wedding staple after a 1968 recording.
Each character has an instrument and a theme, written in four days for a Moscow children's theatre to teach the orchestra.
fields.Listen: The boy's jaunty C-major theme in the strings, leaping up through C, E, and G with a spring in its step.
fields.Clue: Written in four days in 1936 for Natalia Sats's Central Children's Theatre in Moscow, each character has its own instrument and theme: a flute for the bird, an oboe for the duck, a clarinet for the cat, a bassoon for the grandfather, three horns for the predator, and strings for the boy.

fields.Audio: [sound:Prokofiev (Romeo  Juliet - Montagues  Capulets (Dance of the Knights)).mp3]
fields.Description: The Bolshoi rejected it as undanceable, and Prokofiev first gave it a happy ending, later dropped. Dance of the Knights is its best-known number.
fields.Listen: The “Dance of the Knights”: a heavy, stomping E-minor march, the strings' dotted theme climbing an arpeggio (E, G, B, E) over thudding brass and bass drum.
fields.Clue: Its “Dance of the Knights” stomps through the Capulets' ball; the Bolshoi rejected it as undanceable, its composer first gave it a happy ending, and it premiered in Brno in 1938.

fields.Description: Puccini died before finishing it; Arturo Toscanini stopped the premiere where the composer had left off. Contains “Nessun dorma”.
fields.Listen: The climax of “Nessun dorma”: the tenor holds a ringing high B on “Vincerò!” as the full orchestra sweeps the D-major melody to its close.
fields.Clue: Prince Calaf sings “Nessun dorma” after solving the princess's three riddles and daring her to learn his name by dawn; the slave girl Liù kills herself rather than reveal it, and its composer died before finishing it, so Arturo Toscanini stopped the premiere at that point.

fields.Work: Music for the Funeral of Queen Mary
fields.Audio: [sound:Purcell (Music for the Funeral of Queen Mary - March).mp3]
[sound:Rachmoninoff (Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini, 18th Var.).mp3]
fields.Description: Twenty-four variations for piano and orchestra on Paganini's 24th Caprice; the Dies irae chant also runs through it.
fields.Listen: The eighteenth variation: the piano sings Paganini's tune turned upside down and slowed into a lush D-flat-major melody, before the strings take it up.
fields.Clue: Twenty-four variations for piano and orchestra on the last of the violin caprices, written at Hertenstein in 1934; the Dies irae runs through it, and its eighteenth variation is by far the most famous.

fields.Description: Written as a ballet for Ida Rubinstein; Ravel called it “a piece for orchestra without music”.
fields.Listen: This piece opens with a snare drum quietly tapping its insistent 3/4 rhythm over pizzicato violas and cellos; then the solo flute begins the long, sinuous C-major melody.
fields.Clue: Written as a ballet for Ida Rubinstein in 1928, it repeats one C-major melody in two halves over an unchanging snare-drum rhythm in a single long crescendo, modulating only near the end; its composer called it “a piece for orchestra without music”.

fields.Audio: [sound:Respighi (Pines of Rome - Pines of the Appian Way).mp3]
fields.Description: Four scenes of Rome's pine trees; the third calls for a recording of a nightingale, and the last marches a Roman legion up the Appian Way.
fields.Listen: This movement opens with a hushed, ominous march tread in the low strings, piano, and timpani over a deep organ B-flat, as a legion advances in the misty dawn.
fields.Clue: Its four scenes of trees in the Italian capital end with a legion marching up a consular road at dawn, with six buccine (ancient horns, usually played on flugelhorns); the third calls for a phonograph recording of a nightingale, and it is the second of its composer's Roman trilogy.

fields.Movement: The Young Prince and the Young Princess
fields.Description: A symphonic suite on the Arabian Nights in which a solo violin is the storyteller, returning between the sultan's brass theme.
fields.Listen: The Young Prince and the Young Princess: the violins sing a tender, gently swaying G-major love song, decorated by clarinet flourishes.
fields.Clue: A symphonic suite on the Arabian Nights in which a solo violin plays the storyteller who postpones her execution by spinning tales, between the sultan Shahriar's stern brass theme; its movements depict a Kalendar prince, a festival at Baghdad, and a ship wrecked on a rock topped by a bronze horseman.

fields.Audio: [sound:Rimsky-Korsakov (Tale of Tsar Salton - Flight Of The Bumblebee).mp3]
fields.Description: After Pushkin's fairy tale; Prince Gvidon is turned into a bumblebee to visit his father, which is the scene of Flight of the Bumblebee.
fields.Listen: A non-stop buzz of chromatic sixteenth notes in the violins, swarming up and down at breakneck speed.
fields.Clue: Its Prince Gvidon, cast adrift in a barrel with his mother, is turned by the Swan Princess into a bumblebee so he can visit his father, the scene of a famous chromatic interlude; after Pushkin's verse fairy tale.

fields.Description: Written in about three weeks and hissed at its 1816 Rome premiere, partly by supporters of Giovanni Paisiello's older setting. Figaro makes his entrance with Largo al factotum, and the overture was borrowed from two earlier Rossini operas.
fields.Listen: The overture's slow introduction in E major: forceful tutti chords, then a graceful violin melody over plucked strings, here under Arturo Toscanini.
fields.Clue: Written in about three weeks and hissed at its 1816 Rome premiere, partly by partisans of Giovanni Paisiello's older setting; Figaro makes his entrance with “Largo al factotum”, Rosina sings “Una voce poco fa”, and its overture was borrowed from two earlier operas.

fields.Description: Written in weeks and hissed off at its 1816 Rome premiere, partly by supporters of Giovanni Paisiello's older setting. Figaro's Largo al factotum opens it.
Rossini's last opera, written at thirty-seven; he wrote no more operas in the thirty-nine years he had left, and its final galop became the Lone Ranger theme.
fields.Listen: This overture opens with five solo cellos alone: a rising E-minor arpeggio and a hushed, songful dawn over soft basses and timpani rolls.
fields.Clue: Its overture moves from a dawn for cellos through a storm and a “Call to the Cows” for cor anglais and flute to a galloping finale launched by trumpets; in its composer's last opera, written at thirty-seven, the hero shoots an apple from his son Jemmy's head.

fields.Description: Suppressed by Saint-Saëns during his lifetime except The Swan, for fear the jokes would damage his reputation; Tortoises is the can-can played very slowly.
fields.Listen: Aquarium: glassy runs on the glass harmonica (often a glockenspiel or celesta) and rippling two-piano arpeggios over muted strings, gliding in A minor.
fields.Clue: Its Aquarium uses a glass harmonica, its Tortoises plays the can-can very slowly, and its Fossils quotes its composer's own Danse macabre on xylophone; he suppressed this “grand zoological fantasy” in his lifetime except for the cello solo The Swan.

fields.Description: Suppressed by Saint-Saëns during his lifetime except The Swan, for fear the jokes would damage his reputation; Tortoises is the can-can played very slowly.
A tone poem after a poem by Henri Cazalis: Death calls the skeletons from their graves at midnight to dance; the xylophone is their rattling bones, and a cockcrow ends it.
fields.Listen: This piece opens with a harp striking D twelve times for midnight over soft string chords; then the solo violin, its E string tuned down to E-flat, grates out a tritone (A and E-flat).
fields.Clue: A tone poem after Henri Cazalis's poem: Death fiddles in a graveyard at midnight, the xylophone rattles the skeletons' bones, the Dies irae turns into a waltz, and an oboe's cockcrow ends the dance; its composer quoted it in the Fossils of his zoological suite.

fields.Description: Death tunes his fiddle with the E string lowered to E-flat and calls skeletons up at midnight; the xylophone is their rattling bones, and a cockcrow ends it.

fields.Movement: mvt. II · Allegro moderato – Presto – Maestoso – Allegro
fields.Description: Dedicated to the memory of Liszt, who died weeks after its 1886 London premiere. It is laid out in two large parts rather than four movements, and adds organ and piano four hands.
fields.Listen: The scherzo: a restless C-minor dance in the strings, with stamping accents and quick, scurrying figures.
fields.Clue: Dedicated to the memory of Liszt, who died weeks after its 1886 London premiere, this C-minor work is laid out in two large parts and adds piano four hands and a keyboard instrument whose blazing C-major chord launches the finale.

fields.Movement: mvt. II · Allegro moderato – Presto – Maestoso – Allegro
fields.Description: The “Organ” Symphony, dedicated to Liszt's memory, in two large parts, adding organ and piano four hands. Its theme is a transformed Dies irae.
Not a setting of the prayer: it is Ellen's third song from Walter Scott's Lady of the Lake, which only later had the Latin text fitted to it.
fields.Listen: Ellen's prayer: a serene vocal melody that opens on a long held note and rises gently, over rippling piano triplets like a harp.
fields.Clue: Not a setting of the Latin prayer: it is Ellen's third song from Walter Scott's The Lady of the Lake, sung to the Virgin while she hides in a cave, in Adam Storck's German translation; the Latin text was fitted to it later.

fields.Description: Written as a protest piece against Russian censorship of the Finnish press, and performed under disguised titles to evade it. Its hymn section was later given words as a national song.
fields.Listen: This tone poem opens with snarling, menacing chords in the low brass over a timpani roll, answered by grave woodwind chorales.
fields.Clue: Written in 1899 for a press celebration protesting Russian censorship, it was performed under disguised titles such as Happy Feelings at the Awakening of Finnish Spring; its hymn section was later given words and sung as a national song.

fields.Description: Six tone poems on Bohemian history and landscape, from the castle of Vyšehrad to the Hussite mountain of Blaník; Smetana wrote them after going deaf.
fields.Listen: Over rippling flutes and clarinets, the violins sing the flowing E-minor river theme, climbing E, F-sharp, G, A, B, then B, C, C, B.
fields.Clue: Its second tone poem follows a river from two springs past a hunt, a peasant wedding, nymphs by moonlight, and the St John's Rapids to Vyšehrad, on a tune adapted from “La Mantovana”, also the source of “Hatikvah”; six tone poems on Bohemian history and landscape, written after its composer went deaf.

fields.Description: Written as a choral piece with mocking words after Austria's defeat at Königgrätz; the orchestral version became Austria's unofficial anthem.
fields.Listen: This waltz opens with hushed tremolo violins and a rising horn call; then the swaying D-major waltz climbs on the same notes: D, D, F-sharp, A, A.
fields.Clue: Written in 1867 for the Vienna Men's Choral Association, with mocking words after Austria's defeat at Königgrätz; the orchestral version became Austria's unofficial anthem, and Stanley Kubrick set a spacecraft docking to it in 2001: A Space Odyssey.

fields.Description: Strauss's most famous operetta: Eisenstein and his wife each go masked to Prince Orlofsky's ball, where Dr. Falke takes revenge for an old prank.
fields.Listen: A lilting Viennese waltz in the strings, with a swaying, hesitating upbeat.
fields.Clue: Its waltz Du und du draws on the ball at Prince Orlofsky's, where Eisenstein flirts with his own masked wife and Dr. Falke takes revenge for an old prank; the maid Adele sings the “Laughing Song”, and Rosalinde a csárdás.

fields.Description: After Nietzsche's book, in nine sections; its sunrise opening became famous through 2001: A Space Odyssey.
fields.Listen: This tone poem opens with a low C held on organ, contrabassoon, and basses; then the trumpets rise C, G, high C, the full orchestra blazes a major-then-minor chord (E, then E-flat), and the timpani pound C and G.
fields.Clue: After Nietzsche's book, in nine sections including “Of the Backworldsmen”, a chromatic fugue “Of Science”, and a waltz-like “Dance Song”; its sunrise opening, trumpets rising C, G, C, became famous through 2001: A Space Odyssey, and it ends ambiguously between B major and C.

fields.Description: Stravinsky's first Sergei Diaghilev commission, written at twenty-seven after Anatoly Lyadov was too slow, and the work that made him famous overnight.
fields.Listen: The Finale: over shimmering string tremolo, the solo horn sings a gentle B-major Russian folk tune, which then builds through the orchestra to a blazing brass climax.
fields.Clue: Its composer's first commission from Sergei Diaghilev, written at twenty-seven after Anatoly Lyadov was too slow: Prince Ivan captures a magical bird and frees thirteen princesses from the immortal sorcerer Kashchei by smashing the egg holding his soul, and the finale builds a horn's folk tune to a blazing climax.

fields.Description: Its 1913 Paris premiere caused a riot, with Vaslav Nijinsky shouting counts from the wings. A pagan sacrifice, ending with the chosen maiden dancing herself to death.
fields.Listen: The Sacrificial Dance: violent chords hammered in irregular groupings, the metre changing almost every bar as the chosen maiden dances.
fields.Clue: Its 1913 Paris premiere caused a riot, with Vaslav Nijinsky shouting counts from the wings; its first part, “The Adoration of the Earth”, opens with a bassoon high in its register, and in the second a chosen maiden dances herself to death.

fields.Description: Tchaikovsky's last symphony ends with a slow movement that dies away into silence; he conducted the premiere nine days before his death. The first movement quotes the Russian Orthodox requiem chant, and the third is a march that audiences often applaud as if it were the end.
fields.Listen: The famous second theme: the muted violins and cellos sing a soaring, tender D-major melody, its first phrase falling F-sharp, E, D, over soft, swaying chords.
fields.Clue: Its composer's last symphony, premiered nine days before his death: the first movement opens with a bassoon in the depths and marks a passage pppppp, the second is a limping waltz in 5/4, the third a march that audiences often applaud as if it were the end, and it closes with a slow movement that dies away.

fields.Description: Marks Napoleon's retreat from Moscow and is scored for cannon and church bells. Tchaikovsky himself thought it loud and insincere.
fields.Listen: This piece opens with four solo cellos and two violas intoning the Orthodox hymn “O Lord, save thy people” in hushed E-flat-major harmony.
fields.Clue: It marks Napoleon's retreat from Moscow, pitting “La Marseillaise” against “God Save the Tsar”, and it is scored for cannon fire and church bells; its composer thought it loud and noisy, written “without much love”.

fields.Description: Written for a concert for Serbian soldiers wounded fighting the Ottoman Turks, it quotes Serbian folk songs and the Russian imperial anthem “God Save the Tsar”.
fields.Listen: This march opens with a sombre, trudging B-flat-minor tune, a Serbian folk song, in the bassoons and violas over a tramping accompaniment.
fields.Clue: Written for an 1876 concert for Serbian soldiers wounded fighting the Ottoman Turks, it builds on Serbian folk songs and quotes the Russian imperial anthem “God Save the Tsar”, which returns in triumph at the end.

fields.Description: Tchaikovsky's last ballet, from E. T. A. Hoffmann via Dumas. The Sugar Plum Fairy's variation uses the celesta, which he had found in Paris and kept secret to use first.
fields.Listen: The Dance of the Mirlitons: three flutes in close harmony pipe a light, dotted D-major tune over pizzicato strings.
fields.Clue: Its composer's last ballet, from E. T. A. Hoffmann via Dumas: Drosselmeyer's Christmas gift becomes a prince and leads Clara to the Land of Sweets, where the Sugar Plum Fairy's variation features a celesta he had found in Paris and kept secret.

fields.Audio: [sound:Tchaikovsky (Nutcracker - Dance of the Sugar Plum Fairy) (1).mp3]
fields.Description: Tchaikovsky's last ballet, from E. T. A. Hoffmann via Dumas: Clara's nutcracker becomes a prince and takes her to the Land of Sweets.
fields.Listen: The celesta, a bell-like keyboard, picks out a dainty E-minor tune over pizzicato strings, answered by a low bass clarinet.

fields.Description: Tchaikovsky's last ballet, from E. T. A. Hoffmann via Dumas. The Sugar Plum Fairy's variation uses the celesta, which he had found in Paris and kept secret to use first.
fields.Listen: Brass fanfare answered by skipping strings, toy-soldier crispness.

fields.Description: Tchaikovsky's last ballet, from E. T. A. Hoffmann via Dumas. The Sugar Plum Fairy's variation uses the celesta, which he had found in Paris and kept secret to use first.
fields.Listen: A slow descending scale in the strings, plain and enormous, building to a full-orchestra climax.

fields.Description: Tchaikovsky's last ballet, from E. T. A. Hoffmann via Dumas. The Sugar Plum Fairy's variation uses the celesta, which he had found in Paris and kept secret to use first.
fields.Listen: Piccolo and flute chirping high over a plodding bassoon ostinato.

fields.Description: Tchaikovsky's last ballet, from E. T. A. Hoffmann via Dumas. The Sugar Plum Fairy's variation uses the celesta, which he had found in Paris and kept secret to use first.
fields.Listen: Very fast Russian dance with tambourine, accelerating to a stamping finish in under ninety seconds.

fields.Audio: [sound:Tchaikovsky (Nutcracker - Waltz of the Flowers).mp3][sound:cmc-Tchaikovsky (The Nutcracker Waltz of the Flowers).mp3]
fields.Description: Tchaikovsky's last ballet, from E. T. A. Hoffmann via Dumas. The Sugar Plum Fairy's variation uses the celesta, which he had found in Paris and kept secret to use first.
fields.Listen: This waltz opens with a gentle woodwind introduction and a sweeping harp cadenza before the horns announce the waltz theme.

fields.Description: Nikolai Rubinstein told him it was worthless and unplayable; Tchaikovsky refused to change a note and dedicated it to Hans von Bülow instead. The famous opening never returns.
An overture-fantasy written on Mily Balakirev's advice and revised twice over ten years. The love theme is one of the most recognized melodies in orchestral music.
fields.Listen: Turbulent, syncopated orchestral writing, the strings slashing like swords: the music of the feuding families.
fields.Clue: An overture-fantasy written on Mily Balakirev's advice and revised twice over ten years: a hushed chorale for Friar Laurence, syncopated fight music with clashing cymbals, and a soaring love theme, first on cor anglais and violas.

fields.Description: Tchaikovsky's own favourite of his ballets, choreographed by Marius Petipa to a detailed plan the composer followed. The Rose Adagio balances Aurora on one point four times.
fields.Listen: The Garland Waltz: a broad, sweeping waltz for full orchestra, its swirling tune rising over a buoyant oom-pah accompaniment.
fields.Clue: Its composer's own favourite of his ballets, choreographed by Marius Petipa to a plan he followed bar by bar: the wicked fairy Carabosse curses Princess Aurora at her christening, the Lilac Fairy softens it to a hundred years' sleep, and the Garland Waltz precedes the Rose Adagio.

fields.Description: The 1877 Moscow premiere failed and the version now danced is the 1895 Marius Petipa and Lev Ivanov revival staged after Tchaikovsky's death. Odette and Odile are danced by one ballerina.
fields.Listen: Two bassoons chug a staccato accompaniment under a quick, stepping oboe duet in a minor key, as four cygnets dance with linked arms.
fields.Clue: Its 1877 Moscow premiere failed, and the version now danced is the 1895 revival by Marius Petipa and Lev Ivanov; Prince Siegfried falls for a princess turned into a bird by the sorcerer von Rothbart, whose daughter Odile, danced by the same ballerina, performs thirty-two fouettés.

fields.Description: The 1877 Moscow premiere failed and the version now danced is the 1895 Marius Petipa and Lev Ivanov revival staged after Tchaikovsky's death. Odette and Odile are danced by one ballerina.
fields.Listen: Crisp brass-led ceremonial march.

fields.Description: The 1877 Moscow premiere failed and the version now danced is the 1895 Marius Petipa and Lev Ivanov revival staged after Tchaikovsky's death. Odette and Odile are danced by one ballerina.
fields.Listen: Long sweeping A major waltz with full orchestral swing; the big set-piece dance.

fields.Description: The 1877 Moscow premiere failed and the version now danced is the 1895 Marius Petipa and Lev Ivanov revival staged after Tchaikovsky's death. Odette and Odile are danced by one ballerina.
fields.Listen: Plaintive oboe swan theme over rippling harp in B minor; lavish string writing and a prominent violin solo.

fields.Description: Commissioned for Cairo and first staged there in 1871, though not for the Suez Canal's opening as often claimed. Ends with the lovers sealed alive in a vault beneath the temple.
fields.Listen: The Triumphal Scene: a grand, ceremonial march for chorus, stage band, and orchestra, its long straight trumpets blazing out the famous fanfare.
fields.Clue: Commissioned for Cairo and first staged there in 1871: Radamès defeats Ethiopia and returns in a Triumphal March with long straight trumpets, but Amneris's jealousy dooms him, and the lovers are sealed alive in a vault beneath the temple.

fields.Description: A plot of swapped babies and a gypsy's revenge, containing the Anvil Chorus and the Miserere. Enrico Caruso said all it needs is the four greatest singers in the world.
fields.Listen: The Anvil Chorus: the gypsies hail the dawn in a swinging chorus, “Vedi! le fosche notturne spoglie”, striking anvils on the beat.
fields.Clue: A plot of swapped babies and a gypsy's revenge: Azucena threw her own child into the fire by mistake, Manrico sings “Di quella pira”, and the Count di Luna learns too late that he has executed his brother; the gypsies strike anvils in Act II.

fields.Description: After Dumas's La Dame aux camélias. The 1853 Venice premiere failed, partly because the consumptive heroine was sung by a large and visibly healthy soprano.
fields.Listen: The brindisi “Libiamo ne' lieti calici”: a swinging B-flat-major drinking song in 3/8, the tenor leading, then the soprano and the full chorus.
fields.Clue: After Dumas fils's La Dame aux camélias: a Paris courtesan sings “Sempre libera” but gives up Alfredo at his father Germont's request and dies of consumption; its 1853 Venice premiere failed, partly because the dying heroine was sung by a visibly healthy soprano.

fields.Description: Written for the anniversary of Alessandro Manzoni's death, and criticized as an opera in church dress; the Dies irae returns like a refrain.
fields.Listen: The Dies irae: hammering G-minor chords for full orchestra, the bass drum slamming on the offbeats as the chorus shrieks “Dies irae!”
fields.Clue: Written for the first anniversary of Alessandro Manzoni's death and premiered in Milan in 1874; its Dies irae, with bass-drum blows on the offbeats, returns like a refrain, and critics called it an opera in church dress.

fields.Description: Verdi fought the Venetian censors, who objected to a king's assassination; the monarch became a duke. The jester finds his own daughter in the sack.
fields.Listen: The Duke's “La donna è mobile”: a jaunty, swaggering B-major tenor tune in 3/8 over a thumping orchestral accompaniment.
fields.Clue: Its composer fought Venetian censors over a king's assassination, so the monarch became the Duke of Mantua; the hunchbacked jester, cursed by Count Monterone, hires Sparafucile to kill the Duke, then hears “La donna è mobile” and finds his own daughter Gilda dying in the sack.

fields.Description: Four violin concertos published with sonnets, probably Vivaldi's own, whose lines are written into the score beside the barking dog, the sleeping shepherd, and the ice.
fields.Listen: In G minor: a languid, sighing passage broken by sudden, loud bursts of thunder in the strings.
fields.Clue: Four violin concertos published in 1725 with sonnets, probably its composer's own, whose lines are written into the score beside a barking dog, a sleeping goatherd, a cuckoo, and ice; they open The Contest Between Harmony and Invention.

fields.Description: Four violin concertos published with sonnets, probably Vivaldi's own, whose lines are written into the score beside the barking dog, the sleeping shepherd, and the ice.
fields.Listen: Shivering F-minor music: repeated chords and rapid figures in the strings, the solo violin's teeth chattering in the frost.

fields.Description: Four violin concertos published with sonnets, probably Vivaldi's own, whose lines are written into the score beside the barking dog, the sleeping shepherd, and the ice.
fields.Listen: This concerto opens with the full strings' bright E-major ritornello (E, then G-sharp, G-sharp, G-sharp, F-sharp, E, up to B); then the solo violins trill and chirp like birds over a hushed accompaniment.

fields.Description: The second part of the Ring: the twins Siegmund and Sieglinde fall in love, and Wotan punishes his daughter Brünnhilde by putting her to sleep inside a ring of fire. Act III opens with the Ride of the Valkyries.
A swan knight who must never be asked his name. Its third-act prelude leads to the Bridal Chorus, universally used as the wedding processional.
fields.Listen: The Bridal Chorus, “Treulich geführt ziehet dahin”: a gentle B-flat-major processional, the tune known in English as “Here Comes the Bride”.
fields.Clue: A swan knight defends Elsa of Brabant against Telramund and Ortrud on condition that she never ask his name; its Act III prelude leads into the Bridal Chorus, used everywhere as a wedding processional, and he reveals that he is Parsifal's son.

fields.Description: A swan knight who must never be asked his name. Its third-act prelude leads to the Bridal Chorus, universally used as the wedding processional.
fields.Listen: The Act III Prelude: whirling, festive string figures in G major; then the trombones and horns blaze out a fanfare theme.

fields.Description: Opens with the Tristan chord, an unresolved dissonance often called the start of modern harmony. The first Tristan died weeks after the premiere.
fields.Listen: Isolde's Liebestod, “Mild und leise wie er lächelt”: the soprano's line rises over a long, surging orchestral swell toward the B-major resolution withheld since the Prelude.
fields.Clue: It opens with a chord (F, B, D-sharp, G-sharp) that never resolves, often called the start of modern harmony, and ends with a “love-death”; Brangäne swaps a death potion for a love potion, the tenor who created the hero died weeks after the 1865 Munich premiere, and its composer wrote it while in love with Mathilde Wesendonck.

fields.Description: Its Toccata finale is the standard wedding recessional. Widor played at Saint-Sulpice for sixty-four years.
fields.Listen: The Toccata: rapid, detached broken chords in the hands in F major over a slow, stately melody in the pedals, building to full organ.
fields.Clue: Its F-major Toccata finale, with rapid broken chords over a slow pedal melody, is the standard wedding recessional; its composer, who played at Saint-Sulpice in Paris for sixty-four years, wrote ten such symphonies for his instrument.

fields.Description: Collected English folk song and edited the English Hymnal; the Fantasia on a Theme by Thomas Tallis sets a string orchestra against a distant second one.
After a George Meredith poem, begun in 1914 and revised after the war, and dedicated to the violinist Marie Hall.
fields.Listen: After hushed held chords, the solo violin climbs alone in a free, unaccompanied cadenza, trilling and soaring in pentatonic arabesques like a bird rising.
fields.Clue: A romance for violin and orchestra after a George Meredith poem, begun in 1914 and revised after the war; it was dedicated to the violinist Marie Hall, and its unbarred solo cadenzas depict a bird rising out of sight.

fields.Description: Its minuet is marked so fast it is really a scherzo, and the finale's theme is let out a few notes at a time in a teasing slow introduction.
fields.Listen: This symphony opens on a dissonant chord pointing away from the home key (a C dominant seventh resolving to F) before a slow, searching introduction.
fields.Clue: Its minuet is marked so fast it is really a scherzo, and the finale's theme is let out a few notes at a time in a teasing slow introduction.

fields.Clue: Written at Heiligenstadt in the year of the testament in which he admitted his deafness, and one of his most cheerful works.

Beethoven dedicated it to Napoleon, then scratched out the title page when Napoleon crowned himself emperor. Twice the usual length, with a funeral march second and a finale of variations on a theme from his ballet The Creatures of Prometheus.
fields.Listen: This symphony opens with two hammered E-flat chords; then the cellos state the theme as a broken E-flat arpeggio that slips down onto a foreign C-sharp.
fields.Clue: Its first movement's horn enters with the theme four bars early, over the wrong chord, which Ferdinand Ries took for a mistake; it was dedicated to Napoleon until he crowned himself emperor, and its finale varies a theme from The Creatures of Prometheus.

fields.Listen: The funeral march opens sotto voce: the violins intone a C-minor dirge over growling double-bass grace notes that imitate muffled drums, and the oboe then takes up the theme.

fields.Description: The “Eroica”. Beethoven dedicated it to Napoleon then scratched the title out when he declared himself emperor. Twice the usual length, with a funeral march second.
fields.Listen: Light, fast, whispered scherzo; three horns in the trio playing hunting calls.

fields.Listen: This symphony opens with a slow introduction: a forte D-major chord, then a gentle woodwind melody in thirds over held strings.

fields.Description: The “Eroica”. Beethoven dedicated it to Napoleon then scratched the title out when he declared himself emperor. Twice the usual length, with a funeral march second.
fields.Listen: Variations on a bare skeleton of a bass line, including a full fugue, then a slow hymn-like statement before a sudden Presto.

fields.Listen: The Allegro vivace's main theme: a bright B-flat-major tune in the violins, all staccato repeated notes and leaping arpeggios, answered by the full orchestra.
fields.Clue: Schumann called it a slender Greek maiden between two Norse giants, the “Eroica” and the Fifth.

fields.Description: The four-note opening figure recurs across all four movements, and the scherzo runs into a C major finale adding trombones, piccolo, and contrabassoon.
fields.Listen: Scherzo creeping up from the double basses, then horns bark the short-short-short-long rhythm; ends in a long dark crescendo that runs straight into the finale without stopping.

fields.Description: Five movements with titles, including a brook scene whose birdcalls (nightingale, quail, and cuckoo) are named in the score, and a thunderstorm that runs straight into the finale. Beethoven called it “more the expression of feeling than painting”.
fields.Listen: This symphony's first movement: a rustic F-major tune over a drone in the low strings, its short motifs repeated many times over without being developed.

fields.Listen: The storm begins pianissimo, with a distant rumble in the low strings and scattered raindrops in the second violins, then breaks fortissimo with timpani and tremolo strings.

fields.Listen: A bright, compact F-major Allegro vivace in 3/4: full-orchestra phrases answered by lighter woodwind replies, with sudden accents off the beat.
fields.Clue: The shortest of his mature symphonies. Beethoven called it “my little symphony in F” and said it was less popular than the Seventh because it was so much better.

fields.Listen: Bare open fifths, as though the orchestra were tuning, out of which the D minor theme assembles itself. Granitic; the opening returns as a full-orchestra unison.

fields.Description: Took Brahms over twenty years, under the shadow of Beethoven; Hans von Bülow called it “Beethoven's Tenth”. Its finale's big tune resembles the Ode to Joy, and when this was pointed out Brahms said any fool could see that.

fields.Clue: Twenty years in the making under the shadow of Beethoven, it opens over a pounding timpani pedal; Hans von Bülow called it “Beethoven's Tenth”, and its finale's alphorn theme came from a birthday card to Clara Schumann.

fields.Clue: Written to thank the University of Breslau for an honorary doctorate, it strings together student songs, including “Wir hatten gebauet ein stattliches Haus” and the “Fuchslied”, before ending with “Gaudeamus igitur”.

In five movements, the extra one a solemn, archaic movement inspired by a cardinal's installation at Cologne Cathedral. Written after Schumann moved to Düsseldorf, it was the last of his symphonies to be composed.
fields.Listen: This symphony opens with a buoyant, surging E-flat theme in 3/4, its hemiolas pulling against the bar line, with the horns prominent.
fields.Clue: In five movements, the extra one a solemn, archaic movement with trombones inspired by a cardinal's installation at Cologne Cathedral; written after its composer moved to Düsseldorf in 1850, it has a nickname that names a river.

fields.Description: The “Rhenish”, in five movements, with a solemn extra one written after seeing a cardinal's ceremony at Cologne Cathedral.
fields.Listen: Solemn brass chorale in E-flat minor, trombones leading — the cathedral movement, and it is the fourth of five.

fields.Listen: Slow Adagio opening, then a horn call built on a falling minor third with a flattened seventh; driving E minor, folk-flavoured tunes in flutes and oboes.

fields.Description: Written in New York while Dvořák ran the National Conservatory, drawing on spirituals and on Longfellow's Hiawatha. The Largo's cor anglais melody was later given words as “Goin' Home” by his pupil William Arms Fisher.
fields.Listen: Hushed brass and woodwind chords lead the music into D-flat major; then, over muted strings, the cor anglais sings the melody later called “Goin' Home”, opening long F, A-flat, A-flat.

fields.Listen: Hard-driving triangle-and-timpani scherzo with abrupt gear changes; the first movement's theme intrudes.

fields.Description: Written in America. Brahms said that had he known such a concerto was possible he would have written one. Dvořák quoted his own song for his dying sister-in-law.
fields.Listen: This concerto opens with a quiet clarinet theme in B minor over low strings that swells into a full-orchestra statement; then the horn sings the lyrical second theme.

fields.Listen: The first dance, a fiery C-major furiant for full orchestra: stamping accents and quick switches between groupings of two and three.

fields.Description: Written in three days in the Czech community of Spillville, Iowa, during Dvořák's American years; its tunes are pentatonic, and the third movement takes a birdcall from the scarlet tanager.
fields.Listen: Over shimmering tremolo violins, the viola sings the pentatonic F-major main theme.
fields.Clue: Its composer wrote this F-major piece for four strings in three days in the Czech community of Spillville, Iowa; its tunes are pentatonic, and the third movement borrows a scarlet tanager's call.

A showcase of orchestral virtuosity on Spanish themes, dedicated to the sixty-seven players of its premiere, whose names Rimsky-Korsakov wrote into the score.
fields.Listen: The Alborada: the full orchestra bursts out with a brilliant A-major dance in a swinging 2/4, the clarinet and then the solo violin answering with flourishes.
fields.Clue: Its outer movements are near-identical Alboradas, Asturian morning songs, around a set of variations, a “Scene and Gypsy Song”, and a closing Fandango asturiano; it was dedicated to the sixty-seven players of its 1887 St Petersburg premiere, whose names its composer wrote into the score.

Built on Russian Orthodox chants, moving from the solemnity of Holy Week to the bells and rejoicing of Easter morning.
fields.Listen: This overture opens with a slow, chant-like D-minor melody in the woodwinds and strings, an Orthodox hymn, rising toward the first bell-like climax.
fields.Clue: A concert overture built on chants from the Obikhod, the Orthodox liturgy, moving from the solemnity of Holy Week to the bells and rejoicing of the resurrection; its slow introduction shifts between 5/2, 3/1, and 2/1, with a solo violin cadenza marked dolce a piacere.

fields.Listen: The Sea and Sinbad's Ship: surging, wave-like string arpeggios under the stern sultan's theme in the low brass and woodwinds.
