fields.Description: The prologue to Wagner's Ring: Alberich steals the Rhine gold and forges the ring, which Wotan takes from him. It opens on an E-flat chord held for 136 bars.
fields.Listen: Before the gods' entry: Donner's hammer-call (B-flat, D, F) rings out in the brass as he gathers the mists into a thunderstorm, clearing the way for the rainbow bridge.
fields.Clue: The prologue to its composer's tetralogy: the dwarf Alberich renounces love to steal the Rhinemaidens' gold and forge a ring, which Wotan tricks from him to pay the giants Fasolt and Fafner for building Valhalla; it opens on an E-flat chord held for 136 bars.

fields.Audio: [sound:Wagner (Die Meistersinger, Act III - Dance of the Apprentices)_n.mp3]
fields.Description: Wagner's only mature comedy: the knight Walther wins the song contest and Eva's hand with the cobbler Hans Sachs's help, while the pedant Beckmesser caricatures the critic Eduard Hanslick.
fields.Listen: The Dance of the Apprentices: a graceful, lilting C-major dance in three for the apprentices and girls on the festival meadow by the river.
fields.Clue: Its composer's only mature comedy: the knight Walther wins the song contest and Eva's hand with the cobbler Hans Sachs's help, while the pedantic marker Beckmesser, a caricature of the critic Eduard Hanslick, chalks up his mistakes; Sachs's apprentice David and his fellows dance before the guilds march in.

fields.Description: Wagner's only mature comedy: the knight Walther wins the song contest and Eva's hand with the cobbler Hans Sachs's help, while the pedant Beckmesser caricatures the critic Eduard Hanslick.
fields.Listen: This prelude opens with the Mastersingers' pompous C-major march theme in the full orchestra, broad and dignified.

fields.Description: The second part of the Ring: the twins Siegmund and Sieglinde fall in love, and Wotan punishes his daughter Brünnhilde by putting her to sleep inside a ring of fire. Act III opens with the Ride of the Valkyries.
fields.Listen: Siegmund's “Winterstürme wichen dem Wonnemond”: a tender, lilting B-flat-major song of spring for tenor, the harp and strings swelling beneath, as the door blows open on the moonlit night.
fields.Clue: The second part of its composer's tetralogy: the twins Siegmund and Sieglinde fall in love, and he draws the sword Nothung from an ash tree; Wotan punishes his daughter Brünnhilde for defending Siegmund by putting her to sleep inside a ring of fire, and Act III opens with a famous ride of warrior maidens.

fields.Movement: Act III · Sailors' Chorus (“Steuermann, lass die Wacht!”)
fields.Description: Wagner's first characteristic opera, from a storm-tossed sea voyage of his own. Senta's ballad contains the germ of the whole score.
fields.Listen: The Act III Sailors' Chorus, “Steuermann, lass die Wacht!”: the Norwegian crew roars a stamping, boisterous song on the quay, then calls out to the silent ghost ship.
fields.Clue: Its composer's first characteristic opera, drawn from his own storm-tossed sea voyage: Senta's ballad tells of a sea captain cursed to sail forever until redeemed by a faithful woman, the spinning girls sing “Summ und brumm”, and the Norwegian sailors taunt a silent ghost ship in Act III.

fields.Description: Wagner's first characteristic opera, from a storm-tossed sea voyage of his own. Senta's ballad contains the germ of the whole score.
fields.Listen: This overture opens with stormy string tremolo while the horns blast the Dutchman's motif in hollow fifths (A, D, A).

fields.Description: The last part of the Ring: Hagen murders Siegfried, and Brünnhilde rides into his funeral pyre as the Rhine overflows and Valhalla burns.
fields.Listen: The Funeral March opens almost inaudibly, with hushed, muffled strokes on the timpani and low strings: the start of a solemn procession of leitmotifs.
fields.Clue: The last part of its composer's tetralogy: Hagen murders Siegfried with a spear, and Brünnhilde rides her horse Grane into his funeral pyre as the Rhine overflows and Valhalla burns.

fields.Listen: Dawn: the horn calls rise over the orchestra as the hero sets out, and the flowing Rhine theme takes over in a swelling E-flat major.

fields.Description: Wagner's last opera, a “festival play for the consecration of the stage”: the innocent fool Parsifal heals the wounded Grail king Amfortas. Bayreuth long kept it to itself.
fields.Listen: This prelude opens with the Communion theme in bare unison for violins, cellos, clarinet, and bassoon, without harmony: A-flat, C, E-flat, F, G, rising slowly and falling back.
fields.Clue: Its composer's last opera, a “festival play for the consecration of the stage”: the “pure fool” heals the Grail king Amfortas with the spear that wounded him, after resisting Kundry in Klingsor's magic garden; its Grail theme is the Dresden Amen, and Bayreuth long kept it to itself.

fields.Description: The second Ring opera, with the Ride of the Valkyries and Wotan's farewell, ending with Brünnhilde asleep on a rock ringed by fire.
Wagner's early grand opera on the Roman tribune Cola di Rienzi; its 1842 success in Dresden launched his career.
fields.Listen: This overture opens with a single trumpet holding a long, swelling A, three times, before the strings sing the noble prayer theme.
fields.Clue: Its composer's early grand opera, after Edward Bulwer-Lytton's novel, on a fourteenth-century Roman tribune; its 1842 success in Dresden launched his career, its overture is built on the hero's prayer “Allmächt'ger Vater”, and it was a favourite of Adolf Hitler.

fields.Description: The third part of the Ring: Siegfried reforges the sword Nothung, kills the dragon Fafner, and wakes Brünnhilde on her fiery rock.
fields.Listen: The forging song, “Hoho! Hoho! Hohei!”: the tenor works the bellows and hammers the sword's pieces over a pounding orchestra with anvil-like strokes.
fields.Clue: The third part of its composer's tetralogy: the hero reforges the sword Nothung, kills the dragon Fafner, understands a woodbird's song after tasting the dragon's blood, and wakes Brünnhilde on her fiery rock.

fields.Description: The third part of the Ring: Siegfried reforges the sword Nothung, kills the dragon Fafner, and wakes Brünnhilde on her fiery rock.
fields.Listen: Forest Murmurs: murky, divided low strings stir before rustling string figures and woodwind birdcalls fill the forest.

fields.Description: Its 1861 Paris revision put the ballet in Act I instead of Act II, so the Jockey Club members who came late rioted and closed it after three nights.
fields.Listen: This overture opens with the Pilgrims' Chorus as a hushed E-major chorale for clarinets, horns, and bassoons before the cellos' sighing counter-melody.
fields.Clue: Its 1861 Paris revision put the ballet in Act I instead of Act II, so members of the Jockey Club who arrived late rioted and closed it after three nights; its minstrel hero, back from Venus's mountain, shocks the Wartburg song contest, and Wolfram sings “O du, mein holder Abendstern”.

fields.Clue: At the Tuba mirum of its Dies irae, four brass bands placed at the corners of the hall and sixteen timpani blaze out; commissioned by the French state, it is the one work its composer said he would save from the flames.

Schumann's Op. 2, twelve short dances imagining the masked ball in Jean Paul's novel Flegeljahre; a clock striking six ends the ball.
fields.Listen: A few bars of introduction, then the first dance: a sweeping, carefree D-major waltz.
fields.Clue: Its composer's Op. 2: twelve short dances imagining the masked ball in Jean Paul's novel Flegeljahre, where the twins Walt and Vult court Wina; a clock strikes six to end the ball as the opening waltz returns combined with the Grossvatertanz.

fields.Description: Twenty-one short pieces portraying masked revellers, friends such as Chopin and Paganini, and Schumann's own two sides, Florestan and Eusebius; most are built on the letters A–S–C–H.
fields.Listen: The Préambule: grand, festive A-flat-major chords in a stately dance rhythm before the music quickens into a whirl.
fields.Clue: Twenty-one short piano pieces portraying masked revellers at a ball, friends such as Chopin and Paganini, Clara Wieck as “Chiarina”, and its composer's own two sides, Florestan and Eusebius; most are built on A–S–C–H, the hometown of his fiancée Ernestine von Fricken, and it ends with a march against the Philistines.

fields.Description: Sixteen songs to Heinrich Heine's poems, tracing a love affair to its bitter end; “Ich grolle nicht” is the defiant climax.
fields.Listen: “Ich grolle nicht” (“I bear no grudge”): defiant, hammering repeated chords in C major under the singer's bitter claim that he bears no grudge though his heart is breaking.
fields.Clue: Its sixteen songs set Heinrich Heine's poems of a love affair to its bitter end, from “Im wunderschönen Monat Mai” through the defiant “Ich grolle nicht” to the last song's long piano postlude; written in 1840, its composer's “year of song”.

fields.Listen: The last song, “Die alten, bösen Lieder”: a heavy, march-like song in which the poet orders a huge coffin for his old, wicked songs, ending in a long, tender piano postlude.

fields.Clue: Thirteen short “scenes from childhood” for piano, written for adults to hear, opening with “Of Foreign Lands and Peoples” and ending with “The Poet Speaks”; the seventh, Träumerei, is the most famous.

fields.Clue: Eight piano fantasies named after E. T. A. Hoffmann's mad bandmaster Johannes Kreisler and dedicated to Chopin; written in a few days in 1838 while its composer was in love with Clara Wieck, they alternate frantic and dreamy moods.

fields.Clue: A work for piano and four strings with a double bass in place of the second violin, written for the amateur cellist Sylvester Paumgartner of Steyr; its fourth movement varies its composer's own song about a fish, and rising sextuplets run through most of its movements.

fields.Description: Twenty Wilhelm Müller poems: a journeyman miller follows a brook, loses the girl to a hunter, and drowns himself; the brook sings the last song.
fields.Listen: “Das Wandern” (“Wandering”): a bright, strophic song whose piano's steady running figures turn like a mill wheel as the young journeyman sings that wandering is his joy.
fields.Clue: Its twenty Wilhelm Müller poems follow a journeyman who sings of wandering in the first song, follows a brook to a mill, loses the owner's daughter to a green-clad hunter, and drowns himself; the brook sings him a lullaby in the last song.

Schubert set Goethe's ballad at eighteen: one singer voices narrator, father, son, and the Erlking over relentless piano triplets, which stop dead before the last line, “the child was dead”.
fields.Listen: This song opens with the piano hammering triplet octaves, the galloping horse, under a menacing rising figure in the bass; then the narrator asks “Wer reitet so spät durch Nacht und Wind?”
fields.Clue: Its composer set Goethe's ballad at eighteen: one singer voices narrator, father, son, and a supernatural seducer over relentless piano triplets, the boy's cries rising a step each time, until the triplets stop dead before the last line, “the child was dead”.

fields.Description: Four linked movements on a theme from his song Der Wanderer, and so difficult that Schubert broke down playing it and said the devil could play it.
fields.Listen: This piece opens with hammering C-major chords in a long, short-short rhythm, the rhythm of its composer's song “Der Wanderer”, then a fast rising arpeggio.
fields.Clue: Four linked movements for solo piano built on a theme from its composer's song of a lonely traveller, “Ich komme vom Gebirge her”; so hard that he broke down playing it, saying “the devil may play it”, it was later arranged by Liszt for piano and orchestra.

fields.Listen: The Adagio: the song's own melody, slow and sombre in C-sharp minor, in hushed chords, as the theme for variations.

fields.Description: Written at seventeen, a scene from Goethe's Faust; the spinning wheel stops when Gretchen remembers Faust's kiss.
fields.Listen: The piano's right hand whirls a constant sixteenth-note figure while the left hand treads like a foot pedal, under the girl's anxious “Meine Ruh' ist hin, mein Herz ist schwer”.
fields.Clue: Written at seventeen on a scene from Goethe's Faust: the piano's whirring right hand is a spinning wheel, which stops when the heroine remembers her lover's kiss (“sein Kuss!”) before faltering back into motion.

fields.Clue: The only one of its composer's string quartets published in his lifetime; its minuet quotes his song “Die Götter Griechenlands”, and its slow movement borrows an entr'acte from his incidental music to a play by Helmina von Chézy.

fields.Description: Written at nineteen for a private amateur orchestra, with no clarinets, trumpets or drums, and the most Mozartian thing he wrote.
Two complete movements and a scherzo sketched for piano, left in 1822. The score lay with Schubert's friend Anselm Hüttenbrenner until 1865, and why Schubert abandoned it is unknown.
fields.Listen: This symphony opens with the cellos and basses alone, hushed in unison in B minor; then the violins shiver in sixteenths under a plaintive oboe-and-clarinet melody.
fields.Clue: Two complete movements, in B minor and E major, and a scherzo sketched for piano, left in 1822; the score lay with its composer's friend Anselm Hüttenbrenner until 1865. It opens with the low strings alone, and its second theme is a famous cello tune over syncopated accompaniment.

fields.Clue: Schumann found this C-major symphony among the papers of its composer's brother Ferdinand a decade after his death, Mendelssohn premiered it in Leipzig in 1839, and Schumann praised its “heavenly length”; its finale echoes the “Ode to Joy”.

fields.Clue: The second of a pair published in 1836 and dedicated to Countess d'Apponyi, this D-flat-major piece spins its melody like a Bellini duet for one hand.

fields.Listen: This piece opens with the right hand leaping between octave D-sharps like a tolling little bell; then the G-sharp-minor melody sounds beneath the high, repeated D-sharp.
fields.Clue: Its composer's piano study on the bell-rondo finale of the B-minor Second Violin Concerto by the Genoese virtuoso whose caprices he also transcribed; the right hand leaps constantly across more than two octaves to a high, ringing D-sharp.

fields.Clue: After Victor Hugo's poem about the Cossack hetman tied naked to a wild horse and carried across the steppes; its composer reworked it from his piano study of the same name, adding a triumphant march as the hero is hailed by the Cossacks.

fields.Listen: The hushed opening: muffled octave Gs low in the bass, then a slow descending scale with an exotic augmented second; the gesture repeats before the music gathers force.
fields.Clue: A single half-hour movement whose four sections work both as the movements of a sonata and as the parts of one sonata form, built by thematic transformation from motifs on its first page; Humphrey Searle orchestrated it for Frederick Ashton's ballet Marguerite and Armand.

fields.Clue: Its B-flat-minor slow movement, which doubles as the scherzo, opens with pizzicato strings and harp before a cor anglais melody, drawing the jibe that no Haydn or Beethoven symphony uses that instrument; in three cyclic movements, it was dedicated to its composer's pupil Henri Duparc.

fields.Description: Franck's only symphony, in three movements bound by cyclic themes; its slow movement doubles as the scherzo.

fields.Description: Subtitled The Poem of Fire, it is scored for a colour organ (luce) meant to bathe the hall in coloured light.
fields.Listen: This tone poem opens with a hazy, sustained chord, the “mystic chord” built on fourths (C, F-sharp, B-flat, E, A, D), hushed in the low strings, horns, and harp, with no clear key.
fields.Clue: Subtitled The Poem of Fire, it is scored for piano, orchestra, wordless chorus, and a colour organ (luce) meant to bathe the hall in coloured light; its harmony grows from a single six-note chord.

fields.Description: Written for Birmingham in English, modelled on Handel, opening unusually with the prophet's curse before any overture.
fields.Listen: A calm, consoling arioso for baritone over gentle strings: “For the mountains shall depart, and the hills be removed, but thy kindness shall not depart from me”.
fields.Clue: Its prophet sings “For the mountains shall depart”, from Isaiah, shortly before he rises to heaven in a fiery chariot; written in English for the 1846 Birmingham Festival, it opens with his curse of drought before the overture, and he defeats the priests of Baal.

fields.Clue: Its Jägerlied (Hunting Song), in A major with horn calls, is one of forty-eight short lyrical piano pieces in eight books, each a melody over an accompaniment; its composer resisted attaching titles, insisting music says things more precisely than language, and others depict a spinning wheel and Venetian gondolas.

fields.Clue: Its slow A-minor introduction grew from a melody its composer sketched in 1829 in the ruined chapel of Holyrood Palace, Edinburgh; finished thirteen years later and dedicated to Queen Victoria, it runs its four movements without a break.

Mi chiamano Mimì”; after Henri Murger's stories, the painter Marcello loves the flirt Musetta, who sings “Quando m'en vo'”, and the philosopher Colline bids farewell to his coat.

fields.Listen: Colline's farewell to the old overcoat he will pawn for the dying Mimì, “Vecchia zimarra, senti”: a solemn bass melody over a slow orchestral tread, here sung by Feodor Chaliapin.

fields.Movement: Act IV · “O Mimì, tu più non torni”
fields.Description: Puccini and Ruggero Leoncavallo raced to set the same Henri Murger stories; Puccini's won. Mimì's candle goes out in Act I, and she dies in a Paris garret at the end.
fields.Listen: The Act IV duet “O Mimì, tu più non torni”: the tenor mourns “o giorni belli, piccole mani, odorosi capelli”, then the baritone admits his brush still paints Musetta's face, here Beniamino Gigli and Giuseppe De Luca.

fields.Description: Puccini and Ruggero Leoncavallo raced to set the same Henri Murger stories; Puccini's won. Mimì's candle goes out in Act I, and she dies in a Paris garret at the end.
fields.Listen: Mimì introduces herself, “Sì. Mi chiamano Mimì”: plain, conversational phrases on repeated notes, climbing step by step over warm strings before the melody opens out.

fields.Description: Puccini and Ruggero Leoncavallo raced to set the same Henri Murger stories; Puccini's won. Mimì's candle goes out in Act I, and she dies in a Paris garret at the end.
fields.Listen: The Act I love duet “O soave fanciulla”: the tenor greets Mimì in the moonlight before the soprano joins him, here Enrico Caruso and Nellie Melba in 1907.

fields.Description: Puccini and Ruggero Leoncavallo raced to set the same Henri Murger stories; Puccini's won. Mimì's candle goes out in Act I, and she dies in a Paris garret at the end.
fields.Listen: Mimì's quiet farewell to Rodolfo, “Donde lieta uscì al tuo grido d'amore, torna sola Mimì al solitario nido”, a resigned soprano line over muted strings, here sung by Nellie Melba in 1907.

fields.Description: The 1904 La Scala premiere was a fiasco; Puccini revised it into two acts and it became a staple. Butterfly waits through the night with the Humming Chorus.
fields.Listen: The heroine's farewell to her small son, “Tu, tu, piccolo Iddio!”: an anguished soprano line straining high over a full, surging orchestra as she bids him look well at his mother's face.
fields.Clue: Its fifteen-year-old Nagasaki geisha waits through the night for the American naval officer who married her while an offstage chorus hums; when he returns with an American wife, Kate, she bids farewell to their son and kills herself with her father's dagger. Its 1904 La Scala premiere was a fiasco.

fields.Listen: The later part of “Un bel dì, vedremo”, in G-flat major: the soprano imagines her husband calling her by his pet names, and her line swells to its climax of faith as the orchestra surges beneath.

fields.Description: The 1904 La Scala premiere was a fiasco; Puccini revised it into two acts and it became a staple. Butterfly waits through the night with the Humming Chorus.
fields.Listen: Japanese pentatonic tunes and whole-tone colour woven through Italian lyricism; a humming offstage chorus and a long orchestral vigil.

fields.Description: A melodrama in real Roman locations. Tosca stabs Scarpia, the mock execution proves real, and she throws herself from the Castel Sant'Angelo.
fields.Listen: Scarpia's “Va, Tosca!”: over a tolling ostinato of bells, organ, and cannon, the baritone plots aloud as the cardinal's procession enters, before chorus and full orchestra blaze out the Te Deum.
fields.Clue: Its Act I ends as the police chief Scarpia, plotting to possess the heroine, cries that she makes him forget God while a Te Deum celebrates a supposed victory over Napoleon at Marengo; set in real Roman locations, it ends with the singer leaping from the Castel Sant'Angelo after her lover's mock execution proves real.

fields.Description: A melodrama in real Roman locations. Tosca stabs Scarpia, the mock execution proves real, and she throws herself from the Castel Sant'Angelo.
fields.Listen: “Vissi d'arte, vissi d'amore”: the soprano's hushed E-flat-minor prayer, opening on long, sustained notes over soft strings, asking why God repays her devotion so.

fields.Description: A melodrama in real Roman locations. Tosca stabs Scarpia, the mock execution proves real, and she throws herself from the Castel Sant'Angelo.
fields.Listen: “E lucevan le stelle”, in B minor: the tenor half-speaks his memories on repeated notes (“e olezzava la terra, stridea l'uscio dell'orto”) while the solo clarinet sings the melody.

fields.Description: Puccini died before finishing it; Arturo Toscanini stopped the premiere where the composer had left off. Contains “Nessun dorma”.
fields.Listen: This opera opens with crashing, dissonant chords, a brutal stamping motif, before the Mandarin's proclamation “Popolo di Pekino!”

Rossini's last opera before thirty-nine years of near silence. The overture runs storm, pastoral cor anglais and a cavalry galop that became the Lone Ranger theme.

Written in under three weeks and hissed at its 1816 Rome premiere, partly by supporters of Giovanni Paisiello's older setting of Pierre Beaumarchais's play; it soon became the most popular comic opera of its age.
fields.Listen: The end of the orchestral introduction, then Figaro bursts in with “Largo al factotum della città” and “La ran la le ra”, a baritone patter over a skipping 6/8 accompaniment.
fields.Clue: Figaro introduces himself as the town's indispensable jack-of-all-trades, boasting “Ah, che bel vivere” and crying his own name, “Figaro! Figaro! Figaro!”, before Count Almaviva hires him to win Rosina from her guardian, Doctor Bartolo.

fields.Description: Written in weeks and hissed off at its 1816 Rome premiere, partly by supporters of Giovanni Paisiello's older setting. Figaro's Largo al factotum opens it.
Written in under a month when Rossini was twenty-one. Its first-act finale dissolves into nonsense syllables as the characters lose their heads.

A one-act farce for Venice whose overture, with its exposed oboe writing, outlived the opera.
Neither little nor solemn, as Rossini noted, scored for twelve singers, two pianos, and harmonium, and inscribed asking God whether he had written sacred music or damned music.

fields.Description: Dedicated to his patron Nadezhda von Meck, whom he never met; the third movement is played entirely pizzicato.
fields.Listen: Restless F-minor music in a lilting, syncopated 9/8, the strings sighing over a swaying pulse.
fields.Clue: Dedicated to its composer's patron Nadezhda von Meck, whom he never met, to whom he explained its opening brass fanfare as Fate; its third movement is played entirely pizzicato, and its finale quotes the folk song “In the field there stood a birch tree”.

fields.Description: Dedicated to his patron Nadezhda von Meck, whom he never met. The brass fanfare is fate; the third movement is played entirely pizzicato.
Dedicated to his patron Nadezhda von Meck, whom he never met. The brass fanfare is fate; the third movement is played entirely pizzicato.

fields.Movement: mvt. II · Andantino in modo di Canzona
fields.Description: Dedicated to his patron Nadezhda von Meck, whom he never met; the third movement is played entirely pizzicato.
fields.Listen: The Andantino in modo di canzona: a melancholy B-flat-minor oboe melody over pizzicato strings.

fields.Movement: mvt. II · Andante cantabile con alcuna licenza
fields.Description: A fate motto returns in every movement, minor at the start and major at the end. Tchaikovsky privately judged it insincere after conducting it.
fields.Listen: The Andante cantabile: after hushed low-string chords, the solo horn sings its long, yearning D-major melody.
fields.Clue: Its motto, first intoned by low clarinets in E minor, returns in every movement and blazes in E major at the end; its slow movement has a famous horn solo, and its composer privately judged it insincere after conducting it.

fields.Description: A fate motto returns in every movement, minor at the start and major at the end. Tchaikovsky privately judged it insincere after conducting it.
fields.Listen: This symphony opens with two clarinets low in their register intoning the dark E-minor motto, a funeral-march tune (G, two quick Gs, up to A, G, F-sharp, G, E), over hushed low strings.

fields.Description: A fate motto returns in every movement, minor at the start and major at the end. Tchaikovsky privately judged it insincere after conducting it.
fields.Listen: A waltz where the scherzo should be, elegant and slightly weary; the motto creeps in at the end on clarinet and bassoon.

fields.Movement: mvt. IV · Finale. Andante maestoso – Allegro vivace
fields.Description: A fate motto returns in every movement, minor at the start and major at the end. Tchaikovsky privately judged it insincere after conducting it.
fields.Listen: The fate motto turned major and triumphant in the slow introduction, then a driving finale and a march-like blaze to close.

fields.Description: The “Pathétique”, ending with a slow movement that dies away, and premiered nine days before the composer's death. Its first movement quotes the Russian requiem chant.
fields.Listen: A waltz in five beats to the bar, so it never quite settles; lilting and lopsided.

fields.Description: Tchaikovsky's last symphony ends with a slow movement that dies away into silence; he conducted the premiere nine days before his death. The first movement quotes the Russian Orthodox requiem chant, and the third is a march that audiences often applaud as if it were the end.
fields.Listen: Scurrying string triplets in G major out of which a march slowly assembles, a jaunty fragment in the woodwinds.

fields.Description: After Pushkin's verse novel: Onegin rejects Tatiana's letter, kills his friend Lensky in a duel, and years later is rejected by her in turn.
fields.Listen: The Act III Polonaise: a grand, festive dance in stately triple time, with brass fanfares, opening the St Petersburg ball.
fields.Clue: After Pushkin's verse novel: Tatiana writes a long letter declaring her love to a bored dandy who rejects her; he kills his friend Lensky in a duel, and years later, as Prince Gremin's wife, she rejects him in turn. Its Act III ball opens with a Polonaise.

fields.Description: After Pushkin's verse novel: Onegin rejects Tatiana's letter, kills his friend Lensky in a duel, and years later is rejected by her in turn.
fields.Listen: The Act II Waltz: a lilting A-major waltz for the Larins' name-day party, with the chorus of guests gossiping over it.

fields.Description: Tchaikovsky's last ballet, from E. T. A. Hoffmann via Dumas. The Sugar Plum Fairy's variation uses the celesta, which he had found in Paris and kept secret to use first.
fields.Listen: Drowsy swaying G minor over a drone, muted strings, and tambourine.

fields.Description: Nikolai Rubinstein told him it was worthless and unplayable; Tchaikovsky refused to change a note and dedicated it to Hans von Bülow instead. The famous opening never returns.
fields.Listen: This concerto opens with the horns' four descending notes (F, D-flat, C, B-flat); then the piano crashes in with huge D-flat-major chords under the strings' sweeping melody.
fields.Clue: Its grand opening theme never returns; Nikolai Rubinstein called it worthless and unplayable, so its composer dedicated it to Hans von Bülow, who premiered it in Boston in 1875, and its finale is built on a Ukrainian dance.

fields.Listen: The finale: a driving B-flat-minor Ukrainian dance theme, hammered out by the piano in syncopated rhythm.

fields.Listen: This ballet opens with the snarling, stormy brass music of the wicked fairy Carabosse before the Lilac Fairy's gentle, curling theme over harp.

fields.Listen: A hushed, lyrical scene: a gentle melody over rippling harp and strings, gathering intensity.

fields.Description: Leopold Auer, its intended dedicatee, called it unplayable, and after the 1881 Vienna premiere Eduard Hanslick wrote that it “stinks to the ear”. It is now among the most performed violin concertos.
fields.Listen: This concerto opens with a gentle, hushed orchestral introduction in the violins; then the soloist enters with a short cadenza-like passage before singing the lyrical D-major main theme.
fields.Clue: Leopold Auer, its intended dedicatee, called it unplayable, Adolph Brodsky premiered it in Vienna in 1881, and Eduard Hanslick wrote that it “stinks to the ear”; its middle movement is a Canzonetta, and its finale a Russian peasant dance.

fields.Description: Leopold Auer, its intended dedicatee, called it unplayable, and after the 1881 Vienna premiere Eduard Hanslick wrote that it “stinks to the ear”. It is now among the most performed violin concertos.
fields.Listen: The finale: a fiery Russian folk dance, the soloist racing through rapid runs over stamping orchestral accents.

fields.Description: A plot of swapped babies and a gypsy's revenge, containing the Anvil Chorus and the Miserere. Enrico Caruso said all it needs is the four greatest singers in the world.
fields.Listen: Leonora's “Tacea la notte placida”: the soprano recalls the calm, starry night she first heard the troubadour's serenade, in a gently swaying A-flat-major cantabile.

fields.Listen: Tenor and soprano trade phrases, he ardent and she deflecting with light coloratura.

fields.Description: Verdi's first great success, on the Hebrews' captivity in Babylon; the chorus “Va, pensiero” became an anthem of Italian unification.
fields.Listen: The Hebrew slaves' chorus “Va, pensiero, sull'ali dorate”: a long, swaying melody sung almost entirely in unison, longing for the lost homeland.
fields.Clue: Its composer's first great success, on the Hebrews' captivity in Babylon: the Babylonian king is struck mad for declaring himself a god, Abigaille learns she was born a slave, and the exiles' chorus “Va, pensiero” became an anthem of Italian unification.

fields.Movement: Act II · “Credo in un Dio crudel”
fields.Description: Verdi's penultimate opera, after Shakespeare, with a libretto by Arrigo Boito; Iago's “Credo” is Boito's invention, not Shakespeare's.
fields.Listen: Iago's lead-in to his Credo, “Vanne; la tua meta già vedo… e il tuo dimone son io”; then, over snarling unison brass trills, “Credo in un Dio crudel”.
fields.Clue: Its composer's penultimate opera, after Shakespeare, with a libretto by Arrigo Boito, who invented Iago's nihilistic “Credo”; it opens in a storm with “Esultate!”, and Desdemona sings the Willow Song and an “Ave Maria” before she is smothered.

fields.Description: Written for the anniversary of Alessandro Manzoni's death, and criticized as an opera in church dress. The Dies irae returns like a refrain, with the bass drum on the off-beat.
fields.Listen: Bass drum hammering on every beat, full chorus shrieking, brass shattering — the loudest music Verdi wrote, and it recurs through the work.

fields.Description: Written for the anniversary of Alessandro Manzoni's death, and criticized as an opera in church dress; the Dies irae returns like a refrain.
fields.Listen: The Lacrymosa: a slow, sighing B-flat-minor lament begun by the mezzo-soprano and taken up by the other soloists and the chorus over throbbing strings.

fields.Description: Written for the anniversary of Alessandro Manzoni's death, and criticized as an opera in church dress; the Dies irae returns like a refrain.
fields.Listen: This work opens with muted cellos sinking softly through an A-minor phrase as the chorus murmurs “Requiem aeternam” almost inaudibly.

fields.Description: Verdi fought the Venetian censors, who objected to a king's assassination; the monarch became a duke. The jester finds his own daughter in the sack.
fields.Listen: The famous quartet: four characters singing four different things at once, two outside in the storm and two inside.

fields.Description: Verdi fought the Venetian censors, who objected to a king's assassination; the monarch became a duke. The jester finds his own daughter in the sack.
fields.Listen: The courtiers' “Zitti, zitti, moviamo a vendetta”: a whispered, scurrying male chorus, staccato and hushed, as they abduct the jester's daughter.

fields.Description: Written for London and his most tightly argued symphony, prompted by hearing Brahms's Third and by Czech nationalist feeling.

fields.Clue: Its first movement runs “from dawn to noon on the sea”; its composer wrote most of these three symphonic sketches inland, in Burgundy, and put Hokusai's Great Wave on the score's cover.

Three orchestral pieces, Nuages, Fêtes, and Sirènes, the last adding a wordless female chorus.
fields.Listen: Clarinets and bassoons drift in slow, alternating fifths and thirds, borrowed from Mussorgsky; then the cor anglais sounds a haunting motif.
fields.Clue: Its first piece, Nuages, depicts slow-moving clouds; the second, Fêtes, brings a procession of muted trumpets, and the third, Sirènes, adds a wordless women's chorus.

fields.Description: Three orchestral pieces, Nuages, Fêtes, and Sirènes, the last adding a wordless female chorus.
fields.Listen: Fêtes opens with whirling triplet figures in the strings and woodwinds, animé et très rythmé: a festival in full swing.

fields.Clue: Debussy's only completed opera, an almost word-for-word setting of Maurice Maeterlinck's Symbolist play: Golaud finds a mysterious girl weeping by a spring in the forest, marries her, and kills his half-brother out of jealousy.

fields.Listen: Lever du jour: murmuring flute, clarinet, and harp ripples like a brook, while the low strings rise in a broad D-major sunrise melody and piccolo birdcalls chirp above.
fields.Clue: Its third part opens with a sunrise, the murmuring woodwinds depicting brooks and birds; written for Sergei Diaghilev's Ballets Russes after Longus's pastoral romance, it is its composer's largest score, a “choreographic symphony” with wordless chorus, in which pirates seize the heroine until Pan rescues her.

Three poems by Aloysius Bertrand: the water nymph Ondine, a hanged man on the gallows, and the goblin Scarbo, which Ravel meant to be harder than Balakirev's Islamey.
fields.Listen: Ondine: a shimmering, whispered figuration of rapid repeated chords high in the right hand, in C-sharp major, while the left hand sings the water nymph's melody beneath.

fields.Clue: Prisoners let out into the courtyard sing “O welche Lust, in freier Luft” in this opera, whose heroine disguises herself as a young man to free her husband Florestan; its composer wrote four overtures for it.

fields.Listen: This overture opens with hushed, scurrying strings in C major; then the Turkish percussion (triangle, cymbals, and bass drum) bursts in with the full orchestra.

fields.Description: A Singspiel with spoken dialogue, full of Masonic symbolism, premiered in a suburban Vienna theatre weeks before Mozart's death.
fields.Listen: Papageno's strophic song “Der Vogelfänger bin ich ja”: a jaunty, folk-like tune for baritone, each verse punctuated by his little five-note panpipe scale.
fields.Clue: The bird-catcher Papageno introduces himself in “Der Vogelfänger bin ich ja” in this Singspiel full of Masonic symbolism; Tamino falls for a portrait in “Dies Bildnis ist bezaubernd schön”, and its composer died weeks after its 1791 premiere.

fields.Description: A Singspiel with spoken dialogue, full of Masonic symbolism, premiered in a suburban Vienna theatre weeks before Mozart's death. The Queen of the Night's aria reaches top F.
fields.Listen: Bright, simple, singsong baritone tune accompanied by glockenspiel.

fields.Description: A Singspiel with spoken dialogue, full of Masonic symbolism, premiered in a suburban Vienna theatre weeks before Mozart's death. The Queen of the Night's aria reaches top F.
fields.Listen: Very slow, very low bass solo with male chorus answering; hushed and ceremonial.

fields.Description: A Singspiel with spoken dialogue, full of Masonic symbolism, premiered in a suburban Vienna theatre weeks before Mozart's death.
fields.Listen: This overture opens with three solemn E-flat-major chords, the Masonic “threefold knock”, followed by a hushed, mysterious Adagio.

fields.Description: A Singspiel with spoken dialogue, full of Masonic symbolism, premiered in a suburban Vienna theatre weeks before Mozart's death. The Queen of the Night's aria reaches top F.
fields.Listen: Stammered Pa-pa-pa duet, fast and comic, two voices tripping over each other.

fields.Audio: [sound:Mozart (Die Zauberflote - Queen of the Night 1).mp3][sound:cmc-Mozart (Die Zauberflote Der Holle Rache (Queen of the Night))_n.mp3]
fields.Movement: Act II · “Der Hölle Rache” (Queen of the Night)
fields.Description: A Singspiel with spoken dialogue, full of Masonic symbolism, premiered in a suburban Vienna theatre weeks before Mozart's death.
fields.Listen: The Queen of the Night's revenge aria, “Der Hölle Rache kocht in meinem Herzen” (“Hell's vengeance boils in my heart”), hurled out in furious D minor over agitated strings.

fields.Description: Premiered in Prague in 1787. The Commendatore's statue arrives to trombones and drags the unrepentant Don to hell; the overture was reportedly written the night before.
fields.Listen: The “Champagne Aria”, “Fin ch'han dal vino”: headlong B-flat-major patter for baritone as the hero orders a party, the orchestra racing to keep up.
fields.Clue: Its hero orders a wild party in the “Champagne Aria”, woos Zerlina in “Là ci darem la mano”, and is dragged to hell by the statue of the murdered Commendatore; Leporello's “Catalogue Aria” counts 1,003 conquests in Spain.

fields.Description: Premiered in Prague in 1787. The Commendatore's statue arrives to trombones and drags the unrepentant Don to hell; the overture was reportedly written the night before.
fields.Listen: Shocked, halting ensemble over tremolo strings, immediately after the killing.

fields.Description: Premiered in Prague in 1787. The Commendatore's statue arrives to trombones and drags the unrepentant Don to hell; the overture was reportedly written the night before.
fields.Listen: This overture opens with two hammering D-minor chords and a slow, grim Andante, the music of the stone guest, with syncopated strings and eerie rising and falling scales.

fields.Description: Written in June 1787, a few weeks after his father's death; it parodies incompetent composers and players.
fields.Listen: The opening: a deliberately plodding, four-square F-major tune for two horns and strings, stopping and starting on stock phrases.
fields.Clue: Its horns play wrong notes, its first violin's cadenza loses its way in a whole-tone scale, and its finale ends in a crash of chords in different keys.

fields.Description: A serenade for strings, K. 525, written in 1787 while Mozart was working on Don Giovanni. One of its five original movements is lost.
fields.Listen: This serenade opens with a unison “rocket” in the strings, up and back down a G-major arpeggio (G, D, G, D, G, D, G, B, D), brisk and symmetrical.

fields.Description: A serenade for strings, K. 525, written in 1787 while Mozart was working on Don Giovanni. One of its five original movements is lost.
A serenade for strings, K. 525, written in 1787 while Mozart was working on Don Giovanni. One of its five original movements is lost.
fields.Listen: Very short minuet, sharply accented, with a smooth trio.

fields.Description: A serenade for strings, K. 525, written in 1787 while Mozart was working on Don Giovanni. One of its five original movements is lost.
fields.Listen: Fast chattering rondo, phrases flicking between loud and quiet.

fields.Description: Mozart's first mature opera seria, for Munich: a king vows to sacrifice the first person he meets ashore and it is his son.
fields.Listen: The king's bravura aria “Fuor del mar ho un mar in seno” (“Saved from the sea, I have a sea within my breast”): a D-major tenor line bristling with runs over a stormy orchestra.
fields.Clue: Its Cretan king compares his inner turmoil to the sea in “Fuor del mar”, having vowed to Neptune that he would sacrifice the first person he met ashore, who proves to be his son Idamante; an opera seria written for Munich in 1781.

fields.Description: Mozart's first mature opera seria, for Munich: a king vows to sacrifice the first person he meets ashore and it is his son.
fields.Listen: This overture opens with forceful D-major unison chords and rushing violin scales, broken by sudden quiet turns to the minor.

fields.Description: Mozart's first mature opera seria, for Munich: a king vows to sacrifice the first person he meets ashore and it is his son.

fields.Audio: [sound:Mozart (Le nozze di Figaro - Non piu andrai...).mp3]
fields.Description: After Pierre Beaumarchais's banned play, with the political speech removed to satisfy the censor. Its second act ends in a twenty-minute continuous finale.
fields.Listen: The valet's mock-military send-off to the page, “Non più andrai, farfallone amoroso”: a swaggering C-major march for baritone, later with trumpets and drums.
fields.Clue: Its valet teases the page Cherubino, packed off to the army, in “Non più andrai”, which its composer later quoted in the supper scene of Don Giovanni; after Beaumarchais's banned play, its second act ends in a long continuous finale.

fields.Audio: [sound:Mozart (Le nozze di Figaro - Overture).mp3][sound:cmc-Mozart (Le nozze di Figaro Overture).mp3]
fields.Description: After Pierre Beaumarchais's banned play, with the political speech removed to satisfy the censor. Its second act ends in a twenty-minute continuous finale.
fields.Listen: This overture opens with a whispered, rushing unison figure in the strings and bassoons, circling around D, before the full orchestra bursts in, forte.

fields.Audio: [sound:Mozart (Le nozze di Figaro - Voi, che sapete...).mp3]
fields.Description: After Pierre Beaumarchais's banned play, with the political speech removed to satisfy the censor. Its second act ends in a twenty-minute continuous finale.
fields.Listen: Gentle, slightly breathless mezzo aria over a plucked, guitar-like accompaniment.

fields.Audio: [sound:Mozart (Piano Quintet, mvI).mp3][sound:cmc-Mozart (Quintet for Piano and Winds mvt. I).mp3]

fields.Description: Written in Paris in the summer of 1778, when Mozart's mother died there.
fields.Listen: The opening Allegro maestoso: a march-like A-minor melody in dotted rhythm, high in the right hand, over hammering repeated chords in the left.
fields.Clue: The first of Mozart's two minor-key piano sonatas; its Andante cantabile con espressione is torn by a stormy middle section, and its finale is a breathless Presto in A minor.

fields.Description: Unusually, none of its movements is in sonata form: it opens with a theme and variations and ends with the Rondo alla turca, imitating a janissary band.
fields.Listen: The theme: a graceful A-major Andante grazioso in a lilting 6/8, opening on C-sharp, D, C-sharp in a dotted siciliana rhythm.

fields.Description: Unusually, none of its movements is in sonata form: it opens with a theme and variations and ends with the Rondo alla turca, imitating a janissary band.
Published in 1785 with the Fantasy in C minor, K. 475, as its prelude, and dedicated to his pupil Therese von Trattner.
fields.Listen: The opening: a forte arpeggio rising in octaves, C, E-flat, G, C, E-flat, answered softly, then the same call on the dominant.
fields.Clue: One of only two minor-key piano sonatas by Mozart, often said to anticipate Beethoven's Pathétique in the same key; its middle movement is an Adagio in E-flat.

fields.Audio: [sound:cmc-Mozart (Quintet for Piano and Winds mvt. I).mp3]

fields.Description: Commissioned anonymously by a count who wanted to pass it off as his own. Mozart died at the Lacrimosa; Franz Xaver Süssmayr completed it, and the widow concealed the fact.
Commissioned anonymously by a count who wanted to pass it off as his own. Mozart died at the Lacrimosa; Franz Xaver Süssmayr completed it, and the widow concealed the fact.
fields.Listen: Dark low wind colour — bassoons and basset horns — chorus entering low and staggered, then a lone soprano on Te decet hymnus.

fields.Description: Commissioned anonymously by a count who wanted to pass it off as his own. Mozart died at the Lacrimosa; Franz Xaver Süssmayr completed it, and the widow concealed the fact.
fields.Listen: Brisk double fugue for chorus, ending on a bare unharmonized chord.

fields.Description: Commissioned anonymously by a count who wanted to pass it off as his own. Mozart died at the Lacrimosa; Franz Xaver Süssmayr completed it, and the widow concealed the fact.
fields.Listen: Stabbing dotted chorus entries on the word Rex; collapses to a hushed salva me.

fields.Description: Commissioned anonymously by a count who wanted to pass it off as his own. Mozart died at the Lacrimosa; Franz Xaver Süssmayr completed it, and the widow concealed the fact.
fields.Listen: Bright D major, very brief, running straight into the Osanna fugue.

fields.Description: Commissioned anonymously by a count who wanted to pass it off as his own. Mozart died at the Lacrimosa; Franz Xaver Süssmayr completed it, and the widow concealed the fact.
fields.Listen: Solo trombone duets with the bass soloist, then tenor, alto, and soprano enter in turn and combine.

fields.Description: Completed in November 1784, the fourth of the six quartets dedicated to Haydn.
fields.Listen: The opening: a hunting-horn call in 6/8 in the first violin, B-flat major, over the second violin's echoing horn fifths.
fields.Clue: Its slow movement, in E-flat, is the only Adagio among the six quartets dedicated to Haydn; its nickname comes from its opening, not from Mozart.

fields.Description: The last of the six quartets dedicated to Haydn, finished in January 1785; after its introduction the music is sunny C major.
fields.Listen: The slow introduction: a soft pulsing C in the cello, then the viola's A-flat, the second violin's E-flat, and the first violin's A-natural, clashing chromatically before any key is clear.
fields.Clue: Its slow introduction was attacked by the composer Giuseppe Sarti as full of errors, and early copyists were said to have returned the parts as misprinted.

fields.Description: Made from a serenade Mozart wrote in 1782 for the ennoblement of Sigmund Haffner the Younger in Salzburg, then reworked for Vienna with flutes and clarinets added.
fields.Listen: This symphony opens with a bold unison theme leaping two octaves on D, then a quiet answer, in a festive D major with trumpets and drums.
fields.Clue: Its composer told his father its finale should go as fast as possible; it was reworked as a symphony from a serenade written in 1782 for the ennoblement of a Salzburg family friend, with flutes and clarinets added.

fields.Description: Its slow movement unusually keeps trumpets and timpani; Count Johann Joseph Anton Thun-Hohenstein was Mozart's host for its premiere.
fields.Listen: The slow introduction: a forte unison C in dotted rhythm, then soft, searching phrases in the strings that turn toward minor.
fields.Clue: Mozart wrote it in about four days in 1783 for a concert in an Upper Austrian city where he stopped with Constanze on the way home from Salzburg, having brought no symphony with him.

fields.Description: The first of three symphonies written in about six weeks in the summer of 1788, with no known commission or performance in Mozart's lifetime.
fields.Listen: The slow introduction: majestic E-flat chords in dotted rhythms with timpani, against sweeping descending scales in the violins.
fields.Clue: Of his last three symphonies, it alone has clarinets and no oboes, and the trio of its minuet is a Ländler for the clarinets.

fields.Description: One of only two symphonies he wrote in a minor key, both in G minor; he later revised it to add clarinets.
fields.Listen: This symphony opens with the violas' throbbing accompaniment; then the violins sigh the agitated G-minor theme: E-flat, D, D; E-flat, D, D; E-flat, D, D, up to B-flat.
fields.Clue: One of only two symphonies its composer wrote in a minor key, both in G minor; it was revised to add clarinets, and its finale's development opens with a unison leap through eleven of the twelve pitches.

fields.Description: One of only two symphonies he wrote in a minor key, both in G minor; he later revised it to add clarinets.
fields.Listen: The Andante: a gentle E-flat-major theme in 6/8 built on repeated notes, the strings entering one after another.

fields.Description: One of only two he wrote in a minor key, opening without any introduction on a whispered viola accompaniment before the tune.
One of only two he wrote in a minor key, opening without any introduction on a whispered viola accompaniment before the tune.
Mozart's last symphony, the third he wrote in the summer of 1788. Its finale combines five themes in fugal counterpoint at once; the nickname probably came from Johann Peter Salomon.
fields.Listen: This symphony opens with a loud unison C and a triplet run from G up to C, answered by a quiet, lyrical phrase, with trumpets and drums.
fields.Clue: Its composer's last symphony, the third he wrote in the summer of 1788; its finale combines five themes, including the four-note C, D, F, E, in fugal counterpoint, and its nickname probably came from Johann Peter Salomon.

fields.Audio: [sound:Gluck (Iphiegnie en Aulide - Jupiter, lance la foundre).mp3]
[sound:Gluck (Orfeu ed Euridice - Che faro senza Euridice_)_n.mp3]
fields.Description: Gluck's first “reform” opera, with the librettist Ranieri de' Calzabigi, stripping away da capo display in favour of the drama; Orfeo was written for the castrato Gaetano Guadagni.
fields.Listen: The hero's lament, a calm C-major melody, “Che farò senza Euridice? Dove andrò senza il mio ben?”, that returns like a rondo refrain.
fields.Clue: After he looks back and loses his wife a second time, its hero, written for the castrato Gaetano Guadagni, sings a lament that Eduard Hanslick said would suit “I have found her” as well as “I have lost her”; its composer's first “reform” opera, with Ranieri de' Calzabigi.

fields.Description: Gluck's first “reform” opera, with the librettist Ranieri de' Calzabigi, stripping away da capo display in favour of the drama; Orfeo was written for the castrato Gaetano Guadagni.
fields.Listen: The heroine's agitated aria “Che fiero momento”: urgent soprano phrases over restless, throbbing strings as she pleads with her husband, who will not look at her.

fields.Description: A treatise, not a piece: Guido's guide to teaching chant and composing organum, one of the most copied music textbooks of the Middle Ages. His letter Epistola de ignoto cantu introduced the syllables ut, re, mi, fa, sol, and la, taken from the hymn Ut queant laxis.
fields.Clue: A treatise, not a piece: an eleventh-century Benedictine monk's guide to teaching chant and composing organum, one of the most copied music textbooks of the Middle Ages; its author's letter Epistola de ignoto cantu introduced the syllables ut, re, mi, fa, sol, and la, from the hymn “Ut queant laxis”.

fields.Description: A morality play with music, the earliest surviving of its kind, in which the Virtues sing and only the Devil is forbidden music and must shout.
fields.Listen: A single unaccompanied female voice in plainchant, its line arcing through wide leaps and long melismas with no harmony at all.
fields.Clue: The earliest surviving morality play with music, by a Benedictine abbess: the Virtues and the Soul sing, and only the Devil is denied music and must shout his lines.

fields.Description: The Notre Dame repertory of organum attributed to Léonin and revised by Pérotin, the foundation of Western polyphonic notation.
fields.Listen: Two voices: plainchant held in very long drones beneath one florid upper line — organum, the oldest polyphony in the deck.

fields.Work: Le Jeu de Robin et de Marion
fields.Audio: [sound:Adam de la Halle (Le Jeu de Robin et de Marion).mp3]
fields.Description: The earliest surviving French secular play with music, a shepherdess resisting a knight, written by a trouvère at the Angevin court in Naples.
fields.Listen: Medieval monophonic song and dance with spoken dialogue and repeated refrains; one line, no harmony.

fields.Description: The earliest complete polyphonic Mass Ordinary by a single identified composer, written for Reims Cathedral, where Machaut endowed a weekly performance.
fields.Listen: Four voices in angular fourteenth-century polyphony, the tenor built on a slow chant line in repeating rhythmic patterns, with bare fifths and octaves at the cadences.
fields.Clue: The earliest complete polyphonic setting of the Mass Ordinary by a single identified composer, probably for a weekly Saturday Mass he and his brother endowed at Reims Cathedral; its Gloria and Credo are syllabic, and its other movements are isorhythmic.

fields.Description: A mass on the most-set secular tune of the Renaissance, a soldier's song used by more than forty composers.
fields.Listen: Four voices in flowing fifteenth-century polyphony, the tenor carrying a secular tune in long notes beneath the others.
fields.Clue: Built on the most-set secular tune of the Renaissance, a soldier's song used by more than forty composers; in the last Agnus Dei, following a riddle about a crab, the tenor sings the tune backwards in full values, then forwards at half length.

fields.Description: Josquin's last mass, built throughout on a plainchant hymn rather than quoting it in one voice: paraphrase technique taken to its conclusion.
fields.Listen: Four unaccompanied voices in Phrygian-mode imitation on E, each phrase of the plainchant hymn tune passed from voice to voice.
fields.Clue: Its composer's last mass paraphrases Thomas Aquinas's Corpus Christi hymn in all four voices throughout, rather than holding it in the tenor; this Franco-Flemish composer also wrote two masses on “L'homme armé”.

fields.Description: A motet for forty voices, probably written to answer an Italian forty-part work heard in London.
fields.Listen: The voices enter one by one in imitation, passing the opening phrase around the choirs in a slowly widening wave of sound, until all sing together.
fields.Clue: A motet for forty voices in eight choirs of five, probably written to answer a forty-part work by Alessandro Striggio heard in London, and perhaps first sung at Arundel House or Nonsuch Palace; its Latin text means “I have never put my hope in any other”.

fields.Description: Twenty-nine motets on the Song of Songs, dedicated to Pope Gregory XIII with an apology for having set secular love poetry earlier in his career.
fields.Listen: Unaccompanied Latin polyphony, smooth stepwise lines, every dissonance resolved — the model of Counter-Reformation clarity.

fields.Description: Byrd's most expansive Anglican setting, for two five-part choirs, written by a lifelong Catholic who also composed Latin masses for recusant worship.
fields.Listen: Anglican service music in English, full choir in expansive counterpoint, far grander than his short services.

fields.Description: An English madrigal of studied melancholy, its refrain of fa-la-la set against the grief of the text rather than lightening it.
fields.Listen: English madrigal: sharp dissonance and word-painting, with a sudden bright fa-la-la refrain against the gloom.

fields.Description: One of the first printed works to mark its dynamics and to specify which instruments play, written for the antiphonal galleries of St Mark's, Venice.
fields.Listen: Two spaced brass-and-viol choirs answering each other across a church, with the words piano and forte printed in the parts — written dynamics, apparently for the first time.

fields.Description: Seven pavans for five viols and lute, published in 1604, each beginning with the falling “tear” motif of Dowland's song “Flow, my tears”. He punned on his own name: Semper Dowland semper dolens (“always Dowland, always doleful”).
fields.Listen: The viol consort and lute open with the falling four-note “tear” motif (long A, G, F, long E) of the song “Flow, my tears”.
fields.Clue: Seven pavans for five viols and lute, published in 1604, each beginning with the falling “tear” motif of Dowland's song “Flow, my tears”. He punned on his own name: Semper Dowland semper dolens (“always Dowland, always doleful”).

fields.Description: The earliest opera to survive complete, performed in Florence in 1600 for a Medici wedding. Peri sang Orpheus, and the ending was changed to a happy one for the occasion.
fields.Listen: The Prologue: La Tragedia sings her verses in a simple, declamatory line over sparse sustained continuo, following the rhythm of speech, each stanza framed by a short ritornello.
fields.Clue: Its Prologue is sung by La Tragedia; the earliest opera to survive complete, it was performed in Florence in 1600 for the wedding of Henry IV and Marie de' Medici, with its composer singing Orfeo and a happy ending in which the hero brings his wife back.

fields.Movement: Act II · “Thanks to these lonesome vales”
fields.Description: Purcell's only true opera, with a libretto by Nahum Tate, perhaps first given at a girls' school in Chelsea.
fields.Listen: Belinda's “Thanks to these lonesome vales”: a bright soprano air in D minor over a short repeating ground bass, as the royal hunt rests in a grove.
fields.Clue: Belinda sings “Thanks to these lonesome vales” in its grove scene; after her Trojan lover, tricked by a sorceress's false Mercury, sails away, the Carthaginian queen sings “When I am laid in earth” over a descending chromatic ground. Libretto by Nahum Tate.

fields.Description: Twelve concertos published in 1714, after Corelli's death, that set the model for the concerto grosso; No. 8 is the “Christmas” Concerto.
fields.Listen: Stately Italian string writing in which a small group of soloists alternates with the full string band.
fields.Clue: Twelve concertos published in 1714 after their composer's death, setting a concertino of two violins and cello against the ripieno; No. 8, “made for Christmas night”, ends with a 12/8 Pastorale.

fields.Description: Over two hundred harpsichord pieces grouped into ordres and given descriptive titles rather than dance names; Couperin was called le Grand.
fields.Listen: Solo harpsichord in the French court style: a short, dance-like piece thick with agréments (trills, mordents, and slides).
fields.Clue: Over two hundred harpsichord pieces grouped into twenty-seven ordres and given fanciful titles such as Les Barricades mystérieuses rather than dance names; its composer was called “le Grand”.

fields.Description: Three suites played by musicians on a barge following George I up the Thames in 1717; the king is said to have had them repeated three times.
fields.Listen: Bright F-major Baroque dance music in which the horns echo the strings, written to be played outdoors.

fields.Description: One of over 550 single-movement keyboard sonatas Domenico Scarlatti wrote in Spain for Queen Maria Barbara, full of hand-crossing and guitar imitations; Ralph Kirkpatrick catalogued them with K numbers.
fields.Listen: A single-movement harpsichord sonata in F major: a lilting melody over a steady bass, in two halves, each repeated.
fields.Clue: Over 550 single-movement keyboard pieces, mostly in two repeated halves, written in Spain for Queen Maria Barbara and full of hand-crossing and guitar imitations; thirty were published as Essercizi in 1738, and Ralph Kirkpatrick catalogued them with K numbers.

fields.Description: Three collections of “table music” published by subscription in 1733, each running from an overture-suite through quartet, concerto, trio, and solo sonata to a conclusion; Handel was among the subscribers.
fields.Listen: Brisk, festive Baroque ensemble music: strings and winds trading lively counterpoint over harpsichord continuo.
fields.Clue: Three collections of “table music” published by subscription in 1733, each running from an overture-suite through quartet, concerto, trio, and solo sonata to a closing “Conclusion”, meant to accompany banquets; Handel was among the subscribers.

fields.Description: Fourteen fugues and four canons on one subject, left unfinished at Bach's death; the last fugue breaks off soon after the B–A–C–H motif enters.
fields.Listen: A fugue on this work's single D-minor subject (D, A, F, D, C-sharp, D, E, F), worked in strict four-voice counterpoint.
fields.Clue: Fourteen contrapuncti and four canons on one D-minor subject, left unfinished at its composer's death; the last fugue breaks off soon after a motif spelling his own name (B-flat, A, C, B-natural) enters.

fields.Description: From the last years of Johann Stamitz, founder of the Mannheim school, whose orchestra was famous for the long crescendo and the rising “Mannheim rocket” that Mozart and Beethoven inherited.
fields.Listen: A bright E-flat Mannheim symphony: hammered opening chords, then a long orchestral crescendo over tremolo strings, with abrupt loud–soft contrasts.
fields.Clue: From the last years of the founder of the Mannheim school, whose orchestra was famous for the long crescendo and the rising “Mannheim rocket” that Mozart and Beethoven inherited.

fields.Description: The “Eroica”. Beethoven dedicated it to Napoleon then scratched the title out when he declared himself emperor. Twice the usual length, with a funeral march second.
The touchstone of violin virtuosity; the theme of No. 24 has been varied by Brahms, Liszt, Rachmaninoff, and Witold Lutosławski.
fields.Listen: Unaccompanied violin: rapid E-major arpeggios bounced across all four strings with ricochet bowing.
fields.Clue: Twenty-four unaccompanied pieces published as its composer's Op. 1; No. 9 imitates flutes and horns as “The Hunt”, No. 13 is nicknamed “The Devil's Laughter”, and the A-minor theme of No. 24 was varied by Brahms, Liszt, Rachmaninoff, and Witold Lutosławski.

fields.Description: The founding German Romantic opera: the huntsman Max casts magic bullets in the Wolf's Glen to win a shooting contest and Agathe's hand. The Wolf's Glen scene is the model of melodrama.
fields.Listen: The overture's slow introduction: after a hushed opening, four horns sing a calm, hymn-like chorale over quiet strings.
fields.Clue: The founding German Romantic opera, after a tale in Johann Apel's book of ghost stories: the huntsman Max casts magic bullets with Caspar in the Wolf's Glen to win a shooting contest and Agathe's hand, the last bullet belonging to the devil Samiel; its overture opens with a horn quartet.

fields.Description: Twenty-four short pieces, one in every major and minor key in circle-of-fifths order, finished in Majorca; No. 15 is the “Raindrop”.
fields.Listen: A short piano piece built entirely from one figure and one mood, like each of the set's twenty-four.
fields.Clue: Twenty-four short piano pieces, one in every major and minor key around the circle of fifths, finished in Majorca; Hans von Bülow called the E-minor one “Suffocation”, and No. 15's repeated A-flat suggests falling rain.

fields.Description: The “Spring”, sketched in four days in 1841 after a poem about spring blooming in the valley; Mendelssohn conducted the premiere.
Written as a choral piece with mocking words after Austria's defeat at Königgrätz; the orchestral version became Austria's unofficial anthem.

fields.Movement: Die Walküre, Act III · Ride of the Valkyries
fields.Description: Four operas on the curse of a ring forged from the Rhine gold, woven from leitmotifs; the whole cycle was first staged at Wagner's Bayreuth Festspielhaus in 1876.
fields.Listen: The Ride of the Valkyries: swirling string trills and shrieking woodwinds, then horns and trombones hammer out the galloping B-minor Valkyrie theme.
fields.Clue: Four operas on the curse of a gold band forged from the Rhine gold, woven from over sixty leitmotifs and first staged complete at its composer's Bayreuth Festspielhaus in 1876; it calls for a new family of tubas, and its second opera's last act opens with a famous ride.

fields.Description: A symphony in six songs for tenor and alto on Chinese poems in Hans Bethge's German versions; Mahler avoided numbering it as his Ninth, and it ends on the repeated word “ewig”.
fields.Listen: Horns ring out over the full orchestra in a brief, bright outburst that falls away.
fields.Clue: A symphony in six songs for tenor and alto on Chinese poems in Hans Bethge's German versions; its composer avoided numbering it as his Ninth, and its last song, “Der Abschied”, takes half an hour and ends on the repeated word “ewig”.

fields.Description: The Czech national comic opera: Mařenka is promised to the simple-minded Vašek, but her beloved Jeník outwits the marriage broker Kecal.
fields.Listen: This overture opens with a bright F-major burst for the full orchestra; then the strings race off in a breathless fugato, entering one after another in perpetual motion.
fields.Clue: The Czech national comic opera: Mařenka is promised to the stammering Vašek, but her beloved Jeník takes the marriage broker Kecal's three hundred gulden on condition that she marry “Tobias Micha's son”, which he turns out to be; its third act has a furiant and a comedians' dance.

fields.Description: Omits the Dies irae except its closing Pie Jesu, and ends with In Paradisum. Fauré said he wrote it “for pleasure” and saw death as a happy deliverance rather than a terror; it has been called a lullaby of death.
fields.Listen: A hushed choir with organ and low strings in gentle, consoling chords, setting the Latin rite for the dead without drama.
fields.Clue: Its soprano sings the Pie Jesu, the only part of the Dies irae it sets, and its baritone the Libera me; it ends with In Paradisum from the burial service, and its composer saw death as “a happy deliverance”, not a terror.

fields.Description: Ten short piano pieces by an American composer; the first, To a Wild Rose, was nearly thrown away and became the best-known American piano miniature.
fields.Listen: Short, intimate Romantic piano writing: a simple, song-like melody over gentle chords, in a minor key.
fields.Clue: Ten short piano pieces named for a farm in Peterborough, New Hampshire, later the site of an artists' colony; the first, To a Wild Rose, was rescued from the wastebasket by its composer's wife, and others include To a Water-Lily and By a Meadow Brook.

fields.Description: A setting of John Henry Newman's poem following a soul from its deathbed to judgment; a disastrous 1900 Birmingham premiere did not stop it becoming an English choral staple.
fields.Listen: The orchestral Prelude: a hushed, winding theme in the muted violas and woodwinds, then sighing chromatic motifs full of Wagnerian yearning.
fields.Clue: Its tenor hero opens “Jesu, Maria – I am near to death”; after his death his Soul is led to judgment by an Angel, a mezzo-soprano, and at the climax the score demands that “for one moment must every instrument exert its fullest force” as he glimpses God. It sets John Henry Newman's poem, and its 1900 Birmingham premiere was a disaster.

fields.Description: Twelve piano pieces in four books evoking Spanish places, of legendary difficulty. Debussy said no music had ever achieved such diverse impressions.
fields.Listen: Dense solo piano writing in Spanish dance rhythms: the hands interlock in guitar-like strummed chords and flamenco ornaments.
fields.Clue: Twelve piano pieces in four books that open with Evocación and include Triana and El Albaicín; Alicia de Larrocha made the first complete recording, and Ravel was asked to orchestrate it for Ida Rubinstein.

fields.Audio: [sound:Manuel de Falla (El sombrero de tres picos).mp3]
fields.Description: A Sergei Diaghilev ballet with sets and costumes by Picasso, on an Andalusian tale of a magistrate pursuing a miller's wife. Ends with a jota.
fields.Listen: Spanish dance rhythms in brilliant, hard-edged orchestral writing: brassy fanfares, castanets, and stamping accents.
fields.Clue: A Sergei Diaghilev ballet with sets and costumes by Picasso, after Pedro Antonio de Alarcón's tale of a magistrate who pursues a miller's wife; the miller dances a farruca, the “fate” knock of Beethoven's Fifth sounds at his arrest, and it ends with a jota as the magistrate's effigy is tossed in a blanket.

fields.Description: Smyth's Cornish opera about villagers who lure ships onto rocks. She was also a suffragette who conducted The March of the Women with a toothbrush from a prison window.
fields.Listen: Big late-Romantic sea music: surging strings and a brass chorale — the Cornish coast in sound.

fields.Description: Twenty-one poems by Albert Giraud, in German translation, in three groups of seven; its ensemble of flute, clarinet, violin, cello, and piano is now called a “Pierrot ensemble”.
fields.Listen: “Gebet an Pierrot” (“Prayer to Pierrot”): over clarinet and piano alone, the reciter cries in Sprechstimme “Pierrot! Mein Lachen hab ich verlernt!” (“I have forgotten how to laugh!”).
fields.Clue: Twenty-one poems by Albert Giraud in German translation, in three groups of seven, for a reciter in Sprechstimme and five players (flute, clarinet, violin, cello, and piano) who double on piccolo, bass clarinet, and viola; in its ninth song the reciter begs for lost laughter.

fields.Description: Its 1913 Paris premiere caused a riot, with Vaslav Nijinsky shouting counts from the wings. A pagan sacrifice, ending with the chosen maiden dancing herself to death.
fields.Listen: Dissonant, folk-like woodwind fragments over irregular, pounding accents in a huge orchestra.

fields.Description: Dedicated to the Czechoslovak armed forces and scored with fourteen trumpets among its extra brass; its movements portray places in his home city of Brno.
fields.Listen: A tender, slow, nostalgic melody in the muted strings and harp.
fields.Clue: Its third movement portrays the Queen's Monastery in its composer's home city of Brno; first written for a Sokol gymnastics festival and dedicated to the Czechoslovak armed forces, it opens with a fanfare for an extra band of trumpets, bass trumpets, and tenor tubas over timpani.

fields.Description: Written after years transcribing Balinese gamelan, it sets a nuclear gamelan of two pianos and percussion inside a Western orchestra.
fields.Listen: Two pianos, xylophone, and bells imitating a Balinese gamelan: interlocking fast ostinati, cyclic and metallic.

fields.Description: Written after Pravda attacked him, and subtitled a Soviet artist's reply to just criticism. Whether the triumphant ending is sincere is still argued.
fields.Listen: This symphony opens with a jagged canon between the low strings and the violins, leaping by sixths in a dotted rhythm in D minor; then the violins sing a long, bleak melody.
fields.Clue: Written after Pravda attacked its composer's opera, and subtitled “a Soviet artist's creative response to just criticism”; it opens with a canon on leaping sixths in D minor, and its D-major finale repeats the note A over and over, a triumph whose sincerity is still argued.

fields.Description: Nine suites fusing Baroque counterpoint with Brazilian folk idiom; No. 5's Aria is the most famous thing Villa-Lobos wrote.
fields.Listen: The Aria (Cantilena) of No. 5: over cellos plucking like guitars, the soprano sings a long, wordless A-minor vocalise.
fields.Clue: Nine suites fusing Baroque counterpoint with Brazilian folk idiom in homage to Bach; No. 5, for soprano and eight cellos, opens with a wordless vocalise, and No. 2's toccata depicts “The Little Train of the Caipira”.

fields.Audio: [sound:Olivier Messiaen (Quartet for the End of Time).mp3]
fields.Description: Composed in a German prisoner-of-war camp and first played there in January 1941, for the only instruments at hand: violin, clarinet, cello, and piano.
fields.Listen: Birdsong-like flourishes and luminous, static harmonies from the four players.
fields.Clue: Composed in the prisoner-of-war camp Stalag VIII-A at Görlitz and first played there in January 1941 for the only instruments at hand (violin, clarinet, cello, and piano); inspired by the angel of Revelation, its third movement, Abîme des oiseaux, is for solo clarinet.

fields.Description: After George Crabbe's poem The Borough, about a Suffolk fisherman suspected in the deaths of his apprentices; its Four Sea Interludes are often played on their own. The 1945 premiere revived English opera.
fields.Listen: The first interlude, Dawn: violins and flutes in a high, thin unison line over rippling harp, clarinet, and viola arpeggios, with swelling brass chords like breaking waves.
fields.Clue: Its Four Sea Interludes (Dawn, Sunday Morning, Moonlight, and Storm) are often played on their own; after George Crabbe's poem The Borough, it ends with the title fisherman rowing out to sink his boat.

fields.Description: A founding work of musique concrète, assembled from recorded sounds of a man breathing, walking, humming, and shouting rather than from instruments.
fields.Listen: No instruments at all: recorded breathing, footsteps, and voice, cut and spliced on tape — musique concrète.

fields.Description: Three movements of silence for any instrument, premiered by David Tudor in 1952 at Woodstock, New York. The point is the ambient sound of the room; Cage said there is no such thing as silence.
fields.Listen: Silence: the performer plays nothing, so what you hear is the room around you.
fields.Clue: Three movements of silence for any instrument, premiered by David Tudor in 1952 at Woodstock, New York. The point is the ambient sound of the room; Cage said there is no such thing as silence.

fields.Description: Premiered in Cologne in 1958 under Stockhausen, Bruno Maderna, and Pierre Boulez; its tempi are derived from the overtone series.
fields.Listen: Dense, pointillist orchestral writing in which bursts of sound pass between groups of players, each moving at its own tempo.
fields.Clue: For three orchestras placed around the audience on three sides, each with its own conductor and tempo, so that chords swing from one to another; premiered in Cologne in 1958 under its composer, Bruno Maderna, and Pierre Boulez.

fields.Description: Xenakis treated the strings as a mass of particles moving by statistical law, plotting glissandi from the kinetic theory of gases.
fields.Listen: Masses of string glissandi sliding at different speeds, with col legno taps and knocks on the instruments' bodies: a statistical cloud of sound rather than melody.
fields.Clue: Its composer treated forty-six strings as a mass of particles moving by statistical law, plotting their glissandi from the kinetic theory of gases and the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution; its title means “actions through probabilities”, and Hermann Scherchen premiered it in Munich in 1957.

fields.Audio: [sound:Krzysztof Penderecki (Threnody for the Victims of Hiroshima).mp3]
fields.Description: Penderecki's breakthrough, first titled by its duration; he renamed it as a dedication after hearing it played, and it won a UNESCO prize in 1961.
fields.Listen: Fifty-two strings shriek in dense quarter-tone clusters at the top of their range, with glissandi and scraping, percussive effects behind the bridge: an abstract wail rather than melody.
fields.Clue: Written in 1960 for fifty-two strings under the abstract title 8'37", its duration, it was renamed in memory of those killed by the atomic bomb; its graphic score calls for quarter-tone clusters, playing between the bridge and tailpiece, and the highest possible note on each instrument.

fields.Description: Fifty-three short figures that any number of players repeat at their own pace over a steady pulse of Cs on the piano; its 1964 premiere launched minimalism.
fields.Listen: The opening cells: the players repeat a short figure leaning on E, with grace notes from C, overlapping in shifting canons over the piano's pulse on high C.
fields.Clue: Fifty-three short figures that any number of players repeat as they choose, staying within a few cells of one another; its 1964 San Francisco premiere launched minimalism, and Steve Reich suggested its steady pulse.

fields.Description: Commissioned by the New York Philharmonic for its 125th anniversary and premiered in 1967 under Seiji Ozawa.
fields.Listen: A Japanese shakuhachi and biwa set against a Western orchestra: breathy, sliding flute attacks and snapping plucked chords amid long silences.
fields.Clue: Commissioned by the New York Philharmonic for its 125th anniversary and premiered in 1967 under Seiji Ozawa, it sets a shakuhachi and a biwa against the orchestra in eleven sections, or variations, the two sound worlds never blending.

fields.Audio: [sound:Peter Maxwell Davies (Eight Songs for a Mad King).mp3]

fields.Description: A four-and-a-half-hour opera by Philip Glass and Robert Wilson with no plot, linked by five “Knee Plays”; the text is numbers, solfège syllables, and spoken fragments.
fields.Listen: Hypnotic, endlessly repeating arpeggio patterns, built up and varied in small additive steps.
fields.Clue: Its closing Knee Play sets a bus driver's tale of two lovers on a park bench; a four-and-a-half-hour opera made with Robert Wilson that has no plot, its text is numbers, solfège syllables, and poems by Christopher Knowles, and its title character is a solo violinist.

fields.Description: A vast site-specific work for hundreds of performers; R. Murray Schafer coined the term soundscape and founded the World Soundscape Project.
fields.Listen: Hundreds of performers distributed through and around the hall — whispering, processions, and antiphonal choirs in space.

fields.Description: Three books of fiendish piano études shaped by Conlon Nancarrow's player-piano rhythms and African polyrhythm; titles include Désordre and L'escalier du diable.
fields.Listen: Fast, glittering piano patterns in overlapping, out-of-phase rhythms that throw up accented melodies.
fields.Clue: Three books of fiendish piano pieces shaped by Conlon Nancarrow's player-piano rhythms and African polyrhythm; in Désordre, the right hand plays only white keys and the left only black, and L'escalier du diable climbs the keyboard endlessly.

fields.Description: Higdon wrote it after her brother's death; it moves toward a passage of Chinese reflex balls and ends with the players ringing them. One of the most performed American orchestral works.
fields.Listen: Shimmering orchestral washes, bells, and rubbed crystal glasses, a flute then a clarinet solo emerging; consonant and slow-moving.
