fields.Description: A slow choral work in Whitacre's close-harmony style, built almost entirely from one word.
fields.Listen: Unaccompanied chorus in dense, slowly shifting close harmony on a single word; clusters that resolve only gradually.

fields.Description: Written for the Venetian girls' orphanage where Vivaldi taught, lost until the 1920s and now among the most performed Baroque choral works.
Twelve concertos for one, two, and four violins, published in Amsterdam in 1711; they made Vivaldi famous across Europe, and Bach arranged several for keyboard.
fields.Listen: Brilliant A-minor string ritornellos, with the violins trading virtuoso solos over harpsichord continuo.
fields.Clue: Twelve concertos for one, two, and four violins, published in Amsterdam in 1711 as its composer's Op. 3; they made him famous across Europe, Bach arranged several for keyboard, and the title means “harmonic inspiration”.

fields.Description: Assembled late in Bach's life, largely from earlier music, it is a Lutheran composer's complete setting of the Catholic Ordinary; it was never performed complete in his lifetime.
fields.Listen: A five-part chorus over full Baroque orchestra with trumpets and timpani, the voices entering in dense imitative counterpoint.
fields.Clue: Its Crucifixus is a passacaglia over a chromatic descending bass heard thirteen times, recycled from the cantata Weinen, Klagen, Sorgen, Zagen; its Lutheran composer never heard this Catholic setting performed complete.

fields.Description: An aria and thirty variations, every third a canon at a widening interval, closing with a quodlibet of popular tunes before the aria returns.
fields.Listen: Keyboard counterpoint over the slow-moving ground bass (G, F-sharp, E, D, B, C, D, G) on which every one of this work's thirty variations is built.
fields.Clue: An aria and thirty variations on its bass line, every third variation a canon at a widening interval, ending with a quodlibet on popular songs; legend says it was written for the insomniac Count Keyserlingk.

fields.Description: Written on a theme that Frederick the Great gave Bach at Potsdam in 1747; it contains two ricercars, ten canons, and a trio sonata with flute for the flute-playing king.
fields.Listen: The King's Theme (thema regium): a C-minor subject that climbs an arpeggio, leaps down a diminished seventh, and slides back chromatically, worked in strict counterpoint.
fields.Clue: Written on a theme Frederick the Great played for its composer at Potsdam in 1747; it contains a six-voice ricercar, a crab canon, and a trio sonata with flute for the flute-playing king.

fields.Description: A comic secular cantata first performed at Zimmermann's coffee house in Leipzig: a father tries to cure his daughter Lieschen of her coffee habit.
fields.Listen: From this secular cantata: lively Baroque arias for a bass father and a soprano daughter over strings and continuo, introduced by a tenor narrator.
fields.Clue: In this comic secular work, first given at Zimmermann's café in Leipzig, the father Schlendrian (“stick-in-the-mud”) threatens to forbid his daughter Lieschen a husband unless she gives up her favourite drink.

fields.Description: Handel's most successful opera for London, on Caesar and Cleopatra in Egypt; the castrato Senesino created Caesar, and Cleopatra seduces him with the aria “V'adoro, pupille”.
fields.Listen: This opera opens with a French overture in stately dotted rhythms.
fields.Clue: Its composer's most successful London opera: the castrato Senesino created its Roman hero, who rages “Empio, dirò, tu sei” when handed his rival Pompey's head, and the Egyptian queen seduces him with “V'adoro, pupille” and laments in “Piangerò la sorte mia”.

fields.Movement: mvt. II · Kräftig bewegt, doch nicht zu schnell
fields.Description: Mahler first called it a tone poem and briefly titled it after Jean Paul's novel Titan. Its third movement turns Frère Jacques into a minor-key funeral march led by a solo double bass, said to follow a woodcut of animals burying a hunter; the gentle Blumine movement was cut after early performances.
fields.Listen: This scherzo opens with the low strings stamping out a rocking octave figure before the woodwinds and violins strike up a rustic A-major Ländler.
fields.Clue: Its second movement is a stamping A-major Ländler, and its third turns “Frère Jacques” into a minor-key funeral march led by a solo double bass; its composer first called it a tone poem, briefly named it after a Jean Paul novel, and cut its gentle Blumine movement.

fields.Description: Mahler found its ending at Hans von Bülow's funeral on hearing Friedrich Klopstock's hymn “Aufersteh'n”. The first movement began as a separate tone poem, Totenfeier.
fields.Listen: After a hushed brass chorale, the alto sings “Der Mensch liegt in größter Not” (“Man lies in direst need”) in a simple, hymn-like D-flat-major line.
fields.Clue: Its fourth movement, “Urlicht”, sets a Wunderhorn poem for alto beginning “O Röschen rot!”; its composer found its ending at Hans von Bülow's funeral on hearing Friedrich Klopstock's hymn “Aufersteh'n”, and its first movement began as the tone poem Totenfeier.

fields.Description: The lightest of Mahler's symphonies: the finale sets a Wunderhorn song that describes heaven through a child's eyes, and the scherzo's solo violin is tuned a tone high to play Death's fiddle.
fields.Listen: The slow movement's coda: the full orchestra suddenly blazes into E major, horns and timpani pounding, before fading back to calm.
fields.Clue: Its slow movement's coda opens a sudden vision of heaven, in the key in which its finale ends: a Wunderhorn song for soprano describing heaven through a child's eyes. In its scherzo, a solo violin tuned a tone high plays Death's fiddle.

fields.Description: Premiered in Munich in 1910 with over a thousand performers, hence its nickname; its second part sets the closing scene of Goethe's Faust.
fields.Listen: Organ, massed choirs, and a huge orchestra in blazing E-flat major.
fields.Clue: Scored for eight soloists, double chorus, boys' choir, and an enormous orchestra, and premiered in Munich in 1910; its first part sets the Pentecost hymn Veni, creator spiritus, and its second sets the closing scene of Goethe's Faust.

fields.Description: His last completed symphony, ending with an adagio that dies away to nothing; Alban Berg heard it as a farewell.
fields.Listen: This symphony opens hesitantly: a halting, irregular rhythm in the cellos and horn, a tolling harp, then a sighing two-note figure (F-sharp, E) in the violins, here in Bruno Walter's 1938 Vienna recording.
fields.Clue: Its first movement opens with a halting rhythm that Leonard Bernstein heard as its composer's irregular heartbeat; his last completed symphony, it has a Rondo-Burleske third movement and ends with an Adagio that dies away to nothing, marked ersterbend.

fields.Description: Five songs on Friedrich Rückert's poems on the deaths of his children; Mahler's own elder daughter died a few years after he wrote them.
fields.Listen: Spare, chamber-like scoring, with bleak woodwind lines around a restrained, grieving voice.
fields.Clue: Five songs chosen from over four hundred poems that Friedrich Rückert wrote after two of his children died; the first opens “Nun will die Sonn' so hell aufgeh'n” (“Now the sun will rise as brightly”), and its composer's own elder daughter died a few years after he wrote them.

fields.Description: Bruckner gave it its nickname himself, and the scherzo of the 1878 revision is a hunting scene.
fields.Listen: Bruckner's sound: horn calls and string tremolos building in great terraced waves to blazing brass.
fields.Clue: Its composer gave it its nickname himself; it opens with a solo horn call over hushed string tremolo, and the scherzo of the 1878 revision is a hunting scene.

fields.Description: Bruckner called it the pride of his life and suggested it as a finale for his unfinished Ninth Symphony.
fields.Listen: This piece opens with the strings pounding a repeated C-major figure while the choir declaims its Latin hymn of praise in bold unison, brass and organ blazing.
fields.Clue: Its composer called it the pride of his life and suggested it as a finale for his unfinished Ninth Symphony; Mahler crossed out the scoring on his copy and wrote “for tongues of angels, the blessed, tormented hearts, and souls purified by fire”.

fields.Description: A Viennese comedy set in the 1740s with anachronistic waltzes, ending in a trio for three women's voices as the Marschallin gives up her young lover Octavian to Sophie.
fields.Listen: The Presentation of the Rose: shimmering high chords on celesta, flutes, and harps for the silver rose, as the young envoy begins “Mir ist die Ehre widerfahren”.
fields.Clue: A Viennese comedy set in the 1740s with anachronistic waltzes: Octavian, a mezzo-soprano trouser role, presents a silver rose to Sophie on behalf of the boorish Baron Ochs, and the Marschallin gives her young lover up to Sophie in a closing trio for three women's voices.

fields.Description: After Wilde. The Dance of the Seven Veils precedes Salome singing to the Baptist's severed head; Mahler could not get it past the Vienna censor.
fields.Listen: A brief, tense vocal phrase of foreboding over the orchestra, which then sinks to a hushed, eerie murmur.
fields.Clue: After Oscar Wilde's play in Hedwig Lachmann's translation: a princess performs the Dance of the Seven Veils for her stepfather Herod, then sings to the Baptist's severed head before Herod has her crushed; Mahler could not get it past the Vienna censor.

fields.Description: Strauss's first opera with Hugo von Hofmannsthal, after Sophocles: Elektra waits to avenge her father Agamemnon, and the recognition of her brother Orest is its emotional heart.
fields.Listen: Hushed, tender orchestral writing swelling beneath an anguished soprano line, the release after the siblings recognise each other.
fields.Clue: His first opera with Hugo von Hofmannsthal, after Sophocles: Agamemnon's daughter waits to avenge her father on Klytämnestra and Aegisth, takes her brother Orest for a stranger until the Recognition Scene, and dances herself to death; the heroine's chord superimposes E and D-flat major.

fields.Description: A rondo on a folk trickster, with a horn theme and a clarinet shriek; Till is tried and hanged, and the epilogue suggests he survives.
The tone poem that made Strauss famous at twenty-four, opening with an upward rush and ending not in triumph but in a sudden cold emptiness.
A tone poem whose hero is Strauss himself: his critics chatter in the woodwinds, his wife Pauline is a solo violin, and he quotes his own earlier works.
fields.Listen: This tone poem opens with the hero's bold, sweeping theme in E-flat major, the horns and cellos climbing an E-flat triad across two octaves.
fields.Clue: A tone poem whose hero is its composer himself: his critics chatter in the woodwinds and tubas, his wife Pauline is a capricious solo violin, battle is joined with offstage trumpets, and his “Works of Peace” quote his own Don Juan and Also sprach Zarathustra.

fields.Description: A dying artist relives his life before his soul is transfigured. Sixty years later Strauss quoted its transfiguration theme at the close of “Im Abendrot”, the last of his Four Last Songs; dying, he said it was just as he had composed it.
fields.Listen: Loud, surging orchestral writing with blazing brass and heaving strings.
fields.Clue: A tone poem in which a dying artist relives his childhood and ideals before his soul is released, with a poem by Alexander Ritter; sixty years later its composer quoted its final theme at the close of “Im Abendrot”, the last of his Four Last Songs.

fields.Description: Revised twice over five years. Its finale's swinging horn theme came from seeing sixteen swans take off, which he called one of the great experiences of his life.
Sibelius's only concerto, revised in 1905; Donald Tovey called its finale a “polonaise for polar bears”.
fields.Listen: The soloist's long, rhapsodic line climbs high over hushed strings.
fields.Clue: Its composer's only concerto, revised in 1905 and premiered in that version by Karl Halíř under Richard Strauss; the soloist enters over muted, divided violins, and Donald Tovey called its finale a “polonaise for polar bears”.

fields.Description: One of the four Lemminkäinen Legends from the Kalevala: a swan glides on the black river around Tuonela, the land of the dead.
fields.Listen: A long, mournful cor anglais solo floats over hushed, divided, muted strings in A minor, a bird gliding on a black river.
fields.Clue: One of the four Lemminkäinen Legends from the Kalevala: a bird glides on the black river around the land of the dead, voiced by a cor anglais over divided, muted strings.

fields.Description: Inspired by a black-and-white reproduction of Arnold Böcklin's painting; it quotes the Dies irae.
fields.Listen: This tone poem opens with a hushed, rocking 5/8 figure in the harp, muted cellos, and timpani in A minor, like oars dipping into dark water.
fields.Clue: Inspired by a black-and-white reproduction of Arnold Böcklin's painting of a rowboat carrying a shrouded figure to a cypress-crowded island; a rocking 5/8 figure depicts Charon's oars, and it quotes the Dies irae.

fields.Description: Begun in Leningrad during the German siege; the score was microfilmed, flown out through Tehran, and played in the West as propaganda, and in 1942 the starving city's own orchestra performed it.
fields.Listen: Broad, striding orchestral writing that subsides into a calm, pastoral passage.
fields.Clue: Begun in Leningrad during the German siege, its score was microfilmed and flown out through Tehran; its first movement repeats an “invasion” march twelve times over a snare-drum ostinato, and the starving city's own orchestra played it in 1942 while Soviet guns shelled the German batteries.

fields.Audio: [sound:cmc-Shostakovich (Lady Macbeth of the Mtsensk District Passacaglia)_n.mp3]
fields.Description: Katerina Izmailova, bored in a merchant's house, murders her father-in-law and husband for her lover. Stalin walked out in 1936, and Pravda condemned it as “Muddle Instead of Music”.
fields.Listen: The Passacaglia, an Act II interlude: a grim ground bass in the low brass and strings builds to crushing, dissonant climaxes for the full orchestra.
fields.Clue: Its bored merchant's wife poisons her father-in-law with mushrooms and murders her husband for her lover Sergei, then drowns herself and a rival on the road to Siberia; Stalin walked out in 1936, and Pravda condemned it as “Muddle Instead of Music”.

fields.Description: The “Classical”, written deliberately as Haydn might have written it had he lived into the twentieth century, and composed away from the piano.
From a film about a clerical error that invents a soldier who does not exist; the Troika is its best-known movement.
fields.Listen: This suite opens with a distant, muted cornet call; then a flute pipes a perky military tune over a soft snare drum.
fields.Clue: Its suite opens and ends with a distant cornet and snare drum, framing the life and funeral of an officer who exists only through a clerk's slip of the pen that the Tsar misreads; from a 1934 film by Aleksandr Faintsimmer, its “Troika” is a sleigh ride with jingling bells.

fields.Description: Prokofiev's second full-length ballet, finished after the war; the clock striking midnight is its famous orchestral effect.
fields.Listen: A lush, bittersweet Romantic melody in the strings, shadowed by sudden grotesque twists of harmony.
fields.Clue: Its heroine must leave the ball by midnight, marked by twelve strokes of a clock in the orchestra over a ticking wood block; finished after the Second World War, it was its composer's second full-length ballet, after Romeo and Juliet.

fields.Description: After Carlo Gozzi's fairy-tale play: a prince cursed to love three oranges must find them. Its March became a concert favourite.
fields.Listen: The March: a jaunty, grotesque tune over a swaggering brass bass, lurching between keys.
fields.Clue: Its March was arranged for violin by Jascha Heifetz; after Carlo Gozzi's play, a hypochondriac prince laughs only when the witch Fata Morgana tumbles over, and she curses him to pine for fruit kept in the giant cook Creonta's castle; it premiered in Chicago in 1921.

fields.Description: A puppet comes to life at a Shrovetide fair. The Petrushka chord superimposes C major and F-sharp major; begun as a piano concert piece.
fields.Listen: The Shrovetide Fair: swirling flute flourishes over bustling, accordion-like string figures, with Russian folk tunes in the winds.
fields.Clue: A ballet in which a showman's three puppets, a sad clown, a Ballerina, and a Moor, come to life at a Shrovetide fair in St Petersburg; its signature chord superimposes C major and F-sharp major, and it began as a concert piece for piano and orchestra.

fields.Description: Written for the Boston Symphony's fiftieth anniversary and dedicated “to the glory of God”; it sets Latin psalms.
fields.Listen: Stark, widely voiced E-minor chords hammered by winds, pianos, and harp, between dry, running oboe and bassoon arpeggios, with no violins or violas.
fields.Clue: Written for the Boston Symphony Orchestra's fiftieth anniversary and dedicated “to the glory of God”, it sets Latin texts from the Vulgate for chorus and an orchestra with no violins, violas, or clarinets; it opens on a widely spaced E-minor chord, and its second movement is a double fugue.

fields.Description: Commissioned by Serge Koussevitzky while Bartók was ill and poor in New York. Its fourth movement parodies the invasion theme from Shostakovich's “Leningrad” Symphony.
fields.Listen: Instruments step forward as soloists, in pairs and sections, against Bartók's brilliant, folk-inflected orchestral writing.
fields.Clue: Commissioned by Serge Koussevitzky while its composer was ill and poor in New York; its movements include the Game of Pairs, an Elegia in “night music” style, and an Interrupted Intermezzo that mocks the invasion theme of Shostakovich's “Leningrad” Symphony.

fields.Description: Judith opens seven doors in her husband's castle, each lit by its own orchestral colour; behind the seventh are his previous wives, alive.
fields.Listen: The fifth door opens: full orchestra with organ blazes out a massive C-major chord as the castle's owner shows Judith his vast domain (“Look, this is my kingdom”).
fields.Clue: Behind the fifth of this opera's seven doors lies its host's vast domain, revealed with a blaze of C major and organ; a dissonant minor-second “blood motif” stains each treasure Judith finds.

fields.Description: 153 progressive piano pieces in six books, from beginner exercises to concert pieces such as the Six Dances in Bulgarian Rhythm that close the last volume.
fields.Listen: A short teaching piece for solo piano: crisp, folk-modal lines in a lopsided, asymmetrical rhythm.
fields.Clue: 153 progressive piano pieces in six books, written partly for its composer's son Péter, ending with the Six Dances in Bulgarian Rhythm.

fields.Description: After Georg Büchner's play Woyzeck: a poor soldier, bullied by his Captain and experimented on by a Doctor, murders his lover Marie. Every scene is built on a closed form, such as a passacaglia or a suite.
fields.Listen: An atonal, fragmented orchestra with sharp contrasts; the voices slide between singing and Sprechstimme.
fields.Clue: Its third act is a set of six inventions, on a theme, a single note B, a rhythm, a chord, a key, and a perpetual motion; the title soldier, bullied by his Captain and experimented on by a Doctor, kills his lover Marie.

fields.Description: Dedicated “to the memory of an angel”, Manon Gropius, the daughter of Alma Mahler, who died at eighteen; its tone row ends with the rising whole tones of Bach's chorale “Es ist genug”, which is quoted in the finale.
fields.Listen: The soloist arpeggiates across the violin's open strings in a twelve-tone row built from stacked thirds, so the music sounds almost tonal.
fields.Clue: Alban Berg's last completed work, dedicated to Manon Gropius, the daughter of Alma Mahler, who died at eighteen; its tone row ends with the rising whole tones of Bach's chorale “Es ist genug”, which is quoted in the finale.

fields.Description: Berg's second opera, after Frank Wedekind's Lulu plays; he died leaving the third act unorchestrated, and Friedrich Cerha completed it in 1979. Lulu ends murdered by Jack the Ripper.
fields.Listen: The “Lied der Lulu”: a high, agile soprano line leaping across wide twelve-tone intervals, “Wenn sich die Menschen um meinetwillen umgebracht haben”, as she insists she has never wanted to seem anything but what she is.
fields.Clue: Its heroine sings this song to her husband Dr. Schön, who has pressed a revolver on her to kill herself, and then shoots him; in the prologue an animal tamer presents her dressed as Pierrot.

fields.Description: A string sextet after a poem by Richard Dehmel, in which a woman confesses on a moonlit walk that she carries another man's child, and her lover forgives her.
fields.Listen: This sextet opens with a dark, slowly descending D-minor line in the violas and cellos over a pedal D, as the couple walk through a cold, moonlit wood.
fields.Clue: A string sextet after a poem by Richard Dehmel, in which a woman confesses on a moonlit walk that she carries another man's child, and her lover forgives her; a Vienna jury rejected it for an unclassified inverted ninth chord, and it moves from D minor to D major.

fields.Description: Romeo and Juliet moved to Manhattan gang turf, with lyrics by Stephen Sondheim and choreography by Jerome Robbins.
fields.Listen: Jazzy, syncopated rhythms and Latin percussion, with the restless tritone that opens “Maria” threaded through the score.
fields.Clue: Its lovers sing “Tonight” on a fire escape and “Somewhere” after a rumble, and a song repeats an E-flat–A tritone on the heroine's name; lyrics by Stephen Sondheim, choreography by Jerome Robbins.

fields.Description: Bernstein's operetta on Voltaire's satire, with lyrics by Richard Wilbur and others; Cunegonde's aria “Glitter and Be Gay” parodies the coloratura showpiece.
fields.Listen: Cunegonde's soprano showpiece, swinging between a mock-tragic waltz lament and dazzling coloratura laughter (“Ha ha ha!”), a parody of Gounod's “Jewel Song”.
fields.Clue: Kept in luxury in Paris, Cunegonde sings the coloratura showpiece “Glitter and Be Gay” in this operetta after Voltaire, with lyrics by Richard Wilbur; it ends with the ensemble “Make Our Garden Grow”.

fields.Description: The Age of Anxiety, after W. H. Auden's poem, effectively a piano concerto, with a jazz masque before the final affirmation.

fields.Work: The Young Person's Guide to the Orchestra
fields.Description: Britten's Op. 34, subtitled Variations and Fugue on a Theme of Purcell; Malcolm Sargent conducted the London Symphony Orchestra in the 1946 educational film it was written for.
fields.Listen: Purcell's Rondeau from Abdelazer, a stately D-minor tune, stated by the full orchestra before each family of instruments plays it in turn.
fields.Clue: After one variation for each instrument, from the piccolo to the percussion, a fugue begun by the piccolo brings them all back while the brass blaze out the theme above it; Eric Crozier wrote its optional narration.

fields.Description: Interleaves the Latin Mass with Wilfred Owen's war poems, written for the consecration of the rebuilt Coventry Cathedral, with soloists chosen from the warring nations.
fields.Listen: The opening Requiem aeternam: bells toll a tritone (C and F-sharp) as the chorus murmurs the Latin text over muted strings.
fields.Clue: Its tenor and baritone sing Wilfred Owen's war poems, including “Strange Meeting” (“I am the enemy you killed, my friend”), between the Latin Mass sections; it was written for the consecration of the rebuilt Coventry Cathedral.

fields.Description: Written for Lincoln Kirstein's Ballet Caravan and choreographed by Eugene Loring, it quotes cowboy songs such as “Git Along, Little Dogies”; Billy is finally shot by Pat Garrett.
fields.Listen: The Open Prairie: wide-spaced open fifths and fourths in the woodwinds over a slow, plodding tread, Copland's sound for the empty plains.
fields.Clue: Aaron Copland's ballet for Lincoln Kirstein's Ballet Caravan, choreographed by Eugene Loring, on a young outlaw finally shot by Pat Garrett; it quotes cowboy songs such as “Git Along, Little Dogies”.

fields.Description: A narrator reads from Lincoln's speeches and letters, ending with the Gettysburg Address, over music that quotes “Camptown Races”; written in 1942 at André Kostelanetz's request.
fields.Listen: The slow, dignified opening: dotted rhythms and open harmonies, with fragments of the folk song “Springfield Mountain” in the woodwinds.
fields.Clue: A narrator reads from a president's speeches and letters, ending with the Gettysburg Address, over music quoting “Camptown Races”; André Kostelanetz commissioned it in 1942.

fields.Description: An “American folk opera” after DuBose Heyward's novel Porgy, set in Catfish Row in Charleston with an all-Black cast; “Summertime” is Clara's lullaby.
fields.Listen: Clara's lullaby “Summertime”: a slow, bluesy soprano melody, “Summertime, and the livin' is easy”, over a gently rocking accompaniment.
fields.Clue: Clara sings the lullaby “Summertime” (“fish are jumpin', and the cotton is high”) in this “American folk opera” set in Catfish Row, Charleston; the dope peddler Sportin' Life doubts the Bible in “It Ain't Necessarily So”, and its disabled hero sets out in his goat cart for New York.

fields.Description: Written in 1906 and subtitled A Cosmic Landscape; Leonard Bernstein borrowed its title for his Harvard lectures.
fields.Listen: Hushed, sustained G-major string chords, the silence against which the solo trumpet asks its atonal phrase (long B-flat, C-sharp, E, long E-flat, long C) and the flutes answer.
fields.Clue: Written in 1906 and subtitled A Cosmic Landscape, it sets three layers at once: hushed offstage strings for “the Silences of the Druids”, a trumpet asking the same atonal phrase seven times, and four flutes growing more frantic in reply. Leonard Bernstein borrowed its title for his Harvard lectures.

fields.Description: An orchestral set: the Saint-Gaudens memorial to the Black 54th Massachusetts regiment, Putnam's Camp, where two marching bands collide, and The Housatonic at Stockbridge.
fields.Listen: Layered orchestral textures in which marches, hymns, and patriotic songs collide, at times in two tempos at once.
fields.Clue: Its composer's “First Orchestral Set”: it opens with the Saint-Gaudens memorial on Boston Common to Robert Gould Shaw and the Black 54th Massachusetts regiment; in Putnam's Camp, a boy dreams as two marching bands collide, and The Housatonic at Stockbridge sets a river mist over the hymn tune “Dorrance”.

fields.Description: Each movement portrays Concord Transcendentalists: Emerson, Hawthorne, The Alcotts, and Thoreau. One passage calls for a board to press down clusters.
fields.Listen: Dense, dissonant, rhapsodic piano writing, layered and rhythmically free, in which echoes of Beethoven's Fifth surface.
fields.Clue: Each of its four movements portrays a Transcendentalist of one Massachusetts town (Emerson, Hawthorne, The Alcotts, and Thoreau); one passage calls for a board to press down clusters, an optional flute joins in the last movement, and its composer published Essays Before a Sonata to explain it.

fields.Work: Fantasia on a Theme by Thomas Tallis
fields.Audio: [sound:Vaughan Williams (Fantasia on a Theme by Thomas Tallis).mp3]
fields.Description: For a string quartet and two string orchestras of different sizes, on a psalm tune by Thomas Tallis; it premiered in Gloucester Cathedral in 1910.
fields.Listen: Rich, sustained string chords in the Phrygian mode, the Tudor psalm tune echoing between a full string orchestra, a distant smaller one, and a solo quartet.
fields.Clue: For a string quartet and two string orchestras of different sizes, on the third of nine psalm tunes its Tudor model wrote for Archbishop Matthew Parker's Psalter (“Why fum'th in fight”); it premiered in Gloucester Cathedral in 1910.

fields.Description: Vaughan Williams's first symphony, for soloists, chorus, and orchestra, on poems by Walt Whitman.
fields.Listen: This symphony opens with a brass fanfare on a B-flat-minor chord; then the full chorus bursts in on a blazing D-major chord, crying “Behold, the sea itself”.
fields.Clue: Its composer's first symphony, for soprano, baritone, chorus, and orchestra, sets poems from Walt Whitman's Leaves of Grass in four movements, the last titled The Explorers; it premiered at the 1910 Leeds Festival.

fields.Description: An elegiac work written after the First World War; Jacqueline du Pré's 1965 recording made it famous.
fields.Listen: This concerto opens with the soloist's declamatory recitative of rich, rolled E-minor chords; then a sad, rocking 9/8 melody steals in, first in the violas.
fields.Clue: Its composer's last major work, written in 1919 at a Sussex cottage in the shadow of the First World War; its under-rehearsed premiere with Felix Salmond failed, and Jacqueline du Pré's 1965 recording with John Barbirolli made it famous.

fields.Description: Fourteen portraits of friends, each headed by initials. Nimrod is his publisher August Jaeger; Elgar claimed a larger unheard theme runs through it, never identified.
fields.Listen: The theme: a halting G-minor melody in the strings, broken into short phrases that begin after a rest, on which every variation is built.

fields.Description: After Walter Scott: forced to marry another man, Lucia kills her husband on the wedding night and appears before the guests in her bloodstained nightgown.
fields.Listen: In the mad scene, the soprano's florid, fragmented coloratura is echoed phrase by phrase by a solo flute, standing in for the glass harmonica.
fields.Clue: After murdering her bridegroom Arturo, the heroine sings the mad scene “Il dolce suono”, written for glass harmonica and now usually accompanied by flute; its sextet “Chi mi frena” follows the signing of a marriage contract.

fields.Description: A comic opera in which the poor Nemorino buys a fake love potion from the quack Dulcamara to win Adina; “Una furtiva lagrima” is its famous tenor aria.
fields.Listen: The tenor sings the melancholy B-flat-minor romanza “Una furtiva lagrima” over harp arpeggios, the bassoon echoing his phrases.
fields.Clue: The poor Nemorino sings “Una furtiva lagrima”, introduced by a solo bassoon, after the quack Dulcamara sells him a love potion that is really Bordeaux wine.

fields.Description: Bellini's masterpiece: a Druid priestess has secretly borne the Roman proconsul two children. “Casta diva” is the model of bel canto melody.
fields.Listen: The soprano spins a long, floating F-major line, “Casta diva” (“chaste goddess”), a prayer to the moon over gently rocking strings, its phrases climbing to sustained high notes.
fields.Clue: A Druid high priestess raises mistletoe to the moon and sings “Casta diva” in this opera, though she has secretly borne two children to the Roman proconsul Pollione.

fields.Description: Among the first operas, premiered at the Mantuan court in 1607 with a libretto by Alessandro Striggio; it opens with a trumpet toccata, and Orfeo's plea “Possente spirto” lulls the ferryman Charon.
fields.Listen: The hero's plea to Charon: a florid tenor line, every phrase ornamented, with obbligato instruments answering between the verses.
fields.Clue: Its hero tries to charm the ferryman Charon with the florid “Possente spirto”, each verse with a different obbligato instrument, and lulls him to sleep; premiered at the Mantuan court in 1607, with a libretto by Alessandro Striggio, it opens with a trumpet toccata.

fields.Description: Monteverdi's last opera, in which Nero's scheming mistress Poppea becomes empress while virtue goes unrewarded; its closing duet “Pur ti miro” may be by another composer.
fields.Listen: The closing love duet “Pur ti miro, pur ti godo”: two high voices intertwining in sensuous suspensions over a repeating four-note descending ground bass.
fields.Clue: Its closing duet, “Pur ti miro”, crowns Nero's scheming mistress as empress after he exiles Ottavia, who sings “Addio, Roma”; virtue goes unrewarded, and the duet may be by another composer.

fields.Description: Despite its name, a five-movement violin concerto, written for Pablo de Sarasate; it helped start the French vogue for Spanish colour.
fields.Listen: This piece opens with a bold D-minor call for the orchestra in a snapping triplet rhythm, answered by the solo violin's flourish.
fields.Clue: Despite its name, a five-movement concerto for violin, written for Pablo de Sarasate, who premiered it in 1875, a month before Carmen; its third movement, an Intermezzo, was long cut, and it helped start the French vogue for Iberian colour.

fields.Description: A violin showpiece on Hungarian gypsy themes, slow and declamatory before an extremely fast final section, written by a virtuoso famous for his pure tone.
fields.Listen: After a stern C-minor orchestral opening, the solo violin enters with a free, rhapsodic lament in gypsy style (G, up to C, D, long E-flat), with sobbing slides.
fields.Clue: A showpiece for violin and orchestra on Hungarian Romani tunes, slow and declamatory before a headlong final dance with left-hand pizzicato; written in 1878 by a Spanish virtuoso famous for his pure tone, its solo opens rising G, C, D, E-flat.

fields.Description: Won a one-act competition in 1890 and launched verismo. Its orchestral Intermezzo is played between the two halves of the single act; almost always staged with Pagliacci.
fields.Listen: The Intermezzo: hushed strings sing a serene F-major melody over harp and organ, then swell to a warm, broad climax on the empty stage.
fields.Clue: Its orchestral Intermezzo plays on an empty stage between the two halves of its single act, before Turiddu bites Alfio's ear to accept a duel; Santuzza curses him with a “mala Pasqua”, and it won Sonzogno's 1890 one-act competition and launched verismo.

fields.Description: The Prologue steps out to say the actors are real people. Canio stabs his wife during the play-within-the-play and tells the audience the comedy is over.
fields.Listen: The tenor alone, in a halting, sobbing declamation over heavy strings, as the clown resolves to go on with the show though his heart is breaking.
fields.Clue: After catching his wife Nedda with her lover, the clown Canio sings “Vesti la giubba” (“Put on the costume”), telling himself to laugh; Tonio's Prologue says actors are real people, and the opera ends “La commedia è finita!” after Canio stabs Nedda and Silvio.

fields.Description: A Venetian melodrama whose ballet, the Dance of the Hours, is far better known than the opera, not least from Fantasia. Its librettist was Arrigo Boito under an anagram.
fields.Listen: Light ballet music in delicate, tiptoeing woodwind and string phrases, from the dance of the hours of the day.
fields.Clue: Its Act III ballet, in which dancers portray the hours of dawn, day, evening, and night, is far better known than the opera, partly from the ostriches and hippos of Fantasia; Arrigo Boito wrote the libretto under an anagram, and the Venetian street singer heroine stabs herself after the aria “Suicidio!”.

fields.Description: A piano suite after Goya's paintings, later expanded into an opera. Granados drowned when his ship was torpedoed returning from its New York premiere in 1916.
fields.Listen: Solo piano in a Spanish idiom: strummed, guitar-like chords, ornamental flourishes, and dark, rich harmonies.
fields.Clue: A piano suite after Goya's paintings, whose fourth piece, Quejas, o la maja y el ruiseñor (The Maiden and the Nightingale), inspired “Bésame mucho”; later expanded into an opera, after whose 1916 New York premiere its composer drowned when the Sussex was torpedoed.

fields.Description: A guitar concerto named for a Bourbon palace garden; Rodrigo, blind from the age of three, wrote it in 1939.
fields.Listen: The Adagio: over the guitar's soft, strummed B-minor chords, the cor anglais sings a long, ornamented, elegiac melody that the guitar then answers.
fields.Clue: A guitar concerto written in 1939 and named for the gardens of a Bourbon palace; its Adagio opens with a B-minor cor anglais melody, its first movement with flamenco hemiolas, and its composer had been blind since the age of three. Miles Davis and Gil Evans recorded its slow movement on Sketches of Spain.

fields.Description: A wedding present for the violinist Eugène Ysaÿe, cyclic in form, whose finale is a strict canon between violin and piano.
fields.Listen: This piece opens with gently rocking ninth chords in the piano; then the violin enters with a lilting theme in 9/8 that returns throughout the work.
fields.Clue: A wedding present for Eugène Ysaÿe, who premiered it in a Brussels gallery as the light failed, playing the last movements from memory in the dark; it is cyclic, and its A-major finale is a strict canon between the two players. Proust drew on it for Vinteuil's music.

fields.Description: Modelled on the slow Spanish court dance, with an optional chorus added later on verses by Robert de Montesquiou.
fields.Listen: Over plucked strings walking a gentle F-sharp-minor arpeggio, the solo flute sings a long, wistful melody, slow and stately.
fields.Clue: Written in 1887 and dedicated to its composer's patron, Countess Élisabeth Greffulhe, whose cousin Robert de Montesquiou wrote verses for an optional chorus; it is modelled on a slow Renaissance court dance, in F-sharp minor.

fields.Description: A setting of the Gloria for soprano, chorus, and orchestra, commissioned by the Koussevitzky Foundation and premiered in Boston in 1961; Poulenc said its irreverent angels came from Benozzo Gozzoli's frescoes and from Benedictine monks he had seen playing football.
fields.Listen: A hushed, slow passage: a floating melody over soft, bittersweet chords in the chorus and orchestra.
fields.Clue: Commissioned by the Koussevitzky Foundation and premiered in Boston in 1961, this setting of the Latin hymn of praise for soprano, chorus, and orchestra has a jaunty “Laudamus te”; its composer said he pictured Benozzo Gozzoli's angels sticking out their tongues and Benedictine monks playing football.

fields.Description: Poulenc's opera after Georges Bernanos on the sixteen Carmelite nuns of Compiègne guillotined in 1794; the fearful Blanche de la Force walks out to die last.
fields.Listen: Hushed, austere, devotional writing: a chant-like line on repeated notes over sustained modal chords.
fields.Clue: Its sixteen nuns of Compiègne go to the guillotine in 1794 singing the Salve Regina, their voices dropping out one by one at each fall of the blade until the fearful Blanche de la Force joins them and dies last; after Georges Bernanos's screenplay.

fields.Description: Nielsen said its title stands for the elemental will to live; in the finale two sets of timpani, on opposite sides of the orchestra, duel.
fields.Listen: Turbulent, clashing writing for the full orchestra, strings and brass driving at full force toward a blazing climax.
fields.Clue: Its composer said its title stands for the elemental will to live; it opens with strings and low brass clashing on C under a stormy D-minor woodwind outburst, and in the finale two sets of timpani on opposite sides of the stage duel. Written in Denmark during the First World War.

fields.Description: Written for the bicentenary of the playwright Ludvig Holberg, it recasts Baroque dances, Praeludium, Sarabande, Gavotte, Air, and Rigaudon, in Romantic string writing.
fields.Listen: The Praeludium: brisk, rippling string figures in a skipping rhythm under a buoyant melody, in Baroque style.
fields.Clue: Written for the bicentenary of the playwright born in Bergen in 1684, the “father of Danish literature”, it recasts Baroque dances (a Praeludium, Sarabande, Gavotte, Air, and Rigaudon) in Romantic writing, first for piano and then for strings.

fields.Audio: [sound:Carl Maria von Weber (Invitation to the Dance).mp3]
fields.Description: A piano rondo Weber dedicated to his wife; Berlioz orchestrated it, and it became the music of the ballet Le Spectre de la rose.
fields.Listen: The slow introduction: a low voice, the gentleman, issues the invitation and a higher voice, the lady, coyly answers, before the brilliant waltz.
fields.Clue: A piano rondo in waltz time dedicated to its composer's wife, with a slow introduction and epilogue in which a gentleman bows and leads a lady onto the ballroom floor; Berlioz orchestrated it, and it became the music of the ballet Le Spectre de la rose.

fields.Description: Written without bar lines or time signatures, with whimsical directions to the player such as très luisant (“very shiny”); the title is Satie's own coinage.
fields.Listen: A slow, hypnotic piano melody winding around a few notes of a modal, vaguely Eastern scale over a plain, unchanging left-hand accompaniment.
fields.Clue: Written without bar lines or time signatures, with whimsical directions such as très luisant (“very shiny”) and sur la langue; the title is its composer's own coinage, perhaps from Knossos or gnosis, and he also wrote three Gymnopédies.

fields.Description: An orchestral piece with no melody or rhythm, only shifting clusters of sound; Stanley Kubrick used it without permission in 2001: A Space Odyssey.
fields.Listen: This piece opens with a vast, hushed cluster of nearly every chromatic note, held by the whole orchestra, its colour slowly shifting.
fields.Clue: An orchestral piece with no melody or rhythm, only slowly shifting clusters (its composer's “micropolyphony”), dedicated to the memory of Mátyás Seiber; Stanley Kubrick used it without permission in 2001: A Space Odyssey.

fields.Description: Sixteen unaccompanied voices in slowly shifting clusters, the technique Ligeti called micropolyphony; like Atmosphères, it was used in 2001: A Space Odyssey.
fields.Listen: Unaccompanied voices, soft and sustained, the notes overlapping so that no pulse or melody can be heard, the sound slowly changing colour.
fields.Clue: For sixteen unaccompanied voices, it opens with sopranos and altos entering one by one on a single F that slowly spreads into clusters, its composer's “micropolyphony”; like Atmosphères, it was used in 2001: A Space Odyssey.

fields.Description: On Richard Nixon's 1972 visit to Mao, with a libretto by Alice Goodman and direction by Peter Sellars; its three acts move from the airport arrival and banquet to Pat Nixon's tour and a revolutionary ballet, then a sleepless last night.
fields.Listen: This aria opens with the baritone stuttering “News, news, news” over pulsing repeated chords, then marvelling that “news has a kind of mystery” and that he shook hands with Chou En-lai.
fields.Clue: Having stepped off the Spirit of '76 onto the Beijing tarmac, the President sings of the mystery of news in a stuttering, hand-shaking aria; Alice Goodman wrote the libretto, and Peter Sellars directed the 1987 Houston premiere.

fields.Description: A four-minute fanfare; Adams likened it to a ride in a terrific sports car that you wish you hadn't taken.
fields.Listen: This piece's woodblock taps an unchanging pulse while clarinets and synthesizers hammer off-beat patterns against it; the trumpets break in with blaring fanfares.
fields.Clue: A “fanfare for orchestra” in which a woodblock pounds out an unchanging pulse against polyrhythms in the winds and synthesizers; its composer likened it to being taken for a spin in a terrific sports car and wishing you hadn't.

fields.Description: A slow piece for violin (or cello) and piano in Pärt's tintinnabuli style, written in 1978 just before he left Estonia; the title means “mirror in the mirror”.
fields.Listen: This piece opens with the piano's gently rising F-major triads under the violin's long, slow notes, which step out from A and back, one note further each time.
fields.Clue: Written in 1978 just before its composer left Estonia, for violin (or cello) and piano in his tintinnabuli style; its German title means “mirror in the mirror”.

fields.Description: A tintinnabuli piece of 1977 that Pärt has arranged for many ensembles, from string quartet to violin and piano; the title means “brothers”.
fields.Listen: Hushed, hymn-like chord sequences over a constant open-fifth drone on A and E, each phrase closed by a soft percussion stroke.
fields.Clue: Written in 1977 in its composer's tintinnabuli style and arranged for many ensembles, from string quartet to twelve cellos; Gidon Kremer and Keith Jarrett recorded the violin-and-piano version on ECM's Tabula Rasa album, and its Latin title means “brothers”.

fields.Description: A double concerto for two violins, prepared piano, and string orchestra in two movements, the fast Ludus and the still Silentium; its 1984 recording, the first in ECM's New Series, brought Pärt to the West.
fields.Listen: In A minor, the two solo violins and strings spin rapid arpeggio patterns in the tintinnabuli style, punctuated by the bell-like prepared piano.
fields.Clue: A double concerto for two violins, prepared piano, and strings in two movements, the fast Ludus and the still Silentium; written for Gidon Kremer and Tatiana Grindenko, its 1984 recording launched ECM's New Series.

fields.Description: Three slow movements for soprano and orchestra on texts of separation between mother and child, one scratched on a Gestapo cell wall in Zakopane by an eighteen-year-old prisoner. A 1992 recording with Dawn Upshaw sold over a million copies.
fields.Listen: Very slow, quiet, and static: a long modal line unfolding in the strings, spare and hypnotic.
fields.Clue: Its three slow movements for soprano and orchestra set texts of separation between mother and child, one a prayer that eighteen-year-old Helena Błażusiakówna scratched on a Gestapo cell wall in Zakopane; it opens with a canon rising slowly through the strings, and a 1992 recording with Dawn Upshaw sold over a million copies.

fields.Description: A setting for soprano of James Agee's prose-poem about a summer evening in his childhood, later the prologue to his novel A Death in the Family.
fields.Listen: A soprano's lilting, rocking melody over gentle woodwinds and strings: a child's memory of a summer evening on the family porch.
fields.Clue: A soprano sets James Agee's prose-poem about an evening in his Tennessee childhood, later the prologue to his novel A Death in the Family; Eleanor Steber commissioned it.

fields.Description: A Romantic showpiece by a Polish virtuoso who wrote it for himself, dedicated to Pablo de Sarasate.
fields.Listen: A Romantic virtuoso concerto: the solo violin sings a long, sweet melody, then breaks into dazzling runs and double stops.
fields.Clue: A Romantic showpiece in D minor by a Polish virtuoso who wrote it for himself and dedicated it to Pablo de Sarasate; its slow movement is a Romance that runs straight into a gypsy-style finale, à la Zingara.

fields.Description: Twelve studies revised twice, each revision easier than the last; Schumann said the earlier version was playable by at most a dozen people alive.
fields.Listen: Romantic virtuoso piano writing: a singing melody wrapped in rippling figuration.
fields.Clue: Twelve piano pieces revised twice, each version easier, the 1852 set dedicated to its composer's teacher Carl Czerny; Schumann said the 1838 version was playable by at most ten or twelve people alive. Titles include Mazeppa, Feux follets, Ricordanza, and Chasse-neige.

fields.Description: Twelve studies revised twice, each revision easier than the last; Schumann said the earlier version was playable by at most a dozen people alive.
Twelve studies revised twice, each revision easier than the last; Schumann said the earlier version was playable by at most a dozen people alive.
Gluck set a Philippe Quinault libretto already famous from Lully's version seventy years earlier, deliberately inviting the comparison.
Gluck's reform opera at its most austere. Its premiere set off the Paris war between his supporters and Niccolò Piccinni's.
The popular setting that Rossini's later version displaced; its partisans sabotaged Rossini's premiere in 1816.
fields.Listen: A bright, lightly scored G-major overture: short, symmetrical phrases in the strings with oboes and horns, opera buffa before Rossini.
fields.Clue: Written for Catherine the Great's court at St Petersburg in 1782, its setting of Beaumarchais's comedy, with Rosina, Count Almaviva, and the resourceful Figaro, was so beloved that its partisans sabotaged Rossini's 1816 premiere of the same play.

fields.Description: The Vienna premiere in 1792 was encored in full at the emperor's order, the only opera known to have been performed twice in one night.
fields.Listen: Classical opera buffa overture, Mozart-adjacent: crisp, symmetrical, string-led, no trombones.

fields.Movement: Act II · “Torna di Tito a lato”
fields.Description: An opera seria written in haste for Leopold II's Prague coronation in 1791, in Mozart's last year, on the emperor Titus forgiving a conspiracy against him.
fields.Listen: Annio's short aria “Torna di Tito a lato”: an earnest mezzo line over light strings in G major.
fields.Clue: Annio urges his friend Sesto to return to the emperor's side and prove his loyalty, after Sesto has agreed in “Parto, parto”, with clarinet obbligato, to set the Capitol on fire for Vitellia; an opera seria written in haste for Leopold II's Prague coronation in 1791.

fields.Description: The model Napoleonic grand opera: a vestal virgin lets the sacred flame go out for love and is sentenced to be buried alive, saved by lightning relighting it.
fields.Listen: Severe, marble-like French classical style: dotted ceremonial rhythms, heavy brass, declamatory vocal writing.

fields.Description: An opéra comique after Walter Scott whose Scottish setting and ghost plot made it one of the most performed French operas of the 19th century.
fields.Listen: French opéra comique: light, tuneful, Scottish-flavoured melodies with spoken dialogue between.

fields.Description: A five-act French grand opera ending with Rachel thrown into a cauldron of boiling oil as the cardinal learns she was his own daughter.
fields.Listen: Grand opéra: huge choral tableaux, brass bands, ceremonial processions, five acts.

fields.Description: Berlioz's opera on the sculptor casting his Perseus, a failure in Paris that survives mainly through its overture and the Roman Carnival overture drawn from it.
Not an opera but a légende dramatique for concert performance, including the Rákóczi March, which Berlioz inserted by sending Faust to Hungary.
Five hours after Virgil, in two halves. Berlioz never saw it complete; only the second half was staged in his lifetime.
Berlioz's last work, a comedy after Much Ado About Nothing that drops the Don John plot entirely and keeps only the sparring lovers.
A water-spirit opera by the writer better known for his tales; Weber's admiring review of it helped define German Romantic opera.
fields.Listen: Early German Romantic opera: supernatural water music, tremolo strings and chromatic harmony under simple song forms.

fields.Description: Weber's through-composed opera, admired by Wagner and sunk by its libretto; its overture survives in the concert hall.
Nicolai's Shakespeare comedy, now heard mostly as its overture. He died two months after the premiere.
fields.Listen: Long hushed moonlit opening, then a bustling comic Allegro; German Romantic, Weber-ish scoring.

fields.Description: A German romantic opera set in England, whose tenor aria Ach so fromm became a staple in its Italian form, M'appari.
fields.Listen: Light German-French tunefulness; The Last Rose of Summer turns up as a plain Irish melody.

fields.Description: A comic opera from the Arabian Nights whose Weimar premiere Liszt conducted; the hostile reception drove Liszt to resign his post there.
fields.Listen: Wagner-influenced chromatic harmony in a comic opera; rich scoring over a light plot.

fields.Description: Rossini's first serious success; its aria Di tanti palpiti was so popular it was nicknamed the rice aria, supposedly written while rice cooked.
A comedy in which a poet on stage manipulates the plot he is writing, staged a year after L'italiana in Algeri and at first dismissed as its mirror image.
Rossini's version, which changes the ending and keeps little of Shakespeare; eclipsed by Verdi's, though its third act was long admired.

fields.Movement: Act II · “Nacqui all'affanno … Non più mesta”
fields.Description: Rossini's Cinderella has no magic: no fairy godmother and a bracelet instead of a slipper, because bare feet were indecent on the Roman stage.
fields.Listen: The slow first part of the heroine's closing rondo, “Nacqui all'affanno e al pianto”: a gently ornamented mezzo-soprano cantabile in E major recalling her life of sorrow, before the brilliant “Non più mesta”.
fields.Clue: Its heroine, a stepdaughter forced into servitude, forgives her stepfather Don Magnifico and her stepsisters in the rondo “Nacqui all'affanno… Non più mesta”; there is no magic: the philosopher Alidoro replaces the fairy godmother, and a bracelet replaces the slipper.

fields.Description: A servant is condemned to death for a theft actually committed by a magpie.
fields.Listen: This overture opens with two snare-drum rolls, then a swaggering G-major march for the full orchestra.
fields.Clue: Its overture opens with snare-drum rolls; the servant Ninetta is condemned to death for stealing a silver spoon actually taken by the title bird, and she sings the prayer “Deh, tu reggi in tal momento”.

fields.Description: The first opera drawn from Walter Scott, beginning the Romantic vogue for Scotland on the Italian stage.
Rossini's last Italian opera before he left for Paris; its overture is among the few of his to use material from the opera itself.
Rossini reused music from an opera written for the tsar's coronation. A count disguises himself first as a hermit, then as a nun.
The opera that made Donizetti's international name, on Anne Boleyn's fall, ending with a mad scene as the cannon announces Henry's new marriage.
Victor Hugo had it banned in Paris as an infringement of his play, forcing a change of title and setting.
Banned in Naples after Mary calls Elizabeth a vile bastard to her face, a confrontation the two queens never had in life.
Banned in Naples for staging Christian martyrdom; Donizetti reworked it for Paris as Les martyrs.
A girl raised by a regiment of French soldiers falls for a Tyrolean peasant, who joins the regiment to win her.
fields.Listen: Marie's rousing regimental song: a jaunty soprano refrain in march rhythm, crying “Il est là!” in praise of “le beau vingt-et-unième”, the regiment that raised her.
fields.Clue: A foundling raised by French soldiers sings “Chacun le sait” in praise of the 21st, and the Tyrolean Tonio, who enlists to win her, sings “Ah! mes amis” with its nine high Cs.

fields.Description: A grand opera in which a novice discovers the woman he loves is the king's mistress; she dies in his arms in the cloister.
Bellini's first success at La Scala, and the opera that established the long-breathed melodic line Chopin admired.
Bellini's Romeo and Juliet comes from Italian sources, not Shakespeare, and Romeo is sung by a mezzo-soprano.
An English romantic opera remembered for the soprano aria I Dreamt I Dwelt in Marble Halls.
fields.Listen: English ballad opera: plain strophic songs with simple accompaniment, aimed at the drawing room.

fields.Description: An early Verdi crusade opera whose chorus of exiles fed nationalist feeling; the Milan archbishop tried to have the baptism scene suppressed.
fields.Listen: Early Verdi: massed patriotic chorus, banda on stage, and a violin solo introducing the trio.

fields.Description: Verdi's first Venice commission, after Hugo. The plot turns on a hunting horn: the hero has sworn to kill himself whenever it sounds, and it sounds at his wedding.
fields.Listen: “O sommo Carlo”: a noble baritone line swelling into a full ensemble with chorus, here in Mattia Battistini's 1906 recording.
fields.Clue: Its composer's first Venice commission, after Victor Hugo: the bandit hero, rival of King Don Carlo and old Silva for Elvira, swears to kill himself when Silva sounds a hunting horn, which sounds at his wedding; at Charlemagne's tomb, the newly elected emperor pardons the conspirators in “O sommo Carlo”.

fields.Description: An early Verdi opera whose line about leaving Italy to him drew nationalist cheers from Risorgimento audiences. Set at the Hun invasion and the founding of Venice.
fields.Listen: Early Verdi: square driving rhythms, loud unison chorus writing, oom-pah accompaniment.

fields.Description: The bridge between Verdi's early manner and his middle period, after Schiller: a father's letter, forced under threat, destroys his daughter's love.
fields.Listen: Built almost entirely on one nervous fast-moving theme rather than a medley.

fields.Description: A Genoese doge poisoned by his own chancellor. Verdi revised it twenty-four years later with Arrigo Boito, adding the council chamber scene, the best thing in it.
fields.Listen: Dark baritone-and-bass writing with unusually little tenor; sombre orchestral colour throughout.

fields.Movement: Act III · “Forse la soglia attinse … Ma se m'è forza perderti”
fields.Description: Censors moved the assassination of a Swedish king to colonial Boston to avoid staging regicide; productions now restore the Swedish setting.
fields.Listen: Riccardo's recitative before his romanza: the tenor resolves to send Renato and his wife back to England, “e la sua sposa… l'Inghilterra”, letting the ocean part them without a farewell.
fields.Clue: Censors forced its composer to move the assassination of Sweden's Gustav III to colonial Boston: the governor Riccardo loves Amelia, wife of his secretary Renato, who rages at his portrait in “Eri tu” before stabbing him at a ball, as the fortune-teller Ulrica predicted.

fields.Description: The plot is set off by a pistol that fires by accident, killing the heroine's father, whose dying curse drives everything after; singers long thought the opera unlucky. Written for St Petersburg.
fields.Listen: This overture opens with three hammered unison Es in the brass; then the strings take up the restless, churning E-minor “fate” motif, here under Arturo Toscanini in 1944.
fields.Clue: Its plot is set off when a pistol thrown down fires by accident, killing the heroine's father, the Marquis of Calatrava, whose dying curse drives everything after; written for St Petersburg, its heroine prays “Pace, pace, mio Dio!” at a hermitage, and singers long thought it unlucky.

fields.Movement: Act III · Ballet of the Queen (“La Peregrina”)
fields.Description: Verdi's grand opera for Paris, after Schiller, on the Spanish Inquisition and Philip II. Cut repeatedly; the Fontainebleau act is often restored, and there are French and Italian versions.
fields.Listen: From the Queen's ballet, “La Peregrina”, the Paris divertissement: graceful, lilting A-major dance music for orchestra, light and courtly.
fields.Clue: Its composer's grand opera for Paris, after Schiller: the Infante loves Elisabeth de Valois, who must marry his father, Philip II, instead; Philip laments “Ella giammai m'amò”, the Grand Inquisitor demands Rodrigo's death, and the Act III ballet tells of the search for the world's most beautiful pearl, “La Peregrina”.

fields.Movement: Act III · “Dal labbro il canto estasiato vola”
fields.Description: Verdi's last opera, written at seventy-nine after Shakespeare's The Merry Wives of Windsor and Henry IV, and only his second comedy.
fields.Listen: Fenton's sonnet, “Dal labbro il canto estasiato vola pei silenzi notturni”: a tenor's rapt, lyrical love song floating over hushed, shimmering strings.
fields.Clue: Its composer's last opera, written near eighty after Shakespeare's The Merry Wives of Windsor and Henry IV: Fenton sings a sonnet in Windsor Park, the fat knight is tipped into the Thames in a laundry basket and pinched by false fairies, and it ends with the fugue “Tutto nel mondo è burla”.

fields.Description: Arrigo Boito's only completed opera, and he later wrote Verdi's Otello and Falstaff librettos. The 1868 premiere was a riot and it was cut drastically.
fields.Listen: Massed chorus and brass fanfares against a mocking bass devil: the Prologue in Heaven, before the drama begins.
fields.Clue: Its title devil whistles in defiance at the heavenly choirs in the Prologue, and Faust and Margherita sing “Lontano, lontano” in her prison cell; its 1868 premiere at La Scala was a fiasco. Its composer later wrote Verdi's last two librettos.

fields.Description: Opens with the Tristan chord, an unresolved dissonance often called the start of modern harmony. The first Tristan died weeks after the premiere.
fields.Listen: This prelude opens with the cellos rising A, F, E; then the woodwinds' unresolved chord (F, B, D-sharp, G-sharp) slides to a dominant seventh, repeated higher each time, with silences between.

fields.Description: A French grand opera in which Hamlet survives to be crowned; Ophelia's mad scene is its coloratura showpiece, and it was among the first operas to use a saxophone.
fields.Listen: A coloratura soprano over a lilting, dance-like accompaniment, with long trills and runs high in the voice.
fields.Clue: A French grand opera after Shakespeare in which the Danish prince survives to be crowned; Ophélie's Act IV mad scene, “À vos jeux, mes amis”, is its coloratura showpiece, and it was among the first operas to use a saxophone.

fields.Description: Gounod's version keeps only the Marguerite story from Goethe, and was long the most performed opera in the world. Includes the Soldiers' Chorus and the Jewel Song.
fields.Listen: The devil crashes the students' fair, bowing in with “Parmi vous, de grâce, permettez-moi de prendre place”, the bass's mock-polite lead-in to his song of the golden calf.
fields.Clue: At a village fair, the devil sings “Le veau d'or”, Valentin's sword shatters against him, and the students hold up their hilts as crosses; its heroine sings the Jewel Song, and it keeps only the Marguerite story from Goethe.

fields.Description: Gounod's version gives the lovers four duets and keeps Juliet alive long enough for a final scene together, unlike Shakespeare.
Offenbach's satire on the Second Empire dressed as Greek myth, with Paris abducting Helen and the gods behaving like Parisians.
An Offenbach opérette set in Peru, containing the Letter Song and a tipsy aria for a starving street singer.

fields.Movement: Act II · “Comme autrefois dans la nuit sombre”
fields.Description: Bizet's Ceylon opera, remembered for the tenor-baritone duet Au fond du temple saint, in which two friends swear their friendship over a rivalry.
fields.Listen: Leïla's Act II cavatina: a soprano line over softly pulsing horns, here in Amelita Galli-Curci's historic recording.
fields.Clue: Leïla recalls the night she hid a fugitive in the cavatina “Comme autrefois dans la nuit sombre” in this opera set in Ceylon, best known for the tenor-baritone friendship duet “Au fond du temple saint”.

fields.Description: Chabrier's comic opera about a king of Poland trying to escape his own throne. The theatre burned down after three performances.
fields.Listen: Sparkling French comic-opera writing in bright dance rhythms, with surprising chromatic harmonies.
fields.Clue: Its prelude alternates E-major triads and dominant-ninth chords in a passage Ravel said changed the course of harmony; Henri de Valois tries to escape the Polish throne, and the Opéra-Comique burned down after its third performance.

fields.Description: The Gilbert and Sullivan hit that made them famous, satirizing a First Lord of the Admiralty who never went to sea.

fields.Movement: Act II · “When the foeman bares his steel”
fields.Description: Premiered in New York to secure the American copyright, after Pinafore had been pirated. Its hero is apprenticed to pirates by mistake.
fields.Listen: “When the foeman bares his steel”: the Sergeant's police chorus marches with quaking bravado, punctuated by their comic “Tarantara!”, as they prepare to face the buccaneers.
fields.Clue: Premiered in New York in 1879 to secure the American copyright after Pinafore had been copied without payment; its Cornish hero, Frederic, was apprenticed to buccaneers by mistake and, born on 29 February, must serve until his twenty-first birthday, in 1940, and the Major-General knows all things “animal, vegetable, and mineral”.

fields.Description: Set in a fictional Japan to make English satire safe; its Lord High Executioner has a little list of people who would not be missed.
fields.Listen: From a 1914 Edison medley: Nanki-Poo's “A wandering minstrel I, a thing of shreds and patches”, a bright, lilting tune with pseudo-Japanese colouring in the orchestra.
fields.Clue: Set in a fictional Titipu to make English satire safe: a wandering minstrel, really the emperor's son Nanki-Poo, loves Yum-Yum, one of “three little maids from school”, and Ko-Ko, the Lord High Executioner, has “a little list” of people who would not be missed.

fields.Description: Deaf from 1874, Smetana wrote the cycle Má vlast, whose second movement Vltava traces the river from two springs to Prague.
A festival opera on the mythical founder of Prague, written to open the Czech National Theatre and reserved by Smetana for state occasions.
A water nymph who gives up her voice for a prince, so the title role is silent through much of the middle act. Contains the Song to the Moon.
fields.Listen: Harp arpeggios in a slow 3/8 shimmer before the soprano's long, floating melody to the moon, “Měsíčku na nebi hlubokém”.
fields.Clue: Its water-nymph heroine sings the “Song to the Moon” before asking the witch Ježibaba to make her human, at the price of her voice, to win a prince.

fields.Description: Left unfinished at Mussorgsky's death and completed by Rimsky-Korsakov, then again by Shostakovich. Ends with Old Believers burning themselves alive.
Rimsky-Korsakov's first opera, with Ivan the Terrible as a bass role Feodor Chaliapin made his own.

fields.Work: The Legend of the Invisible City of Kitezh
fields.Audio: [sound:cmc-Rimsky-Korsakov (The Legend of the Invisible City of Kitezh).mp3]
fields.Description: A Russian city made invisible to save it from the Tatars, often called the Russian Parsifal.
Rimsky-Korsakov's last opera, banned by the censor for satirizing the Tsar's conduct of the Russo-Japanese War; he died before it was staged.
Remembered almost entirely for the soprano aria Ebben? Ne andrò lontana, used in the film Diva. The heroine is finally carried off by an avalanche.
fields.Listen: The heroine's farewell, “Ebben? Ne andrò lontana”: a soprano line rising in long, yearning phrases over sustained strings.
fields.Clue: Its heroine resolves to leave her father's home for the snows in “Ebben? Ne andrò lontana”, later used in the film Diva; she is finally swept away by an avalanche.

fields.Description: Mascagni's follow-up to Cavalleria rusticana, a gentle Alsatian pastoral remembered mainly for its Cherry Duet.
fields.Listen: Suzel's short, simple soprano song offering a posy of violets, “Son pochi fiori, povere viole”, over light woodwinds and strings.
fields.Clue: The farmer's daughter Suzel offers a birthday posy of violets in “Son pochi fiori” and later shares the “Cherry Duet” with the bachelor landowner whom the rabbi David bets will marry; a gentle Alsatian pastoral, its composer's follow-up to Cavalleria rusticana.

fields.Description: Three one-act operas meant to be played together: the grim Il tabarro, the tragic Suor Angelica and the comic Gianni Schicchi. Premiered at the Met in 1918.
fields.Listen: Dark, conversational verismo singing over the orchestra's slow, flowing C-minor music of the river.
fields.Clue: Three one-act operas premiered together at the Metropolitan Opera in 1918: a grim barge drama on the Seine, a convent tragedy for an all-female cast, and a Florentine comedy in which a schemer impersonates the dead Buoso Donati and his daughter sings “O mio babbino caro”.

fields.Description: The first panel of Il trittico, a grim Seine barge drama in which a bargeman kills his wife's lover and reveals the body under his cloak.
fields.Listen: Dark, conversational verismo singing over the orchestra's slow, flowing C-minor music of the river.
fields.Clue: A bargeman on the Seine suspects his young wife Giorgetta of loving the stevedore Luigi, strangles him, and reveals the body to her at the end; the first panel of its composer's triptych, it premiered at the Met in 1918.

fields.Description: The middle panel of Il trittico, for female voices only: a nun learns her illegitimate child is dead, takes poison, and begs the Virgin for forgiveness.
fields.Listen: Soprano lament over shimmering strings and harp; an all-female cast, no male voices.

fields.Description: A medieval tragedy in which a blind king strangles his daughter-in-law and smears poison on her lips to trap whichever man kisses the corpse.
fields.Listen: Post-Wagnerian Italian: continuous orchestral flow, no set-piece arias, dark low brass.

fields.Description: Massenet's version makes Salome love John the Baptist and kill herself over his body, which is why the Paris Opéra refused it.
Massenet's version of the Abbé Prévost novel; Puccini set the same story a decade later and said Massenet felt it as a Frenchman and he as an Italian.
fields.Listen: Des Grieux's “Ah! fuyez, douce image”: a yearning tenor melody that swells to a passionate climax and falls back.
fields.Clue: About to take holy orders at Saint-Sulpice, the Chevalier des Grieux begs a sweet image to leave him in “Ah! fuyez, douce image”, until his lover arrives and wins him back; after the Abbé Prévost novel, the heroine sings “Adieu, notre petite table” and dies on the road to Le Havre.

fields.Description: After Pierre Corneille; its ballet music is more often played than the opera.
After Goethe's novel. Rejected by the Opéra-Comique as too gloomy and premiered in Vienna instead; contains the Ossian aria.
Massenet wrote the title role for Feodor Chaliapin. The knight dies seeing Dulcinea's face in a star.
A French operetta remembered for its Swing Song, a duet sung on a garden swing.
fields.Listen: French operetta: brisk elegant waltz and polka tunes, light and transparent.

fields.Description: Humperdinck set his sister's nursery-play text in a Wagnerian orchestral idiom; Richard Strauss conducted the premiere and called it a masterpiece.
Humperdinck's second fairy-tale opera, in which a goose-girl and a prince die eating a poisoned loaf.
A fairy-tale allegory in which an Empress with no shadow cannot bear children and must buy one from a dyer's wife. Strauss's largest score; Hofmannsthal's most elaborate libretto.
fields.Listen: Vast orchestra with celesta, glass harmonica, and organ; shimmering fairy-tale colour and very high soprano lines.

fields.Description: Strauss's last collaboration with Hugo von Hofmannsthal, who died before revising it; Strauss set the first act as it stood. A Viennese comedy turning on a sister disguised as a boy.
fields.Listen: Lyric soprano writing over a huge but transparent orchestra, with Viennese waltz tunes recurring throughout.

fields.Description: Strauss's last opera, a conversation piece asking whether words or music come first in opera, set in a château and ending without answering.
fields.Listen: Rich, glowing late-Romantic string writing in A-flat major, a warm melody rising over lush harmonies in chamber-like textures.
fields.Clue: Its composer's last opera, set in a château near Paris in 1775: a poet and a composer court the widowed Countess Madeleine, debating whether words or music come first in opera; it opens with a string sextet played on stage and ends with her undecided after the “Moonlight Music”.

fields.Description: A “musical legend” in which the Renaissance composer saves church polyphony by writing the Pope Marcellus Mass, dictated to him by angels.
fields.Listen: Post-Wagnerian orchestral writing in archaic, modal harmonies that evoke Renaissance polyphony, the strings rising to a radiant climax.
fields.Clue: A “musical legend” in which the Renaissance composer, despairing after his wife's death, has the Mass for Pope Marcellus dictated to him by angels and so saves church polyphony from the Council of Trent; premiered in Munich in 1917 under Bruno Walter.

fields.Description: The operetta that saved its theatre from bankruptcy and swept the world, containing the Vilja Song and the waltz duet.
fields.Listen: Hanna's “Vilja-Lied”: a wistful soprano song of the wood-sprite who lures a young hunter, “Vilja, o Vilja, du Waldmägdelein”, its hushed refrain echoed by the chorus.
fields.Clue: Its rich heroine, Hanna Glawari, sings of a forest sprite in the “Vilja-Lied” at a Pontevedrin party in Paris, and Valencienne writes “I am a respectable wife” on a fan; Count Danilo prefers the dancers at Maxim's, a song Shostakovich's “Leningrad” Symphony is said to quote.

fields.Description: A Lehár operetta whose tenor aria Dein ist mein ganzes Herz was written for Richard Tauber; unusually for operetta, the lovers part.
Schoenberg abandoned tonality around 1908 and by 1923 had systematized the twelve-tone method, in which all twelve pitches sound before any repeats.
Schoenberg's twelve-tone opera in which Moses speaks and Aron sings, so the prophet cannot express what he knows. The third act was never set.

fields.Movement: Act I · “Glück, das mir verblieb” (“Marietta's Lute Song”)

fields.Description: Brecht and Weill's reworking of The Beggar's Opera, opening with the Ballad of Mack the Knife; it ran for years in Berlin until the Nazis banned it.
fields.Listen: Cabaret-style dance-band music with saxophone, banjo, and harmonium, mocking and sour.
fields.Clue: Its composer's reworking with Bertolt Brecht of The Beggar's Opera, premiered in Berlin in 1928: a street singer opens with the “Moritat” of Mack the Knife, the beggar king Peachum's daughter Polly marries Macheath, and a mounted messenger brings a mock-happy ending.

fields.Description: Brecht and Weill's opera about a city founded on money, where the only crime is having none. Its Alabama Song was later covered by The Doors.
Weill's American opera on a Manhattan tenement stoop, with Langston Hughes's lyrics, mixing Broadway idiom with operatic writing.
Written in the Theresienstadt ghetto, where Death goes on strike so that no one can die. Rehearsed but banned, and Ullmann was murdered at Auschwitz weeks later.
fields.Listen: Small ensemble with Weill-like cabaret irony, quoting Deutschland über alles and a Bach chorale.

fields.Description: Schulhoff's only opera, a jazz-inflected Don Juan condemned to be unable to die. He was Jewish and a communist and died in a Nazi internment camp.
fields.Listen: Jazz rhythms and dance-band inflection inside an expressionist opera; saxophone and flatted blues harmony.

fields.Description: A semi-autobiographical opera about a composer and the woman who bore his child, never staged in Janáček's lifetime.
A Prague landlord is transported to the moon and to the Hussite wars, satirizing the philistine in both.
After Alexander Ostrovsky's The Storm: a woman in a Volga town confesses adultery in a thunderstorm and drowns herself. Janáček wrote it in his sixties for Kamila Stösslová.
Drawn from a newspaper comic strip. The vixen is shot and her cubs go on; Janáček asked for its last scene at his funeral.
A 337-year-old singer sustained by an elixir finally refuses to renew it, after a Karel Čapek play about the horror of not dying.
After Dostoevsky's Siberian prison memoir, with almost no plot and no female lead. Janáček's last opera, inscribed that in every creature a spark of God.
After Hans Christian Andersen: a real nightingale outsings a mechanical one and its song brings the Emperor back from death. Its three acts are stylistically distinct.
An opera-oratorio in Latin, with a narrator speaking the audience's own language between scenes and the cast barely moving, masked.
A tale of possession and witch trials Prokofiev never saw staged; he reused its material in his Third Symphony.
A Soviet opera set in Ukraine in 1918; its director was arrested and shot during rehearsals.
Prokofiev's comic opera after Richard Brinsley Sheridan's The Duenna, written in 1940 and held back by the war.
Thirteen scenes after Tolstoy, revised for years under Soviet pressure to strengthen the patriotic half; never staged complete in Prokofiev's lifetime.
After Gogol. A civil servant's nose detaches and outranks him; includes an interlude for percussion alone, and Shostakovich wrote it at twenty-two.
Shostakovich's only operetta, a satire on Moscow housing shortages, which he later dismissed.
A one-act farce set in a clockmaker's shop, where a wife hides her lovers in grandfather clocks. Ravel called it a musical conversation piece.
Gertrude Stein's libretto makes little narrative sense and there are more than four saints. The 1934 premiere used an all-Black cast and cellophane sets.
fields.Listen: Plain, hymn-like tunes as the singers chant Gertrude Stein's circular text: “Saint Ignatius not there. Saint Ignatius staying where. Never heard them speak speak of it.”
fields.Clue: Its Gertrude Stein libretto makes little narrative sense, has many more holy figures than its title promises, and includes the line “Pigeons on the grass alas”; the 1934 Hartford premiere used an all-Black cast and cellophane sets by Florine Stettheimer.

fields.Description: A surrealist farce after Guillaume Apollinaire in which a wife's breasts float away as balloons and her husband bears forty thousand children.
A forty-minute monologue for one soprano on a telephone, after Jean Cocteau, hearing only her side of a conversation with the lover leaving her.
Messiaen's only opera, over four hours, with birdsong transcribed from three continents and an orchestra of around 120 including three ondes Martenot.
A twelve-tone opera in which a prisoner of the Inquisition is allowed to escape into the garden only to find the Grand Inquisitor waiting: hope itself was the final torture.
fields.Listen: Twelve-tone writing used dramatically — three recurring row-based motifs, a huge orchestra, and an offstage chorus.

fields.Description: Nono's first opera, on a migrant worker met with police violence; its Venice premiere was disrupted by neo-fascist protesters.
fields.Listen: Twelve-tone writing with tape, shouted chorus, and projections; deliberately harsh and fragmented.

fields.Description: After a play on the real Carlo Gesualdo murders: a prince kills his wife and her lover. Scored at the edge of audibility, mostly very quiet.
fields.Listen: Extremely quiet and sparse — breath tones, tiny gestures, long silences — under a slow declaimed vocal line.

fields.Description: After Georg Büchner's play, and the opera that reopened the Salzburg Festival in 1947. The crowd is a character; Danton goes to the guillotine arguing with Robespierre about the Terror.
fields.Listen: Neoclassical tonality with sharp ostinati and big declamatory choruses.

fields.Description: Zimmermann's only opera, with simultaneous scenes on stacked stages and film projection, so notoriously difficult that it was long declared unperformable.
