fields.Listen: Several scenes played simultaneously with jazz band, tape, organ, and huge percussion — deliberate sensory overload.

fields.Description: Written for Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau, who had asked for a Lear for decades. The storm is built from tone clusters and quarter tones.
fields.Listen: Microtonal string clusters and extreme vocal range; the title role shouts and speaks as well as sings.

fields.Description: After Antonin Artaud, on the fall of Tenochtitlan: Cortés is a baritone and Montezuma a soprano, with the orchestra spread around the audience.
fields.Listen: Percussion-dominated and spatially separated, with howling and whispering voices over sustained bands of noise.

fields.Audio: [sound:cmc-Ligeti (Le Grand Macabre Mysteries of the Macabre).mp3]
fields.Description: Ligeti's only opera, opening with a prelude for twelve motor horns. Death arrives to end the world and fails, apparently because he is drunk.
A Finnish opera on the medieval bishop of Finland, in Rautavaara's mystical vein.
fields.Listen: Slowly shifting tonal clusters and modal chant fragments over sustained strings.

fields.Description: A Danish opera after Margaret Atwood, cutting between Offred's past and present with the two versions of her sung by different singers.
fields.Listen: Two sopranos as one character; Amazing Grace and Lutheran chorale quoted against grinding dissonance.

fields.Description: A chamber opera for eight singers with a Male and Female Chorus who comment from outside the action and impose a Christian ending on a Roman story.
fields.Listen: Eight singers and twelve players, with two narrators commenting from outside the action in an austere idiom.

fields.Description: A chamber opera for thirteen players, set in a Suffolk village where no girl is virtuous enough to be May Queen, so a grocer's boy is crowned King of the May instead.
fields.Listen: Spiky, comic chamber writing for thirteen players, with fast, chattering recitative.
fields.Clue: After a story by Maupassant: a Suffolk village can find no girl virtuous enough to be May Queen, so a greengrocer's boy is crowned King of the May, gets drunk on spiked lemonade, and runs off for a night.

fields.Description: After Henry James's ghost story: a governess fights the ghosts of Peter Quint and Miss Jessel for the two children in her care.
fields.Listen: The Prologue: a tenor narrator, accompanied only by piano, tells how the governess took her post on one condition, that she never trouble the children's guardian.
fields.Clue: Its Prologue, for tenor and piano, sets up a governess's post at Bly; a twelve-note theme and fifteen variations, one between each scene, carry her struggle with the ghosts of Peter Quint and Miss Jessel.

fields.Description: Britten and Peter Pears cut Shakespeare's text to a libretto, keeping almost only his words; Puck is a speaking acrobat.
fields.Listen: The enchanted wood: sliding string glissandi, celesta and harp, and boys' voices for the fairies.
fields.Clue: Its composer and Peter Pears cut Shakespeare's play into a libretto almost entirely in his words; Oberon is a countertenor written for Alfred Deller, Puck is a speaking acrobat, and the mechanicals' play parodies Donizetti.

fields.Description: A church parable for a Fenland church, after a Japanese Noh play Britten saw in Tokyo. No conductor, monks in procession, and the Madwoman sung by a man.
fields.Listen: Church parable: an all-male cast processing in singing plainchant, seven players, no conductor, and a heterophonic texture drawn from Japanese noh.

fields.Description: Britten's last opera, after Thomas Mann. Aschenbach's thoughts are set as accompanied recitative at the piano, and one baritone sings all seven figures who push him toward death.
fields.Listen: Restless, shimmering orchestral writing as the gondola arrives in Venice; tuned percussion in a gamelan style marks the world of the boy Tadzio.
fields.Clue: Its composer's last opera, after Thomas Mann: Aschenbach's thoughts are set as piano-accompanied recitative, and one baritone sings all seven figures who lure him toward his end.

fields.Work: The Man Who Mistook His Wife for a Hat
fields.Audio: [sound:cmc-Nyman (The Man Who Mistook His Wife for a Hat).mp3]
fields.Description: A chamber opera after Oliver Sacks's case study of a man with visual agnosia, who reaches for his wife's head mistaking it for his hat. Nyman scored it for three singers and a small ensemble.
fields.Listen: Small ensemble in driving repetitive minimalist patterns, with Schumann's Ich grolle nicht quoted as the still centre.

fields.Description: Tavener's icon-like opera on the desert saint, static and ritualistic, written in his Orthodox idiom.
fields.Listen: Orthodox chant-derived drones, bells, and long unison lines; static, ritual, and resolutely consonant.

fields.Description: Turnage's first opera, transposing Oedipus to Thatcher-era East London, with the plague as urban decay and an ending that refuses the myth.
fields.Listen: Jazz and punk inflection in an opera pit: saxophones, drum kit, blues-derived harmony, shouted English.

fields.Description: The first opera written for American television, broadcast by NBC on Christmas Eve 1951; a disabled shepherd boy offers his crutch to the Three Kings and is healed.
fields.Listen: The shepherds' dance: a lively, folk-like dance led by the woodwinds in a rustic, lilting rhythm.
fields.Clue: Its shepherds dance and offer olives and quinces to three kings resting at a poor hut on their way to Bethlehem; the first opera written for American television, broadcast by NBC on Christmas Eve 1951, its disabled shepherd boy offers his crutch as a gift and is healed.

fields.Movement: Act I · “Must the Winter Come So Soon”
fields.Description: Barber's Pulitzer-winning opera to Gian Carlo Menotti's libretto, set in a northern country house where a woman has waited twenty years behind covered mirrors.
fields.Listen: A short, wistful mezzo-soprano lament over hushed strings and woodwinds.
fields.Clue: Erika sings “Must the winter come so soon?” as she and the title character wait for Anatol in a country house whose mirrors have been covered for twenty years.

fields.Description: A one-act opera on a failing suburban marriage, with a jazz trio commenting like an advertising jingle.
On Gandhi's years in South Africa, sung in Sanskrit from the Bhagavad Gita, with Tolstoy, Rabindranath Tagore, and Martin Luther King Jr. watching from above the stage.
fields.Listen: Slowly repeating arpeggios and chords building in layers, minimalist patterns that shift by small steps.
fields.Clue: On Gandhi's years in South Africa, sung in Sanskrit from the Bhagavad Gita, with Tolstoy, Rabindranath Tagore, and Martin Luther King Jr. presiding over its three acts; it ends with Gandhi singing a rising Phrygian scale thirty times.

fields.Description: The third of Glass's portrait operas, after Einstein on the Beach and Satyagraha. Sung in Akkadian, Egyptian, and Hebrew, with the pharaoh written for countertenor.
fields.Listen: Repeating arpeggios that rock between A minor and A major, the bed for the countertenor pharaoh's long, rapt hymn.
fields.Clue: Its countertenor pharaoh sings a long hymn to the sun-disc Aten in the audience's own language, and an offstage chorus answers with Psalm 104 in Hebrew; the third of its composer's “portrait” operas, its other texts are in Akkadian, Egyptian, and Hebrew.

fields.Work: I Was Looking at the Ceiling and Then I Saw the Sky
fields.Audio: [sound:cmc-Adams (I Was Looking at the Ceiling and Then I Saw the Sky).mp3]
fields.Description: A song play for seven singers and a pop band, set around the 1994 Northridge earthquake in Los Angeles.
A Nativity oratorio using medieval mystery texts and Latin American poetry, including Rosario Castellanos on the Tlatelolco massacre.
Usually called the first English opera, a masque for Charles II's court in which the king's mistress sang Venus and their daughter played Cupid.
fields.Listen: Restoration court music for strings and continuo: dotted French-overture rhythms and dances, with recitative in free, declamatory English.
fields.Clue: Usually called the first English opera, this masque for Charles II's court cast the king's mistress Mary Davis as the goddess of love and their daughter as Cupid; its closing chorus was the model for the end of Dido and Aeneas.

fields.Description: A semi-opera on A Midsummer Night's Dream in which none of Shakespeare's characters sing; the score was lost for two centuries.
An intermezzo played between the acts of a serious opera; its Paris revival in 1752 set off the Querelle des Bouffons over French versus Italian style.
fields.Listen: Quick-fire secco recitative in Italian over sparse harpsichord chords: the maid sparring with her master, announcing that she has found herself a match.
fields.Clue: In this comic intermezzo, written to be played between the acts of its composer's serious opera Il prigionier superbo, the maid Serpina tricks her bachelor master Uberto into marriage with the help of the mute servant Vespone; its 1752 Paris revival set off the Querelle des Bouffons.

fields.Description: An opera-ballet in four exotic entrées, one of which introduced a dance of the peace pipe after Rameau saw Native American dancers in Paris.
Rameau's tragédie en musique on the twins who share immortality; its 1737 premiere fuelled the quarrel between his supporters and Lully's.
Handel's first Italian opera for London, written in two weeks from borrowed material. Contains Lascia ch'io pianga.
A Handel magic opera after Ludovico Ariosto: a sorceress turns her discarded lovers into rocks and beasts, and loses her powers when she falls in love herself.
A ballad opera setting new words to popular tunes, satirizing Italian opera and Robert Walpole's government. Its highwayman hero is reprieved because the audience demands it.
fields.Listen: The highwayman's air “Pretty Polly, say”: he asks if her fancy strayed while he was away, and she answers “Without disguise, heaving sighs, doting eyes”, all to a plain, popular strophic tune.
fields.Clue: The highwayman Macheath sings “Pretty Polly, say” to his secret wife, the daughter of the fence Peachum, in this ballad opera; Johann Christoph Pepusch arranged its popular tunes, and it satirized Italian opera and Robert Walpole's government.

fields.Description: Hindemith's painter is Matthias Grünewald, torn between art and the Peasants' War. The Nazis banned it, prompting Wilhelm Furtwängler's public defence and Hindemith's exile.
fields.Listen: Hushed, glowing string chords open the movement; then the trombones softly intone the old hymn “Es sungen drei Engel”.
fields.Clue: Its first movement, an “angel concert”, was drawn from its composer's opera about the painter of the Isenheim Altarpiece, which the Nazis banned despite Wilhelm Furtwängler's public defence.

fields.Description: Begun as a ballet for Léonide Massine, who rejected Hindemith's treatment of Weber; the Turandot scherzo builds a fugue on a Chinese tune Weber had used.
The archetypal Romantic ballet: a peasant girl dies of a broken heart and joins the Wilis, spirits who dance men to death, and saves her betrayer by dancing in his place until dawn.
fields.Listen: Set at night among the Wilis' graves: hushed strings and harp, with first-act themes returning as leitmotifs.
fields.Clue: In this ballet's second act, Myrtha, queen of the Wilis, orders the dead heroine to dance her faithless lover to death, but she shields him until dawn.

fields.Description: A comic ballet in which a girl impersonates the life-size doll an inventor is trying to bring to life.
fields.Listen: A swaggering mazurka for full orchestra, with heavy accents on the second beat.
fields.Clue: Its Act I mazurka is a showpiece for character dancers; the village girl Swanhilda impersonates the toymaker's life-size doll, after a tale by E. T. A. Hoffmann.

fields.Description: Boulez's serial cantata on René Char, for alto and six players including xylorimba, vibraphone, and guitar, its instrumentation drawn from non-Western ensembles.
The archetypal French grand opera, five acts ending in the St Bartholomew's Day Massacre, and the first opera to be performed a thousand times at the Paris Opéra.
fields.Listen: Graceful, elegant orchestral writing in C major for the garden scene at Chenonceau, where Queen Marguerite de Valois holds court.
fields.Clue: Its second act, in the gardens of Chenonceau, opens with Marguerite de Valois's “Ô beau pays de la Touraine”, as she tries to reconcile Catholics and Protestants by marrying Raoul to Valentine; the archetypal French grand opera, with a libretto by Eugène Scribe, it ends in the St Bartholomew's Day Massacre.

fields.Description: A cantata on the writing on the wall, with the chorus shouting “Slain!” at the king's death. Commissioned by the BBC for small forces, it grew into a Leeds Festival showpiece with two extra brass bands.
fields.Listen: Hard-edged chorus and blazing brass in jagged, syncopated rhythms, broken by sudden hushed passages.
fields.Clue: A cantata on the writing on the wall, its text chosen by Osbert Sitwell from Daniel and Psalm 137: the baritone lists the gods of gold, silver, iron, wood, stone, and brass, each with its own instrument, and the chorus shouts “Slain!” at the king's death; commissioned by the BBC for small forces, it grew into a Leeds Festival showpiece with two extra brass bands.

fields.Description: A ballet on an African creation myth scored for a jazz band of seventeen players, written after Milhaud heard jazz in Harlem, with a blues fugue.
A set of piano studies for finger speed by Beethoven's pupil and Liszt's teacher, still standard practice material.
fields.Listen: A finger study for piano: one fast figuration of running scales and arpeggios repeated through changing harmonies, harmonically plain.
fields.Clue: A set of piano studies for finger speed by Beethoven's pupil and Liszt's teacher, still standard practice material.

fields.Description: A comic troupe and an opera seria company are ordered to perform simultaneously to finish before the fireworks. The Composer is sung by a woman.
fields.Listen: This Prologue opens with a brisk, witty orchestral introduction in chamber-sized scoring before the backstage bickering begins.
fields.Clue: Its Prologue is set backstage in the house of the richest man in Vienna, where a comic troupe led by Zerbinetta and a serious opera company are ordered to perform at once to finish before the fireworks; the young Composer is a trouser role for mezzo-soprano, and Bacchus rescues the abandoned heroine.

fields.Description: Puccini's first success, with five librettists and none credited. Ends with the lovers dying in a desert outside New Orleans.
Set in a California gold-rush camp, after David Belasco's play, it premiered at the Metropolitan Opera in 1910 with Enrico Caruso; Minnie wins the bandit Dick Johnson's life in a poker game.
fields.Listen: This opera opens with a surging orchestral prelude: a passionate theme over augmented, whole-tone harmonies, then a syncopated cakewalk rhythm.
fields.Clue: Set in a California gold-rush camp after David Belasco's play, it premiered at the Metropolitan Opera in 1910 with Enrico Caruso as the bandit Ramerrez, alias Dick Johnson, who sings “Ch'ella mi creda” before his planned hanging; the saloon owner Minnie wins his life from Sheriff Jack Rance in a poker game.

fields.Movement: Act III · Lisa's arioso “Akh, istomilas' ya gorem”
fields.Description: After Pushkin: a gambler frightens an old countess to death trying to learn three winning cards, and her ghost returns to name them.
fields.Listen: Lisa's arioso at the Winter Canal, sung here in German: a soprano's long, despairing lament that her life, once bright, has turned to grief, as she waits at midnight for Herman.
fields.Clue: After Pushkin: the gambler Herman frightens an old countess to death trying to learn her secret of three winning cards; her ghost names them (three, seven, ace), Lisa drowns herself in the Winter Canal, and the last card turns up as the title one.

fields.Description: On J. Robert Oppenheimer and the Trinity test, with a libretto assembled from declassified documents, poetry, and the Bhagavad Gita. Ends waiting for the countdown.
fields.Listen: From this opera's first act, in the days before the Trinity test: an urgent orchestral pulse of repeated minor-key figures, with brass surging against the ostinato.
fields.Clue: Its first act ends with the title character singing John Donne's sonnet “Batter my heart, three-person'd God” on the eve of the Trinity test.

fields.Description: On the Achille Lauro hijacking and the murder of a wheelchair-using passenger. Its choruses of exiled Jews and Palestinians made it the most protested modern opera.
fields.Listen: This opera's opening “Chorus of Exiled Palestinians”: slow, keening choral lines over a pulsing orchestra, recalling a father's house razed in 1948.
fields.Clue: It opens with paired choruses of exiled Palestinians and exiled Jews before the hijacking of the Achille Lauro, and the murdered passenger sings “The Aria of the Falling Body”.

fields.Description: A suite from Kodály's opera about a veteran hussar's tall tales, among them beating Napoleon single-handed.
fields.Listen: Colourful, folk-flavoured Hungarian orchestral writing, by turns comic and grand.
fields.Clue: A suite from its composer's opera about a veteran hussar's tall tales, among them beating Napoleon single-handed; it opens with an orchestral “sneeze”, since in Hungary a sneeze means a tale is true, and features the cimbalom and a Viennese Musical Clock.

fields.Nickname: The three parts are exposition, development, and recapitulation, often with a slow introduction and a coda.
fields.Description: The standard first-movement plan in three parts: a statement of two contrasting key areas, a middle section that fragments and modulates them, and a return in which both are heard in the home key.

fields.Nickname: Schematically ABACA or ABACABA; typical of a finale.
fields.Description: A movement in which a recurring main theme alternates with contrasting episodes, returning to the tune each time.

fields.Nickname: ABA; the minuet-and-trio and the da capo aria are both examples.
fields.Description: A three-part plan in which an opening section is followed by a contrasting one and then repeated.

fields.Nickname: AB; the standard shape of a Baroque dance movement.
fields.Description: A two-part plan, each part usually repeated, the first moving away from the home key and the second returning.

fields.Nickname: The Goldbergs, the Diabellis, and the Enigma are the towering sets.
fields.Description: A movement stating a tune and then restating it repeatedly with changes of harmony, rhythm, register, or figuration.

fields.Nickname: Entries alternate subject and answer; the middle is spun from episodes and stretto.
fields.Description: A contrapuntal movement in which a subject stated alone is answered in turn by each entering voice and then developed against itself.

fields.Nickname: A round is the simplest kind; Pachelbel's is built over a ground bass.
fields.Description: A texture in which one voice states a line and another repeats it exactly a fixed distance later, the two sounding together.

fields.Nickname: Basso ostinato; “Dido's Lament” and Purcell's laments generally are built on one.
fields.Description: A short pattern in the lowest part repeated unaltered throughout while the upper parts change above it.

fields.Nickname: Bach's in C minor for organ and the finale of Brahms's Fourth are the models.
fields.Description: Continuous variations over a repeating bass line or harmonic pattern, generally in a slow triple metre.

fields.Nickname: Bach's, ending the D minor Partita for solo violin, is the most celebrated.
fields.Description: Continuous variation over a repeating chord progression rather than a fixed melodic bass.

fields.Nickname: Vivaldi standardized it; the refrain is progressively fragmented and moves through related keys.
fields.Description: The recurring orchestral refrain of a Baroque concerto movement, returning between passages for the soloist.

fields.Nickname: The instruction to go back to the head gives it its name; the staple of opera seria.
fields.Description: An operatic number whose opening section returns after a contrasting middle, the singer expected to ornament the repeat.

fields.Nickname: Common in folk song and hymnody; its opposite is a through-composed setting.
fields.Description: A setting in which every stanza of the text is sung to the same music.

fields.Nickname: Durchkomponiert; Franz Schubert's “Erlkönig” is the standard example.
fields.Description: A setting with new music for each stanza, following the text rather than repeating a tune.

fields.Nickname: The third movement of a Classical symphony until Ludwig van Beethoven replaced it with something faster.
fields.Description: A stately triple-metre movement paired with a lighter contrasting one, after which the first returns.

fields.Nickname: Italian for “joke”; Beethoven made it the standard replacement for the minuet.
fields.Description: A fast triple-metre movement, boisterous or unsettling, that displaced the courtly dance in the symphony.

fields.Nickname: César Franck and Hector Berlioz are its great practitioners.
fields.Description: A multi-movement work unified by bringing back the same theme in later movements.

fields.Nickname: ABCBA; Béla Bartók used it repeatedly, in the fourth and fifth quartets and Concerto for Orchestra.
fields.Description: A symmetrical plan whose sections mirror around a central one.

fields.Nickname: Common in Ludwig van Beethoven's finales.
fields.Description: A finale combining a recurring refrain with the key scheme and development of first-movement design.

fields.Nickname: Franz Liszt invented the type; Strauss's are the most elaborate. Also called a tone poem.
fields.Description: A single-movement orchestral work whose shape follows a story, a piece of literature or a picture rather than an abstract plan.

fields.Nickname: The small group is the concertino, the full body the ripieno; Arcangelo Corelli and George Frideric Handel wrote sets, Bach the Brandenburgs.
fields.Description: A Baroque work setting a small group of soloists against the full body of strings.

fields.Nickname: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart's for violin and viola is the best known.
fields.Description: An orchestral work with two or more soloists, standing between concerto and symphony.

fields.Nickname: Haydn's The Creation is the other standard example; a narrator often carries the plot.
fields.Description: A large unstaged setting of a sacred story for soloists, chorus, and orchestra, without scenery or action.

fields.Nickname: Bach wrote some two hundred surviving sacred ones for the Lutheran year.
fields.Description: A modest vocal work in several movements with instruments, sacred or secular, for church or chamber.

fields.Nickname: Metastasio supplied most of the libretti; Handel and the young Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart wrote them.
fields.Description: The serious 18th-century Italian type on mythological or heroic subjects, built from recitative and da capo arias.

fields.Nickname: The Marriage of Figaro and The Barber of Seville.
fields.Description: The comic Italian type with contemporary characters, ensemble finales, and a bass in a leading role.

fields.Nickname: The Magic Flute and The Abduction from the Seraglio are Mozart's.
fields.Description: A German type alternating sung numbers with spoken dialogue rather than recitative.

fields.Nickname: Cavalleria rusticana and Pagliacci launched it; Giacomo Puccini is its greatest figure.
fields.Description: A late Italian operatic manner taking violent, ordinary contemporary life as its subject.

fields.Nickname: Bellini, Gaetano Donizetti, and the Gioachino Rossini of the serious operas.
fields.Description: An early 19th-century Italian style prizing long-breathed lyrical line, evenness of tone, and florid decoration.

fields.Nickname: Schubert wrote over six hundred; Robert Schumann, Johannes Brahms, and Wolf followed.
fields.Description: A German setting of a lyric poem for solo voice and piano, the keyboard an equal partner rather than accompaniment.
A set of songs ordered to be performed together, linked by narrative, poet, or musical thread.

fields.Nickname: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart's unfinished one, Giuseppe Verdi's, Gabriel Fauré's, and Benjamin Britten's War Requiem.
fields.Description: A setting of the Mass for the dead, taking its name from the opening plea for rest.

fields.Nickname: Josquin, Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina, and Byrd; in the medieval version each voice could carry a different text.
fields.Description: A polyphonic setting of a sacred Latin text, unaccompanied in Renaissance practice.

fields.Nickname: Flourished in Italy and then England; Claudio Monteverdi's eight books trace the shift to the Baroque.
fields.Description: A secular part-song for a handful of unaccompanied voices, closely illustrating its poem.

fields.Nickname: Bach harmonized hundreds and built cantatas and preludes on them.
fields.Description: A Lutheran congregational hymn tune, plain and four-square, used as raw material by later composers.
An organ piece elaborating a hymn tune, played to introduce the congregation's singing of it.

fields.Nickname: Gregorian chant; notated in neumes on a four-line staff.
fields.Description: The unaccompanied single-line liturgical melody of the Western church, unmeasured and modal.

fields.Nickname: Léonin and Pérotin at Notre-Dame took it from parallel motion to florid melisma.
fields.Description: The earliest Western polyphony, adding one or more lines to an existing chant.

fields.Composer: Chopin's Nocturne in E-flat major, Op. 9 No. 2
fields.Nickname: John Field invented the type; Chopin perfected it.
fields.Description: A lyrical, reflective piano piece evoking night, with a singing right hand over spread left-hand harmony.

fields.Nickname: Chopin's and Franz Liszt's are the point at which the exercise became art.
fields.Description: A piece written to drill one technical problem, raised by the Romantics into concert music.

fields.Composer: Debussy's Prelude to the Afternoon of a Faun
fields.Nickname: Bach paired them with fugues; Frédéric Chopin and Debussy wrote independent sets.
fields.Description: A short piece originally introducing something larger, later free-standing and often collected by key.

fields.Composer: Bach's Toccata and Fugue in D minor
fields.Nickname: From the Italian for “touched”; Bach's D minor for organ is the famous one.
fields.Description: A showpiece for keyboard in free style, displaying the player's touch with runs and full chords.

fields.Nickname: Also used for works quoting other music, as in Vaughan Williams's on a theme by Thomas Tallis.
fields.Description: A piece in free form following the composer's invention rather than a set plan.

fields.Nickname: Bach wrote sets for keyboard and for solo violin.
fields.Description: A suite of contrasting dance movements, particularly in German Baroque usage.

fields.Nickname: The French kind opens slow with dotted rhythms; the Italian is fast-slow-fast and grows into the symphony.
fields.Description: The orchestral piece opening an opera or oratorio, or a self-contained concert work in that manner.

fields.Nickname: Liszt's Hungarian set, Brahms's Alto Rhapsody, and his two for solo piano.
fields.Description: A free, episodic single-movement piece of heroic or national character.

fields.Nickname: Ludwig van Beethoven published three sets; Für Elise is a stand-alone one.
fields.Description: A short, light keyboard piece of no great pretension.

fields.Nickname: Franz Schubert and Chopin wrote the best-known sets.
fields.Description: A short lyric keyboard piece written to sound spontaneous.

fields.Nickname: Chopin wrote some sixty, drawing on three distinct folk types.
fields.Description: A Polish triple-metre dance with the accent thrown onto the second or third beat.

fields.Nickname: Chopin's are the national monuments of the type.
fields.Description: A stately Polish processional dance in triple metre with a characteristic short-short-long opening.

fields.Nickname: Plainchant is the central Western repertory of it.
fields.Description: A single unaccompanied melodic line, whether sung by one voice or many in unison.

fields.Nickname: The prevailing texture of the Classical period.
fields.Description: One melody clearly in charge, supported by parts that move with it as accompaniment.

fields.Nickname: Renaissance sacred music and the Baroque fugue are its high points.
fields.Description: Two or more independent melodic lines of comparable interest sounding at once.

fields.Nickname: Characteristic of much traditional music outside Europe.
fields.Description: Several performers elaborating the same melody simultaneously in slightly different ways.

fields.Nickname: Codified in species by Fux; Bach is its supreme practitioner.
fields.Description: The craft of combining independent lines so that each makes sense alone and all agree vertically.

fields.Nickname: Cello or bassoon with harpsichord or organ; the defining sound of the period.
fields.Description: The Baroque accompanying group of a bass instrument and a chord-playing one realizing the harmony from figures.

fields.Nickname: Realising it was an improvised skill every Baroque continuo player had.
fields.Description: A shorthand of numerals under the lowest part telling the keyboard player which chords to fill in.

fields.Nickname: Ubiquitous in Classical keyboard writing; the opening of Mozart's K. 545 is the textbook case.
fields.Description: A left-hand accompaniment breaking each chord into a repeating low-high-middle-high pattern.

fields.Nickname: Holst's Mars and Orff's “O Fortuna” both lean on one.
fields.Description: A short figure repeated persistently at the same pitch while other parts change around it.

fields.Nickname: Named for the organ pedal; typically on the tonic or dominant and used to build tension before a close.
fields.Description: A sustained note, usually in the bass, held while the harmonies above it change and clash against it.

fields.Nickname: Compresses the material and usually signals that the movement is driving to its close.
fields.Description: Overlapping entries of a fugue subject, each beginning before the last has finished.

fields.Nickname: Frequently combined with its opposite in a fugue's later stages.
fields.Description: Restating a theme in longer note values, so it moves at half speed or slower.
Restating a theme in shorter note values, so it moves faster than first heard.

fields.Nickname: A staple of fugue and a required operation on a twelve-tone row.
fields.Description: Turning a melodic line upside down, so every rising interval falls by the same distance and vice versa.

fields.Nickname: One of the four forms of a twelve-tone row, with the original, inversion, and retrograde inversion.
fields.Description: Playing a series of notes backwards, from last to first.

fields.Nickname: Real sequence keeps the intervals exactly; tonal sequence adjusts them to the key.
fields.Description: Immediately repeating a short figure at a higher or lower pitch level, usually more than once.

fields.Nickname: A madrigalism; endemic in the English and Italian madrigal.
fields.Description: Illustrating the literal meaning of the text in the music that sets it, so that 'descend' falls and 'running' hurries.

fields.Nickname: Arnold Schoenberg devised it around 1921; the ordering is a row or series, deployed in four forms and twelve transpositions.
fields.Description: Composing from a fixed ordering of all the chromatic pitches, every one sounded before any returns.

fields.Nickname: Milton Babbitt, Pierre Boulez, and Karlheinz Stockhausen carried it beyond pitch after 1945.
fields.Description: Ordering musical material by a fixed series; in its total form, extending that control to rhythm, dynamics, and attack as well as pitch.

fields.Nickname: Arnold Schoenberg's free period before he systematized the twelve-tone method.
fields.Description: Writing that avoids any tonal centre, so no pitch functions as home.

fields.Composer: Debussy's Prelude to the Afternoon of a Faun
fields.Nickname: Because every step is the same, it has no leading note and no clear centre; Debussy uses it for suspension.
fields.Description: A six-note collection built entirely from equal steps, with no semitone anywhere in it.

fields.Nickname: Also called the diminished scale; central to Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov, Igor Stravinsky, and Olivier Messiaen.
fields.Description: An eight-note collection alternating semitone and tone.

fields.Nickname: Found worldwide in traditional music and used by Claude Debussy, Antonín Dvořák, and Béla Bartók for colour.
fields.Description: A five-note collection with no semitones, the pattern of the black keys.

fields.Nickname: A cadential mannerism in Baroque triple metre; Johannes Brahms uses it constantly.
fields.Description: A rhythmic shift making three groups of two sound where two groups of three are written, or the reverse.

fields.Nickname: Literally “robbed time”; associated above all with Frédéric Chopin.
fields.Description: Flexible performance timing, pushing and holding back against a steady underlying pulse.

fields.Nickname: Signalled by a fermata over a six-four chord; Ludwig van Beethoven began writing his own.
fields.Description: An unaccompanied solo flourish near the end of a concerto movement, once improvised, later written out.

fields.Nickname: The Queen of the Night's arias are the emblem; also a voice type specializing in it.
fields.Description: Elaborate rapid decoration of a vocal line with runs, leaps, and trills.

fields.Nickname: The opposite of syllabic setting; a mark of florid chant and of George Frideric Handel's choruses.
fields.Description: Singing several notes to a single syllable of text.

fields.Nickname: Half-sung, half-spoken: the voice touches the notated pitch and leaves it. Berg uses it in Wozzeck.
fields.Description: A delivery between speech and song, touching each pitch and immediately leaving it.

fields.Nickname: Wagner's Ring is built from them; the parallel device in Hector Berlioz is the idée fixe.
fields.Description: A short recurring musical idea attached to a character, object or notion, transformed as the drama develops.

fields.Audio: [sound:cmc-Berlioz (Symphonie fantastique mvt. V ( Songe d'une nuit du sabbat )).mp3]
fields.Nickname: Berlioz's own term; an ancestor of Wagner's leitmotif.
fields.Description: A single melody standing for the beloved, returning transformed in every movement of a programme symphony.

fields.Audio: [sound:cmc-Berlioz (Symphonie fantastique mvt. V ( Songe d'une nuit du sabbat )).mp3]
fields.Nickname: Its opposite is absolute music; Berlioz, Franz Liszt, and Strauss are its champions.
fields.Description: Instrumental music written to depict a story, scene or idea named outside the notes.

fields.Nickname: Hanslick argued for it against the programme composers; Johannes Brahms is its usual standard-bearer.
fields.Description: Instrumental music understood as needing no story or picture beyond its own patterns.

fields.Nickname: Chant or popular tune, often in long notes in the tenor; the basis of the medieval and Renaissance mass.
fields.Description: An existing melody taken as the fixed structural foundation on which new parts are composed.

fields.Nickname: The rhythmic unit is the talea, the pitch unit the color; Guillaume de Machaut and Guillaume Du Fay use it.
fields.Description: Building a part from a repeating rhythmic pattern and a repeating pitch series of different lengths, so they realign only gradually.

fields.Nickname: A medieval device, from the word for “hiccup”.
fields.Description: Splitting a single melodic line between two voices that alternate note and rest, so each fills the other's silences.

fields.Nickname: Terry Riley, Steve Reich, Philip Glass, and John Adams.
fields.Description: Writing built from short patterns repeated with very gradual change, steady pulse, and static harmony.

fields.Nickname: Reich's Piano Phase and Come Out are the demonstrations.
fields.Description: Starting two identical repeating patterns together and letting one drift slowly ahead of the other.

fields.Nickname: Cage's use of the I Ching; also called chance or indeterminate music.
fields.Description: Composition in which some element is deliberately left to chance or to the performer's choice.
Composition assembled from recorded real-world sound manipulated on tape rather than written for players.

fields.Nickname: Cage's invention; the Sonatas and Interludes is the central work.
fields.Description: A keyboard altered by placing screws, bolts, felt, and rubber between the strings, turning it into a percussion battery.

fields.Nickname: The witches' sabbath in the Symphonie fantastique and Holst's Mars.
fields.Description: Striking the string with the wood of the bow instead of drawing the hair across it.

fields.Nickname: Its opposite, over the fingerboard, is sul tasto.
fields.Description: Bowing very close to the bridge to produce a thin, glassy, and metallic sound.

fields.Nickname: Béla Bartók pizzicato snaps the string against the fingerboard.
fields.Description: Plucking a string instrument's strings with the finger rather than bowing them.

fields.Nickname: The clarinet opening of Rhapsody in Blue is the famous instance.
fields.Description: Sliding continuously or by rapid steps from one pitch to another.

fields.Nickname: A staple of orchestral tension writing.
fields.Description: Rapid reiteration of a single pitch, or rapid alternation between two.

fields.Nickname: Achieved on wind instruments by unconventional fingering and embouchure.
fields.Description: Producing more than one pitch at a time on an instrument built to sound one.

fields.Nickname: The engine of sonata form; the pivot chord is the commonest means.
fields.Description: Moving from one key to another and establishing the new one as home.

fields.Nickname: Prepared, struck, resolved; the central expressive device of Renaissance and Baroque counterpoint.
fields.Description: Holding a note from one chord into the next, where it clashes, and then resolving it downward by step.

fields.Nickname: A leaning note; the sigh figures of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart's slow movements.
fields.Description: An accented note foreign to the chord, resolving by step to the note it displaced.
A close moving from the chord on the fourth degree to the tonic.

fields.Nickname: Also called an interrupted cadence; a favourite way of extending a passage.
fields.Description: A close that sets up a resolution to the tonic and goes somewhere else, usually the submediant.

fields.Nickname: Standard in Renaissance and Baroque practice.
fields.Description: Ending a piece in the minor with a major chord, the crucial degree raised at the last moment.

fields.Nickname: Largely improvised in Baroque practice and indicated by symbols rather than written out.
fields.Description: Decorating a melodic line with small added notes -- trills, turns, mordents, and grace notes.

fields.Nickname: Bach's arias frequently pair a voice with one.
fields.Description: An instrumental part that is essential rather than optional, often duetting with the singer.

fields.Nickname: The larger body answering it is the ripieno or tutti.
fields.Description: The small group of soloists in a Baroque work set against the full ensemble.

fields.Nickname: It arrived with the first operas, in Florence around 1600.
fields.Description: Speech-like singing that follows the rhythm of the words and carries an opera's plot between the arias; secco when only the continuo accompanies it.
A self-contained solo song in an opera, oratorio, or cantata, where the action stops and a character reflects; the Baroque type repeats its first section da capo.

fields.Audio: [sound:cmc-Berlioz (Symphonie fantastique mvt. V ( Songe d'une nuit du sabbat )).mp3]
fields.Nickname: Also quoted by Liszt (Totentanz), Saint-Saëns (Danse macabre), and Rachmaninoff (Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini).
fields.Description: The medieval chant on the Day of Judgement from the Requiem Mass, whose four-note falling opening composers quote to mean death.
The unresolved half-diminished chord F, B, D-sharp, G-sharp in the second bar of a Wagner prelude, often called the start of modern harmony.

fields.Nickname: Written after the letter in names: B-flat, E-flat major.
fields.Description: The sign ♭, which lowers a note by a semitone; its opposite raises one.

fields.Nickname: Written after the letter in names: C-sharp minor, F-sharp major.
fields.Description: The sign ♯, which raises a note by a semitone; its opposite lowers one.

fields.Nickname: The label means spoken dialogue, not comedy: Carmen ends in a murder.
fields.Description: French opera with spoken dialogue between the musical numbers, whatever its mood; named after the Paris theatre that staged it.

fields.Nickname: The Paris Opéra required a ballet in Act II, which is why the Jockey Club wrecked Wagner's 1861 Tannhäuser when he put it in Act I.
fields.Description: The Paris spectacle of the 1830s to 1860s: five acts, a historical subject, massed choruses, a ballet, and lavish staging.

fields.Nickname: Ben Jonson wrote the texts and Inigo Jones the designs for the Stuart ones.
fields.Description: An English court entertainment of the 16th and 17th centuries combining poetry, song, dance, and elaborate scenery, in which courtiers themselves performed.
An 18th-century English stage work of spoken dialogue broken by new words set to popular tunes, usually satirical.
A light stage work with spoken dialogue, catchy songs, and dances, usually comic and sentimental; Jacques Offenbach in Paris, Johann Strauss II and Franz Lehár in Vienna.
A short piece set between larger ones: in the 18th century, a comic opera played between the acts of a serious one; later, an orchestral interlude inside an opera or a short piano piece.
Music written for a spoken play (overtures, entr'actes, songs, and underscoring), often gathered afterwards into a concert suite.
A set of instrumental movements played as one work: in the Baroque, stylized dances (allemande, courante, sarabande, gigue); later, any sequence drawn from a ballet, opera, or play.
Originally a song sung at evening beneath a lover's window; in the Classical period, a light piece in several movements for an outdoor or social occasion.
A short Romantic piano work that captures one mood or scene, often under a fanciful title.
An operatic set piece in which a heroine loses her reason, sung in dazzling coloratura, often with a solo flute echoing her.

fields.Nickname: Cherubino in The Marriage of Figaro and Octavian are the standard examples.
fields.Description: A male character written for a woman's voice, usually a mezzo-soprano playing a youth.

fields.Nickname: Britten wrote Oberon for Alfred Deller.
fields.Description: A male singer using a developed head voice to sing in the alto or even soprano range.

fields.Nickname: A fast rising arpeggio, the signature of Johann Stamitz's Mannheim orchestra; Beethoven's first piano sonata opens with one.
fields.Description: A rapidly rising arpeggio over a crescendo, the trademark of the Elector Palatine's court orchestra under Johann Stamitz in the 1750s.
A German movement of the 1760s and 1770s, named after a play, prizing turbulent emotion; in music, restless minor-key symphonies.
A chord of adjacent notes sounded together, such as a whole row of piano keys pressed with the forearm.

fields.Composer: Ketawang: Puspawarna (“Kinds of Flowers”), played by the court gamelan of the Paku Alaman, Yogyakarta
fields.Nickname: It tunes to the five-note sléndro or the seven-note pélog scale; this recording went into space on the Voyager Golden Record, and Debussy heard a gamelan at the 1889 Paris Exposition.
fields.Description: An Indonesian ensemble of tuned gongs, metallophones, and drums from Java and Bali, whose interlocking patterns influenced Debussy and Britten.
An alto oboe pitched a fifth below the oboe, with a bulb-shaped bell and a darker, melancholy tone; called the English horn in America.

fields.Audio: [sound:Tchaikovsky (Nutcracker - Dance of the Sugar Plum Fairy) (1).mp3]
fields.Nickname: Invented by Auguste Mustel in Paris in 1886.
fields.Description: A keyboard instrument whose hammers strike metal plates, giving a soft, bell-like sound.
An English Restoration hybrid in which a spoken play carries the plot and the music comes in separate episodes, usually sung by minor or supernatural characters.
The serious French opera of Lully and Rameau: five acts on myth or chivalric romance, a prologue praising the king, and dances throughout.
An 18th-century French stage genre of loosely linked acts, each with its own story, in which dance matters as much as singing.

fields.Nickname: The Wolf's Glen scene and the dungeon scene of Beethoven's Fidelio are the standard examples.
fields.Description: Spoken words delivered over or between passages of music.
Music using intervals smaller than a semitone, such as quarter tones.

fields.Nickname: Jean-Jacques Rousseau took the Italian side.
fields.Description: The 1752 to 1754 Paris pamphlet war over whether French or Italian opera was better, set off by an Italian comic intermezzo.
A Renaissance mass built on a plainchant melody that is embellished and passed through every voice rather than held in one.

fields.Composer: Guido of Arezzo's hymn Ut queant laxis
fields.Description: Naming the steps of a scale by syllables (ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la) to teach sight-singing, credited to Guido of Arezzo.
A piece that combines several well-known tunes at once or in quick succession, usually for humour.
A small-scale sacred opera for an all-male cast and a chamber ensemble, staged in a religious building without a conductor, modelled on Japanese Noh.
An early electronic instrument of 1928, played from a keyboard or a ring on a wire, producing gliding, wavering tones.
The Hungarian concert hammered dulcimer, its strings struck with small beaters.

fields.Nickname: The mad scene was first scored for it.
fields.Description: Nested spinning crystal bowls played with wet fingers, invented by Benjamin Franklin in 1761.
A tenor clarinet with an extended low range and a bent neck, favoured by Mozart in his Masonic music.

fields.Nickname: Its solo opens Debussy's Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune, and it plays the bird in Prokofiev's Peter and the Wolf.
fields.Description: A woodwind with no reed, held sideways and sounded by blowing across a hole; Theobald Boehm's keywork of 1847 set the modern metal form.

fields.Nickname: A glissando on it opens Gershwin's Rhapsody in Blue; it plays the cat in Peter and the Wolf; Mozart and Brahms wrote quintets for it.
fields.Description: A single-reed woodwind with a cylindrical bore, so it overblows at the twelfth rather than the octave; its dark low register is the chalumeau.

fields.Nickname: It asks the question in Ives's The Unanswered Question; Louis Armstrong and Miles Davis played it.
fields.Description: The highest brass instrument, a narrow cylindrical tube with a cup mouthpiece and three piston valves; Baroque players had only the valveless natural form.

fields.Nickname: Paganini's 24 Caprices are its virtuoso touchstone.
fields.Description: The highest bowed string instrument, with four strings tuned in fifths (G, D, A, E), whose form was set by the Cremona workshops of Amati, Stradivari, and Guarneri.

fields.Nickname: The sustain pedal lifts all the dampers; John Cage “prepared” one with screws and bolts.
fields.Description: A keyboard instrument whose keys throw felt hammers at strings, invented by Bartolomeo Cristofori in Florence around 1700 and named for playing both soft and loud.

fields.Nickname: Pablo Casals revived Bach's suites; it plays The Swan in Saint-Saëns's Carnival of the Animals.
fields.Description: The bowed string instrument an octave below the viola, strung C, G, D, A, held between the knees and resting on an endpin.

fields.Audio: [sound:Moussorgsky (Pictures at an Exhibition - The Old Castle).mp3]
fields.Composer: The Old Castle in Ravel's orchestration of Pictures at an Exhibition
fields.Nickname: Charlie Parker and John Coltrane made it the voice of jazz; Glazunov and Debussy wrote concert works for it.
fields.Description: A single-reed woodwind with a conical brass body, patented in 1846 by a Belgian maker from Dinant who gave it his name.

fields.Nickname: Paganini commissioned the Berlioz work and never played it; Walton and Bartók wrote concertos for it.
fields.Description: The alto of the bowed string family, a fifth below the violin with a low C string, whose music is written in the alto clef.

fields.Nickname: It plays the duck in Peter and the Wolf; Richard Strauss wrote a concerto for it in 1945.
fields.Description: A double-reed woodwind with a conical bore, which sounds the A the orchestra tunes to.

fields.Composer: Mozart's horn concertos, written for Joseph Leutgeb
fields.Nickname: Its call opens Strauss's Till Eulenspiegel, and three of them play the wolf in Peter and the Wolf.
fields.Description: A coiled brass instrument with a wide flaring bell, played with one hand inside the bell; valves arrived in the 1810s, and before them it changed key with crooks.

fields.Nickname: Beethoven brought it into the symphony in the finale of his Fifth.
fields.Description: A brass instrument that changes pitch with a telescoping slide instead of valves, long tied to church music and to the supernatural in opera.

fields.Composer: The opening solo of Stravinsky's The Rite of Spring
fields.Nickname: It plays the grandfather in Peter and the Wolf and the marching broom in Dukas's The Sorcerer's Apprentice.
fields.Description: The bass of the double-reed woodwinds, its long tube folded back on itself, with the reed on a bent metal crook.

fields.Nickname: Its cadenza opens the Waltz of the Flowers in The Nutcracker.
fields.Description: A plucked instrument of 47 strings whose seven pedals each move one note name by a semitone in every octave, the double-action mechanism perfected by Sébastien Érard.

fields.Nickname: Andrés Segovia built its concert repertoire; Villa-Lobos wrote twelve études for it.
fields.Description: A plucked, fretted instrument with six strings and a flat back, whose classical form was fixed by Antonio de Torres in 19th-century Spain.

fields.Nickname: Domenico Scarlatti wrote 555 sonatas for it; Wanda Landowska revived it in the 20th century.
fields.Description: A keyboard instrument that plucks its strings with quills, so touch cannot change its loudness; players use a second manual or stops instead.

fields.Composer: Bach's Toccata and Fugue in D minor
fields.Nickname: Saint-Saëns's Third Symphony features it; Widor and Vierne wrote “symphonies” for it alone.
fields.Description: A keyboard instrument sounded by wind through ranks of pipes chosen by stops, usually with several manuals and a pedalboard for the feet.

fields.Composer: The Elephant from Saint-Saëns's Carnival of the Animals
fields.Nickname: Plucked, it holds down the rhythm section in jazz; Giovanni Bottesini was its great virtuoso.
fields.Description: The largest and lowest bowed string instrument, tuned in fourths rather than fifths and sounding an octave below its written pitch.

fields.Composer: Beethoven's String Quartet in C-sharp minor, Op. 131
fields.Nickname: Shostakovich wrote 15, as many as his symphonies; Haydn's Op. 76 No. 3 is the “Emperor”.
fields.Description: A chamber work, or the ensemble that plays it, for two violins, viola, and cello; Haydn wrote 68 and established it, and Beethoven's late set pushed it furthest.

fields.Composer: Mendelssohn's Violin Concerto in E minor
fields.Nickname: Vivaldi wrote over 500; Beethoven's Fifth for piano is the “Emperor”.
fields.Description: A work setting a soloist, or a small group, against an orchestra, usually fast–slow–fast, with a solo cadenza near the end of the first movement.

fields.Nickname: Chopin's Op. 64 No. 1 is the “Minute”; Ravel's La valse is its apotheosis and collapse.
fields.Description: A dance in triple time with a strong downbeat, which grew out of the Austrian Ländler to rule the Viennese ballrooms of the 19th century.

fields.Nickname: Machaut's Messe de Nostre Dame is the first complete setting by one composer; Palestrina's for Pope Marcellus supposedly saved polyphony at Trent.
fields.Description: A setting of the central Catholic liturgy, above all its fixed Ordinary: Kyrie, Gloria, Credo, Sanctus, and Agnus Dei.

fields.Nickname: Mahler told Sibelius it “must be like the world; it must embrace everything.”
fields.Description: A large orchestral work, usually in four movements with the first in sonata form, which grew out of the Italian opera overture; Haydn wrote 104.

fields.Nickname: Beethoven wrote 32 for piano; Domenico Scarlatti's 555 are single movements.
fields.Description: An instrumental work in several movements for one player, or one with piano, whose first movement usually runs exposition, development, and recapitulation.

fields.Composer: John Philip Sousa's The Stars and Stripes Forever
fields.Nickname: Elgar's Pomp and Circumstance No. 1 is played at graduations.
fields.Description: Music for soldiers and parades to step to, in duple time with a strong regular beat and a contrasting middle section called the trio; John Philip Sousa was its American master.

fields.Nickname: The 1973 film The Sting revived it; Joplin also wrote an opera, Treemonisha.
fields.Description: A syncopated American piano style of about 1895–1918: an off-beat right hand over a steady “oom-pah” left hand, in march-like strains.

fields.Nickname: Beethoven tuned them an octave apart in his Eighth and Ninth; they answer the brass in the opening of Also sprach Zarathustra.
fields.Description: Large tunable drums with copper bowls and a stretched head, pitched by pedals or screws and played in sets of two to five.

fields.Nickname: Tchaikovsky wrote his as an elegy for Nikolai Rubinstein.
fields.Description: A chamber work, or the ensemble that plays it, for keyboard, violin, and cello.

fields.Nickname: Chopin's Op. 60 is the great piano example.
fields.Description: A song or piece in a lilting 6/8 or 12/8 time imitating the songs of Venetian gondoliers.

A six-voice mass dedicated to Pope Marcellus II, long said to have persuaded the Council of Trent not to ban polyphony because its words stay audible; Hans Pfitzner's opera Palestrina dramatizes the legend.
fields.Listen: The Kyrie: six unaccompanied voices enter one after another in smooth, overlapping imitation on “Kyrie eleison”, each line rising and falling stepwise, the words kept clear.
fields.Clue: A six-voice mass named for a pope who reigned only three weeks in 1555; legend held that its clear text-setting persuaded the Council of Trent not to ban polyphony, a story dramatized in Hans Pfitzner's opera.

fields.Description: One of three Latin masses the Catholic Byrd published in Protestant England without title pages, for services in recusant households; its Agnus Dei builds to an intense plea for peace.
fields.Listen: Four unaccompanied voices enter one after another in slow, overlapping imitation on “Agnus Dei”.
fields.Clue: A Latin mass for a quartet of singers, published around 1593 without a title page by a Catholic composer in Elizabeth I's Protestant England, for secret services in recusant households.

fields.Description: Written at Eszterháza when Prince Nikolaus Esterházy kept his musicians away from their families too long: in the finale the players stop one by one, snuff their candles, and leave, until two muted violins remain. The prince took the hint.
fields.Listen: The finale's Presto: driving, agitated minor-key strings with rushing scales and sharp accents.
fields.Clue: In the finale of this F-sharp-minor symphony of 1772, the players stop one by one, snuff their candles, and walk out until two muted violins remain: its composer's hint to Prince Nikolaus Esterházy that his musicians wanted to go home.

fields.Description: Built on a cycle of eleven chords, each stretched into a section of pulsing repeated patterns for pianos, marimbas, women's voices, clarinets, violin, and cello, with the changes cued by the vibraphone; about an hour long.
fields.Clue: An hour-long piece built on a cycle of eleven chords, each stretched into a section of pulsing patterns for pianos, marimbas, women's voices, clarinets, violin, and cello, the changes cued by the vibraphone; premiered in New York in 1976.

fields.Description: An electronic work that splices a boy's recorded voice singing the Benedicite from the Book of Daniel, the song of the three youths in the fiery furnace, into synthesized tones, first projected from five groups of loudspeakers.
fields.Clue: Its composer's electronic landmark of 1956 splices a boy's recorded voice singing the Benedicite, the canticle of the three young men in Nebuchadnezzar's fiery furnace, into synthesized sine tones and pulses, first projected from five groups of loudspeakers.

fields.Description: Smetana's account of his life, from youthful romance to the tinnitus and deafness that struck him in 1874; he gave the viola the passionate opening theme.
fields.Listen: This quartet opens with a sustained chord and agitated tremolo in the violins and cello; then the viola launches the passionate, surging E-minor theme.
fields.Clue: An autobiographical work for four strings: the viola opens with a passionate E-minor theme, the second movement is a polka, and the finale is cut short by a long, piercing high E in the first violin, the ringing in its composer's ear that came before his deafness.

fields.Description: By the “March King”, who led the U.S. Marine Band before touring the world with his own; the recording is the Marine Band's.
fields.Listen: A brisk four-bar introduction for full band, then the first strain of the E-flat march over an oom-pah bass.
fields.Clue: A march written on a ship home from Europe in 1896, whose final strain adds a famous piccolo obbligato; Congress made it the national march of the United States in 1987.

fields.Description: By a member of Les Six, who said he loved locomotives as others love women or horses; he called the piece a study in mounting speed while the actual tempo slows.
fields.Listen: This piece opens with low strings hissing and sighing like escaping steam; then the orchestra churns into motion as the engine pulls away, gathering speed.
fields.Clue: An orchestral “symphonic movement” of a steam locomotive starting up and thundering along, named for a type of engine with a 2-3-1 wheel arrangement.

fields.Description: The largest work for the prepared piano, which Cage invented for a 1940 dance by Syvilla Fort; the preparations turn the piano into something like a gamelan.
fields.Listen: Sonata V: muted, woody, gong-like tones from the prepared piano in a lilting, dance-like rhythm, in two short repeated halves.
fields.Clue: Twenty pieces written between 1946 and 1948 for a piano “prepared” with screws, bolts, and rubber between its strings, meant to express the nine permanent emotions of Indian aesthetics; sixteen are in two repeated halves, and four freer pieces stand between them.

fields.Description: One of the first major sacred works from behind the Iron Curtain, mixing tone clusters and twelve-tone rows with Gregorian chant.
fields.Listen: The opening hymn: dense choral clusters and swelling cries of “O crux” over a dark, low orchestra.
fields.Clue: A Latin Passion written for the 700th anniversary of Münster Cathedral, whose music spells out B-A-C-H and ends on a blazing E-major chord.

fields.Description: Beach, largely self-taught, belonged to the Second New England School; she wrote it partly in answer to Dvořák's call for an American music drawn from folk song.
fields.Listen: A stormy, surging opening in the full orchestra, like a gale at sea, before a bold theme emerges.
fields.Clue: Built on Irish folk tunes, it was the first symphony composed and published by an American woman, premiered by the Boston Symphony Orchestra in 1896.

fields.Description: Still, later the first Black American to conduct a major U.S. orchestra, prefaced each movement with lines by Paul Laurence Dunbar.
fields.Listen: This symphony opens with a plaintive cor anglais solo in A-flat, bending its notes in the inflections of the blues.
fields.Clue: The first symphony by a Black composer from the United States to be played by a major orchestra, the Rochester Philharmonic under Howard Hanson in 1931; it adds a tenor banjo, builds its themes on the twelve-bar blues, and prefaces each movement with lines by Paul Laurence Dunbar.

fields.Description: Commissioned by Lincoln Kirstein's American Ballet Caravan, which broke up before staging it; the suite was heard in 1943, the full ballet only in 1952.
fields.Listen: The Malambo: after a hushed start, driving, syncopated 6/8 rhythms hammered out by brass, xylophone, and percussion, building relentlessly.
fields.Clue: A ballet of a day on an Argentine cattle ranch, whose suite ends with a malambo, the gauchos' competitive foot-stamping dance.

fields.Description: By a founder of minimalism, who also wrote Composition 1960 #7: a perfect fifth, B and F-sharp, “to be held for a long time”.
fields.Listen: Slow, resonating piano figures in a pure, unfamiliar tuning, blurring into a shimmering haze.
fields.Clue: A minimalist improvisation of five hours or more on a piano retuned in just intonation, performed in the composer's Dream House under Marian Zazeela's lights.

fields.Description: It won the 1932 Wanamaker Prize; Price's reputation revived after a trove of her manuscripts turned up in an abandoned house in Illinois in 2009.
fields.Listen: A syncopated, ragtime-flavoured dance tune, bright and bouncing in the strings.
fields.Clue: Its third movement is a Juba dance; in 1933 it became the first symphony by a Black woman played by a major American orchestra, the Chicago Symphony.

fields.Description: Lili Boulanger, younger sister of the teacher Nadia Boulanger, died at twenty-four in 1918.
fields.Listen: A hushed orchestral introduction of murmuring strings and woodwind.
fields.Clue: A cantata on Goethe's Faust that made its nineteen-year-old composer the first woman to win the Prix de Rome in composition.

fields.Movement: Act III · “When I am laid in earth”
fields.Description: A short opera after Book IV of Virgil's Aeneid; it closes with a chorus of Cupids scattering roses on the queen's tomb, “With drooping wings”.
fields.Listen: The lament's ground bass alone in the low strings, falling slowly by half steps in triple time, before the soprano enters on “When I am laid, am laid in earth”.
fields.Clue: After her Trojan lover sails for Italy, the queen of Carthage takes Belinda's hand and sings this lament, begging “remember me, but ah! forget my fate”, then dies; Nahum Tate's libretto replaces Virgil's gods with a Sorceress and her witches.

fields.Description: Composed in 1802, the year of the Heiligenstadt Testament, as the last of the three sonatas Beethoven grouped as Op. 31.
fields.Listen: The questioning opening: a soft falling fifth, C to F, heard twice over a chord that holds off the home key, then a slow chromatic rise to a pause before the music settles into E-flat major.
fields.Clue: A four-movement sonata with no slow movement: a 2/4 scherzo in sonata form, a minuet whose theme Camille Saint-Saëns took for his Variations on a Theme of Beethoven for two pianos, and a galloping 6/8 finale that gave it its nickname.

fields.Description: The middle movement, Abwesenheit (“Absence”), is a slow lament that runs straight into the finale, Das Wiedersehen (“The Return”), marked vivacissimamente.
fields.Listen: The slow introduction: three soft chords trace the horn-call motto G, F, E-flat, under which Beethoven wrote “Le-be-wohl”, and the third slips deceptively onto C minor.
fields.Clue: Beethoven wrote it when his patron and pupil Archduke Rudolph fled Vienna ahead of Napoleon's army in 1809, heading its movements Farewell, Absence, and Return, and he objected to the French title his publisher printed.

fields.Description: It depicts the Battle of Vitoria in Spain, where British and allied troops routed Joseph Bonaparte's army in June 1813; a huge success in its day, it is now often called Beethoven's weakest work.
fields.Listen: Side drums roll nearer and nearer, trumpets sound the English fanfare in E-flat, and the march on “Rule, Britannia!” begins.
fields.Clue: Written for Johann Nepomuk Maelzel's mechanical panharmonicon and premiered with the Seventh Symphony in December 1813, it pits armies marching to rival tunes, the French to “Malbrough s'en va-t-en guerre”, amid cannon and musket fire, and ends with a fugue on “God Save the King”.

fields.Description: Written in Vienna in July 1789, after Mozart's journey to Potsdam and Berlin, when he was borrowing heavily from his friend Michael Puchberg.
fields.Listen: The opening: a hunting-horn call in bare octaves climbing through the D-major chord in 6/8, answered by a light, ornamented reply in the right hand.
fields.Clue: His last piano sonata, also called the “Trumpet”, supposedly one of six easy sonatas for Princess Friederike of Prussia but among his hardest; its development works the opening call in close canon between the hands.

fields.Description: His only completed sonata for two pianos; he also left four complete sonatas for one piano, four hands, which he played with his sister.
fields.Listen: The opening: both pianos together in bold D-major chords and fanfare figures, before they begin trading phrases.
fields.Clue: Mozart wrote it in 1781 to play with his pupil Josepha Barbara Auernhammer; in 1993 a study in Nature claimed that hearing its first movement briefly raised spatial-reasoning scores, the “Mozart effect”.

fields.Description: A modest concerto for a gifted amateur, scored for strings with pairs of oboes and horns.
fields.Listen: The orchestral opening: a bright, festive C-major tutti in strings, oboes, and horns, before the soloist enters.
fields.Clue: Written in Salzburg for a countess who was the niece of Archbishop Colloredo, and kept as a teaching piece, for which Mozart wrote out several cadenzas; it ends with a rondo in minuet tempo.

fields.Description: Written in Salzburg in January 1777, at twenty-one, and the first of his concertos regularly called a masterpiece.
fields.Listen: The opening: the orchestra's unison call in E-flat, answered at once, in only the second bar, by the solo piano, and the exchange repeats before the orchestra goes on.
fields.Clue: Its nickname garbles the name of Victoire Jenamy, daughter of the ballet master Jean-Georges Noverre, for whom Mozart wrote it; its C-minor Andantino has muted violins, and a slow minuet interrupts its Presto finale.

fields.Description: Completed in February 1788, it is one of only two piano concertos Mozart wrote after 1786; the other is No. 27 in B-flat.
fields.Listen: The orchestral opening: a quiet, marching D-major theme in the strings, then a full, festive tutti with trumpets and drums.
fields.Clue: Mozart played it in Frankfurt in October 1790 during the festivities for Leopold II's coronation; much of its left-hand solo part was never written down and was filled in by the publisher Johann André.

fields.Description: For its Vienna performances Mozart added clarinets, trumpets, and timpani to the orchestra.
fields.Listen: The opening tutti: emphatic E-flat chords from the orchestra in unison, then a graceful theme in the strings, before the two soloists enter together.
fields.Clue: Written in Salzburg around 1779 for Mozart and his sister Maria Anna, “Nannerl”, to play together, and counted as his Piano Concerto No. 10; in Vienna he played it with his pupil Josepha Auernhammer.

fields.Description: Counted as his Piano Concerto No. 7, it is lightly scored for strings with oboes and horns.
fields.Listen: The orchestral opening: a stately F-major tutti in strings, oboes, and horns, before the three soloists enter.
fields.Clue: Written in 1776 for a Salzburg countess and her two daughters; the youngest daughter's part is so easy that Mozart later rearranged the work for two players.

fields.Description: Completed in Vienna on 31 December 1782, the first fruit of Mozart's study of Haydn's Op. 33 quartets.
fields.Listen: The finale opens as a fugue: a subject in long, even notes, G, B, E, C-sharp, D, enters quietly alone and is taken up by each instrument in turn.
fields.Clue: The first of six quartets Mozart dedicated to Haydn as the fruit of “long and laborious effort”; its minuet sets rising chromatic lines against markings that alternate piano and forte on successive beats.

fields.Description: Written in Vienna in August 1786, the summer after The Marriage of Figaro.
fields.Listen: The opening: the four instruments in octaves on a quiet, unhurried D-major theme built from the notes of the chord, which they then answer in harmony.
fields.Clue: A single D-major quartet written between the six dedicated to Haydn and the three for the King of Prussia, and named for the Viennese composer and publisher who issued it.

fields.Movement: No. 21 in D major, K. 575 · mvt. I · Allegretto
fields.Description: His last three string quartets, published by Artaria just after his death in 1791.
fields.Listen: The set opens: a gentle, flowing D-major melody in the first violin over soft accompaniment in the lower strings.
fields.Clue: Meant as a set of six for Friedrich Wilhelm II, a keen amateur cellist, and so giving the cello prominent, high-lying melodies; Mozart finished only three and complained that he had to sell them for a pittance.

fields.Movement: No. 15 in D minor, K. 421 · mvt. I · Allegro moderato
fields.Description: The six include the “Spring”, the “Hunt”, and the “Dissonance”; Mozart wrote them after studying Haydn's Op. 33.
fields.Listen: From the set's only minor-key quartet: a hushed D-minor theme in the first violin that drops an octave from its first note, over throbbing repeated notes below.
fields.Clue: Six string quartets published in 1785 with a dedication to a friend and model, calling them the fruit of “long and laborious effort”; hearing them, the dedicatee told the composer's father that his son was the greatest composer he knew.

fields.Description: In seven movements; four of them were perhaps first heard at the clarinettist Anton Stadler's benefit concert in Vienna in March 1784.
fields.Listen: The Adagio in E-flat: low winds pulse softly, then a solo oboe enters on a long held note that swells and passes its line to a clarinet, the two trading phrases above.
fields.Clue: Scored for twelve wind instruments, basset horns among them, and a double bass, it is the grandest of Mozart's wind serenades; in the film Amadeus, Salieri reads its slow movement in disbelief.

fields.Movement: mvt. I · Adagio maestoso – Allegro con spirito
fields.Description: In seven movements; Mozart later turned its first, fifth, and seventh into a three-movement symphony.
fields.Listen: The slow introduction: grand D-major chords with trumpets and drums, then the Allegro con spirito rushes off in the strings.
fields.Clue: A Salzburg serenade of 1779 for the end of the university term, named for the solo in the second trio of its second minuet, played on the small valveless horn that mail coaches sounded on arrival.

fields.Description: The same family commissioned a symphony from Mozart in 1782, now his No. 35, also named for them.
fields.Listen: A perpetual-motion rondo in G major: the solo violin skitters through unbroken sixteenth notes over light orchestral accompaniment.
fields.Clue: Written in Salzburg for the wedding of a daughter of the city's late burgomaster; three of its eight movements form a violin concerto, and Fritz Kreisler arranged this rondo for violin and piano.

fields.Description: Mozart wrote to his father that the audience applauded in the middle of the first movement, at a passage he had calculated to please them.
fields.Listen: The opening: loud unison D's from the whole orchestra, then a rapid rising D-major scale in the violins, a “Mannheim rocket”, and a soft answer.
fields.Clue: Written for the Concert Spirituel in 1778, on the journey during which Mozart's mother died; its director Joseph Legros found the first slow movement too long, so Mozart wrote another, and it was his first symphony with clarinets.

fields.Description: Completed in Vienna on 6 December 1786, the only one of his mature symphonies in three movements.
fields.Listen: The long slow introduction: emphatic unison D's from the full orchestra, then hushed, searching phrases that darken toward D minor.
fields.Clue: A symphony in three movements with no minuet, first played in the Bohemian capital in January 1787, where The Marriage of Figaro had made Mozart a celebrity; its finale borrows a figure from Figaro's duet “Aprite, presto, aprite”.

fields.Composer: Samuel Barber's Adagio for Strings, named for its marking
fields.Nickname: Johann Nepomuk Maelzel patented the metronome in 1815, and Beethoven was the first major composer to use its markings; rubato is its expressive pushing and pulling.
fields.Description: The speed of a piece, marked with Italian words from largo and adagio through andante and allegro to presto, or with a metronome figure in beats per minute.

fields.Nickname: Its degrees are numbered from the tonic, the fifth being the dominant; the pentatonic, whole-tone, and octatonic kinds are the common alternatives.
fields.Description: A collection of pitches set out in order; the major and minor kinds have seven notes per octave in fixed patterns of whole and half steps, and the chromatic kind has all twelve.

fields.Nickname: The tritone, three whole steps, was called the “devil in music”; the octave spans eight letter names.
fields.Description: The distance between two pitches, named by counting letter names from the lower note to the upper inclusive, so that C up to F is a fourth, and qualified as perfect, major, minor, augmented, or diminished.

fields.Nickname: Named by Roman numerals for the scale degree of its root; the Tristan chord and the Petrushka chord are famous single examples.
fields.Description: Three or more pitches sounded together; the basic kind stacks thirds into a root, third, and fifth, and further thirds give sevenths, ninths, and the thirteenths of jazz.

fields.Nickname: Moving from one to another within a piece is modulation; music without one is atonal.
fields.Description: The scale and home pitch a piece is built on, usually shown by a signature of sharps or flats; two that share a signature but not a tonic are relative, and two that share a tonic but not a mode are parallel.

fields.Composer: The clarinet's opening glissando in Gershwin's Rhapsody in Blue
fields.Nickname: Rewriting music at another pitch level is transposition; a score “in C” shows every part at its sounding pitch.
fields.Description: An instrument whose part is written at a different pitch from the one it sounds, like the B-flat clarinet, whose written C sounds the B-flat below, or the horn in F, sounding a fifth lower than written.

fields.Composer: Haydn's “Surprise” Symphony, whose hushed theme is broken by a fortissimo chord
fields.Nickname: Sforzando marks a sudden accent; Ravel's Boléro is one long crescendo.
fields.Description: Markings for loudness, from pianissimo (pp) through piano, mezzo-piano, mezzo-forte, and forte to fortissimo (ff), with crescendo and diminuendo for gradual change.

fields.Nickname: Marked with dots, slurs, lines, and wedges; string players add bowings such as spiccato and martelé.
fields.Description: How notes are attacked and joined: short and detached in staccato, smoothly connected in legato, held for their full value in tenuto, or stressed with accents.

fields.Nickname: Theme and variations, the fugue, and the ground bass are the other standard designs.
fields.Description: The overall structure of a piece, labelled with letters for its contrasting sections: AB in binary, ABA in ternary, ABACA in rondo; sonata form adds an exposition, development, and recapitulation.

fields.Composer: A concert at the Siam Society, Bangkok
fields.Nickname: Played from memory: the large gong circle carries the core melody and the others elaborate it at once; the Khmer pinpeat is its close relative.
fields.Description: A Thai classical ensemble of wooden xylophones (ranat), circles of tuned gongs (khong wong), a quadruple-reed oboe (pi), and drums, played at temple ceremonies and for masked khon dance-drama.

fields.Composer: Ravi Shankar's alap in Raga Bageshri, on the sitar
fields.Nickname: Both the northern Hindustani and southern Carnatic traditions are built on it; a performance opens with an unmetred alap, and Ravi Shankar brought it to the Beatles and the West.
fields.Description: In Indian classical music, a melodic framework of characteristic notes, phrases, and ornaments, tied to a time of day or a mood, which a performer improvises on over a drone and sets to a rhythmic cycle called a tala.

fields.Composer: Liu Shui (“Flowing Water”), played by Guan Pinghu
fields.Nickname: Guan Pinghu's Liu Shui went into space on the Voyager Golden Record; its relatives include the guzheng zither, the pipa lute, and the bowed erhu.
fields.Description: A seven-stringed, fretless Chinese zither played on a table, its notes bent and slid by the left hand; the instrument of scholars since Confucius, it was one of the four arts of the Chinese gentleman.

fields.Composer: Etenraku, played by the Music Department of the Imperial Household
fields.Nickname: Etenraku is its best-known piece; Japan's other classical traditions include the shakuhachi flute of Zen monks, the shamisen of kabuki, and taiko drumming.
fields.Description: The ancient court music of Japan, brought from China and Korea and played by the shō mouth organ, hichiriki double reed, ryūteki flute, biwa lute, koto zither, and drums in slow, sustained lines.

fields.Composer: Munir Bashir's taqsim in Maqam Rast, on the oud
fields.Nickname: Played by the small takht ensemble of oud, qanun, violin, and darbuka; the Turkish makam and the Persian dastgah are related systems.
fields.Description: The system of melodic modes in Arabic music, each defined by a scale that often uses quarter tones, by characteristic phrases, and by a mood, explored in improvised preludes called taqsim.

fields.Composer: Ceddin Deden, the best-known march of its repertoire
fields.Nickname: Mozart's Rondo alla turca and Die Entführung aus dem Serail imitate it; Ottoman art music proper is built on makam modes and usul rhythmic cycles.
fields.Description: The Ottoman military band of shawms (zurna), trumpets, kettledrums, bass drums, and cymbals, whose sound Haydn, Mozart, and Beethoven imitated as “Turkish” or janissary music.

fields.Composer: Dastgah Shur, played by Faramarz Payvar's ensemble
fields.Nickname: Shur is the most important; its instruments include the tar and setar lutes, the santur dulcimer, the bowed kamancheh, and the tombak drum.
fields.Description: One of the seven principal modal systems of Persian classical music, each a family of short melodies (gusheh) gathered with the others in the radif, on which performers improvise.

fields.Nickname: The jeli, or griots, trace their line to Balla Fasséké, griot of Sundiata Keita; Toumani Diabaté of Mali and Sona Jobarteh of the Gambia are its best-known players.
fields.Description: A twenty-one-stringed West African harp-lute with a large half-calabash body, played by the jeli, the hereditary praise-singers and historians of the Mandé peoples.

fields.Nickname: Two players interlock a leading kushaura part and a following kutsinhira part over a hosho rattle; it is often called a thumb piano.
fields.Description: A Shona instrument of Zimbabwe with over twenty metal tongues on a hardwood board, plucked with the thumbs and a forefinger inside a calabash resonator, and played to call the ancestors at all-night bira ceremonies.
